questions.stem: What is the value of eccentricity for the no-tension condition in a dam?
questions.solution:
**e < B/6** — the resultant must fall within the **middle third** of the base.

> The source states it: **the resultant of all the forces — hydrostatic water pressure, uplift pressure and the self-weight of the dam — should always lie within the MIDDLE THIRD of the base for no tension.**

**The three cases:**

| Eccentricity | Stress at the heel |
|---|---|
| **e < B/6** | **Compression at BOTH toe and heel — no tension** ✓ |
| **e = B/6** | **Stress at the heel becomes exactly ZERO** — the limiting case |
| **e > B/6** | **TENSION develops at the heel — cracking** |

**Where B/6 comes from:**

> The base stress is **σ = P/A ± Pe·y/I**, and for a rectangular base of width B per unit length:
>
> **σ = (P/B)(1 ± 6e/B)**
>
> **The stress goes to zero when 6e/B = 1, that is when e = B/6.**

> **Beyond that the bracket turns negative and the stress becomes tensile.** The rule is arithmetic, not a convention.

> **And "middle third" follows directly**: measured from the centre, ±B/6 spans B/3 — the central third of the base.

**Why no tension is the governing criterion for a gravity dam:**

> **Mass concrete and masonry have negligible tensile strength**, so a tensile stress means a crack.

> **And a crack at the heel is doubly dangerous**, because it does not merely reduce the contact area:

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1. Crack opens at the heel** | Contact area reduced |
| **2. Water enters the crack** | **UPLIFT increases** |
| **3. Increased uplift reduces effective weight** | Eccentricity grows |
| **4. Crack extends further** | **The process ACCELERATES** |

> **The failure is PROGRESSIVE**, which is why no tension is enforced rather than merely preferred.

**The full stability checks for a gravity dam:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **NO TENSION** | **Resultant within the MIDDLE THIRD** |
| **Sliding factor** | **≥ 1.5**; shear friction factor **4 to 5** |
| **Overturning** | Factor of safety **≥ 1.5** |
| **Crushing** | Compressive stress within the allowable |

**And the elementary profile relations:**

> **Without uplift: B = H/√G**
>
> **With uplift: B = H/√(G − c)**

> **Uplift reduces the effective weight, so a wider base is needed for the same height** — and weight is the only thing holding a gravity dam in place.

> **DRAINAGE GALLERIES with relief holes** intercept seepage and cut the uplift, typically to about a third of full head at the drain line — a large gain in stability for a modest cost.

**The middle-third rule is not confined to dams:**

> It governs **retaining walls, chimneys, masonry piers and unreinforced footings** — anywhere a material that cannot take tension carries an eccentric load. **The same B/6 arithmetic applies each time.**

examTip.trick: **σ = (P/B)(1 ± 6e/B)** goes to zero when **e = B/6**. The rule is arithmetic, not a convention — and ±B/6 about the centre spans exactly the **middle third**.
examTip.trap: **B/3 is the WIDTH of the middle third, not the eccentricity limit.** The limit is measured from the centre, so it is half of that: B/6.
examTip.mnemonic: **A heel crack is PROGRESSIVE**: crack → water enters → uplift rises → eccentricity grows → crack extends. That accelerating chain is why no tension is enforced absolutely.

questions.stem: The size of footings depends upon:
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

> The source confirms it: **footings depend upon type of load, bearing capacity of soil, and type of superstructure.**

**The governing equation is simply:**

> **Area required = Load ÷ Safe bearing capacity**

> **Both terms are variables**, which is why both the load side and the soil side appear in the answer.

| Factor | How it enters |
|---|---|
| **TYPE OF LOAD** | Axial, eccentric, inclined, or with moment — changes the pressure **distribution**, not just its magnitude |
| **BEARING CAPACITY of soil** | The denominator — sets the area for a given load |
| **TYPE OF SUPERSTRUCTURE** | Fixes the **load magnitude and pattern**, and how much **settlement** can be tolerated |

**Why the type of load matters separately from its size:**

> **An AXIAL load gives uniform pressure. An ECCENTRIC load gives a trapezoidal or triangular distribution**, with a peak pressure far higher than the average.

> **σ = P/A ± M/Z**, and if e > L/6 the pressure at one edge goes **negative** — meaning the footing would lift off, which soil cannot resist.

> **So an eccentrically loaded footing must be larger than the load alone suggests**, or shaped to bring the resultant back to the centre.

**Why the superstructure type matters:**

| Structure | Consequence for the footing |
|---|---|
| **Framed structure** | Tolerates **more** differential settlement — joints redistribute |
| **Load-bearing masonry** | **Very intolerant** — cracks readily |
| Tall / slender | Large **moments** from wind and earthquake |
| Industrial with machinery | **Vibration** and settlement limits |

> **Masonry is the demanding case**: it has no ductility, so a differential settlement that a frame absorbs will crack a brick wall visibly.

**SETTLEMENT, not bearing capacity, usually governs:**

> **The safe bearing capacity is the LESSER of two values** — the shear-failure value with a factor of safety of **2.5 to 3**, and the pressure that produces the permissible settlement.

| Permissible settlement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Total (isolated footing on sand)** | **40 mm** |
| **Total (on clay)** | **65 – 75 mm** |
| **DIFFERENTIAL** | **Usually the real limit** |
| Angular distortion | **1/500 for framed buildings** |

> **DIFFERENTIAL settlement causes the damage, not total settlement.** A building that settles 100 mm uniformly is undamaged; one that settles 25 mm at one corner and nothing at another cracks.

> **Which is why footings under a single structure are often proportioned for EQUAL PRESSURE rather than equal factor of safety** — equal pressure gives more nearly equal settlement.

**And the minimum depth**, which is a separate question from the size:

> **Below scour depth, below frost depth, below the zone of seasonal moisture change, and at least 500 mm below finished ground level (IS 1904).**

> **Size answers "how much area?"; depth answers "how far down?"** They are decided by different considerations, and this question asks only the first.

examTip.trick: **Area = Load ÷ Safe bearing capacity** — and both terms are variables. The load side brings in the superstructure and the load type; the soil side brings in bearing capacity.
examTip.trap: **Type of load matters beyond its magnitude**: an eccentric load gives σ = P/A ± M/Z, and if e > L/6 the pressure at one edge goes negative — the footing would lift, which soil cannot resist.
examTip.mnemonic: **DIFFERENTIAL settlement causes the damage, not total.** 100 mm uniform is harmless; 25 mm at one corner cracks the building — which is why footings are often proportioned for **equal pressure**.

questions.stem: A turbine develops 10,000 hp under a head of 81 metres at 500 rpm. Identify the turbine.
questions.solution:
**Francis turbine.**

**The specific speed:**

> **N_s = N√P / H^{5/4}**, with **N in rpm, P in kW and H in metres**

**Working:**

> **P = 10,000 hp = 10,000 × 0.746 = 7460 kW**
>
> **H^{5/4} = 81^{1.25}.** Since **81 = 3⁴**, **81^{1.25} = 3⁵ = 243**
>
> **√7460 = 86.37**
>
> **N_s = 500 × 86.37 / 243 = 177.7**

> **177.7 lies in the range 60–300 → FRANCIS turbine** ✓

**Note the clean exponent:** **81 is 3⁴, so 81^{5/4} = 3⁵ = 243 exactly.** Recognising that removes the only awkward step in the calculation — a deliberate choice by the examiner, and a signal that the arithmetic is meant to come out neatly.

**The specific speed ranges:**

| Turbine | **N_s** | Head | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PELTON (single jet)** | **10 – 35** | **> 250 m** | Impulse, tangential |
| Pelton (multi-jet) | 35 – 60 | — | — |
| **FRANCIS** | **60 – 300** | **45 – 400 m** | Reaction, mixed flow |
| **KAPLAN / propeller** | **300 – 1000** | **< 60 m** | Reaction, axial flow |

> **Specific speed RISES as head FALLS** — the single most useful relationship in turbine selection, and the H^{5/4} in the denominator is what drives it.

**A cross-check from the head alone:**

> **81 m sits squarely in the Francis range (45–400 m)** — too low for a Pelton wheel, too high for a Kaplan.

> **The two independent routes agree**, which is worth doing when time allows: the specific speed calculation and the head range should never contradict each other.

**Two unit traps in this calculation:**

| Trap | Note |
|---|---|
| **hp must be converted to kW** | **1 hp = 0.746 kW.** Using 10,000 directly gives N_s = 205 — still Francis here, but wrong in general |
| **The metric N_s formula takes kW** | Some older texts use hp with a different constant; mixing them is a genuine error |

> **Here the answer survives the hp/kW slip because both values fall inside the Francis band** — but that is luck, not method, and near a boundary it would give the wrong turbine.

**What specific speed actually means:**

> **The speed of a geometrically similar turbine producing UNIT POWER under UNIT HEAD.**

> **It is a SHAPE parameter, not a speed.** Two turbines of the same specific speed have the same runner geometry however different their size — which is precisely what makes model testing possible.

> **A model tested in a laboratory predicts the prototype's performance** because the two share a specific speed, and that is why the quantity was invented.

**The runner shapes that go with it:**

| N_s | Runner |
|---|---|
| **Low** | **Narrow buckets, large diameter — small flow, high head** |
| **High** | **Wide axial blades, small diameter — large flow, low head** |

> **High head means small flow for a given power, and small flow means a narrow runner.** The geometry follows from the physics, which is why specific speed and shape are the same statement.

examTip.trick: **81 = 3⁴, so 81^{5/4} = 3⁵ = 243 exactly** — that removes the only awkward step. N_s = 500 × √7460 / 243 = **177.7**, which is in the Francis band (60–300).
examTip.trap: **Convert hp to kW (× 0.746)** — the metric N_s formula takes kW. Here the answer survives the slip because both values land in the Francis band, but near a boundary it would give the wrong turbine.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cross-check from the HEAD alone: 81 m is squarely Francis (45–400 m).** Two independent routes should never disagree. And **specific speed is a SHAPE parameter, not a speed** — which is what makes model testing valid.

questions.stem: For the empty reservoir condition, the maximum compressive force acts:
questions.solution:
**At the heel.**

> The source states both cases: **for reservoir FULL condition the maximum compressive force is at the TOE of the dam; for reservoir EMPTY condition it is at the HEEL. When the reservoir is empty the maximum vertical stress equals 2W/B at the heel and causes zero stress at the toe.**

**Why — it follows from where the resultant sits:**

| Condition | Forces acting | Resultant shifts | Maximum compression |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RESERVOIR FULL** | Self-weight **+ water thrust** pushing downstream | **Toward the TOE** | **At the TOE** |
| **RESERVOIR EMPTY** | **Self-weight ALONE** | **Toward the HEEL** | **At the HEEL** |

> **The reasoning is simply that stress is greatest where the resultant is nearest.**

> **With the reservoir full, the water pushes the resultant downstream toward the toe. With it empty, only the dam's own weight acts — and because a gravity dam's section is a triangle thickening downstream, its centre of gravity lies UPSTREAM of the base centre, throwing the resultant toward the heel.**

**First terminology, since the two are constantly swapped:**

| Term | Position |
|---|---|
| **HEEL** | **UPSTREAM edge of the base — the water side** |
| **TOE** | **DOWNSTREAM edge of the base — the dry side** |

> **A useful anchor: your HEEL is at the BACK, and the water is behind the dam.**

**Why the empty case must be checked at all:**

> **It is not merely the absence of load — it is a genuinely different and sometimes governing case.**

> **The source's own figure is exact: with the reservoir empty, σ_heel = 2W/B and σ_toe = 0.** That is the limiting condition where the resultant sits exactly at the middle-third boundary on the upstream side.

> **Push it further — a section too thin at the top, or an unusually heavy downstream face — and TENSION appears at the TOE.**

> **So both extremes must be checked**: full reservoir for tension at the heel, empty reservoir for tension at the toe. **Designing for only one leaves the other unverified.**

**And the empty case is realistic, not hypothetical:**

| When it occurs | Note |
|---|---|
| **During and just after CONSTRUCTION** | Before first filling |
| **Reservoir drawn down** for inspection or repair | Routine |
| **Emergency drawdown** | After an earthquake, or a safety concern |
| Before the first monsoon | The dam stands complete and empty |

> **A newly completed dam stands empty for months**, so the empty case is the first condition it actually experiences.

**The stress at the base:**

> **σ = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B)**

> **With e = B/6 the bracket becomes (1 ± 1), giving 2ΣV/B at one edge and ZERO at the other** — exactly the values the source quotes.

**The complete set of load cases** a gravity dam is checked for: **reservoir empty**, **reservoir full**, **with and without uplift**, **with and without earthquake**, and **ice and silt pressure** where they apply.

> **The critical combination is not always the obvious one**, which is why every case is computed rather than reasoned about.

examTip.trick: **Stress is greatest where the resultant is nearest.** Empty reservoir → only self-weight → resultant toward the HEEL (the triangular section's centroid is upstream of the base centre).
examTip.trap: **HEEL is upstream (water side); TOE is downstream.** Constantly swapped. Anchor it: your **heel is at the back**, and the water is behind the dam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Empty reservoir gives σ_heel = 2W/B and σ_toe = 0** — from σ = (ΣV/B)(1 ± 6e/B) at e = B/6. Both extremes must be checked: full for tension at the heel, empty for tension at the toe.

questions.stem: The maximum depth of a timber batten is:
questions.solution:
**50 mm.**

> The source states it directly: **the maximum depth of a timber batten should be 50 mm.**

**What a batten is:**

> **A BATTEN is a thin, narrow strip of timber**, used as a support, a fixing ground, or a covering over a joint.

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Supporting roof covering** | Battens carry tiles or slates across the rafters |
| **Fixing ground for panelling** | Fixed to a wall to receive boards |
| **Board-and-batten cladding** | Covering the joints between boards |
| Ceiling and partition framing | Light framing members |

> **The defining property is that a batten is a LIGHT, SECONDARY member**, and the 50 mm limit expresses exactly that: beyond it the piece is no longer a batten but a scantling or a joist.

**The timber size classification** it belongs to:

| Term | Description |
|---|---|
| **BATTEN** | **Thin narrow strip — maximum depth 50 mm** |
| **PLANK** | Wide and flat, thickness usually under 50 mm |
| **BOARD** | Thin, wide, less than about 30 mm thick |
| **SCANTLING** | Small squared timber |
| **BALK / BEAM** | Large squared section |
| Log | Unconverted round timber |

> **The names are defined by SIZE and PROPORTION, not by use**, which is why a table like this is worth carrying: the same piece of timber changes its name with its dimensions.

**Why the maximum depth matters practically:**

> **A batten is nailed, often near its end and often through its thickness.** A deeper section splits more readily when nailed and is heavier to handle on a roof.

> **And a batten spans a short distance between rafters**, so depth beyond 50 mm buys strength that is not needed while adding weight and cost across a very large number of pieces.

**The timber properties that govern its use:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strength along the grain** | **Much greater than across it** — timber is highly ANISOTROPIC |
| **Moisture content** | Governs shrinkage, strength and decay |
| **Seasoning** | Reduces moisture to a stable level before use |
| **Defects** | **Knots, shakes, wanes** reduce strength |

> **Anisotropy is timber's defining characteristic**: it may be ten to twenty times stronger along the grain than across it, which is why timber members are always loaded along the grain and why cross-grain tension is avoided entirely.

**SEASONING**, since it recurs in every timber question:

> **The objective is to reduce moisture content, increase structural stability, and increase resistance to shrinkage, cracking, warping and decay.**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL (air) seasoning** | **Cheap but slow — 2 to 12 months**; stacked with air gaps |
| **KILN seasoning** | **Fast, controlled, more uniform**; costs energy |
| Water seasoning | Sap removed by immersion, then air dried |

> **Timber must be seasoned to roughly the moisture content it will live at**, or it will move after installation — shrinking, cupping and opening joints. **That is the practical reason seasoning matters more than any strength consideration.**

**Common defects:** **KNOTS** (branch bases — reduce strength and deflect grain), **SHAKES** (splits along the grain), **WANE** (bark or a missing edge), **WARP** (bow, cup, twist, spring) and **decay** from fungal attack in damp conditions.

examTip.trick: **A batten is a LIGHT, SECONDARY member**, and 50 mm is where it stops being one. Beyond that depth the piece is a scantling or a joist.
examTip.trap: **Timber names are defined by SIZE and PROPORTION, not by use** — batten, plank, board, scantling, balk. The same timber changes its name with its dimensions.
examTip.mnemonic: **Timber is highly ANISOTROPIC** — often 10–20× stronger along the grain than across it, which is why cross-grain tension is avoided entirely. And **season to the moisture content it will live at**, or it moves after installation.

questions.stem: For supercritical flow, the Froude number should be:
questions.solution:
**Fr > 1.**

**The Froude number:**

> **Fr = V / √(g y)**

> It compares the **flow velocity** with the **speed of a small surface (gravity) wave** in water of that depth.

**The three regimes:**

| | **SUBCRITICAL** | **CRITICAL** | **SUPERCRITICAL** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Froude number** | **Fr < 1** | **Fr = 1** | **Fr > 1** |
| Depth | **Deep** | y_c | **Shallow** |
| Velocity | Slow | V_c | **Fast** |
| Also called | **Tranquil, streaming** | — | **Shooting, torrential, rapid** |
| **Disturbance travels upstream?** | **YES** | Stationary wave | **NO** |
| **Control from** | **DOWNSTREAM** | — | **UPSTREAM** |

**The physical meaning is worth having, because it makes the whole topic memorable:**

> **Fr = 1 means the flow moves exactly as fast as a wave can travel across it.**

> **In SUPERCRITICAL flow the water OUTRUNS ITS OWN WAVES.** A disturbance cannot propagate upstream, so nothing downstream can influence what happens above — **control is from upstream.**

> **In SUBCRITICAL flow waves can travel upstream**, so a downstream gate or weir sets the depth above it — **control is from downstream.**

> **This is the exact hydraulic analogue of the sound barrier**: Fr in open channels plays the role that the Mach number plays in gas flow, and the same reasoning about disturbance propagation applies to both.

**A caution about the source's own wording:** the compilation's explanatory note states "Froude number is greater than 4 for super-critical flow", which is **wrong** — the boundary is **1**, as the keyed option (c) correctly gives. **Fr > 4 is not a definition but a design guideline**: a hydraulic jump with Fr₁ between **4.5 and 9** is the stable, well-dissipating "steady" jump that stilling basins are designed around. The two ideas are unrelated, and the number 4 belongs to the second.

**The critical depth relations:**

> **For a rectangular channel: y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}**, where q is the discharge per unit width.
>
> **V_c = √(g y_c)** — the source's own derivation, which gives Fr = 1 by definition.
>
> **E_min = 1.5 y_c** — at critical depth the specific energy is a minimum.

> **And the critical state is where specific energy is MINIMUM for a given discharge, or discharge is MAXIMUM for a given specific energy.** Those are two views of the same point on the E–y curve.

**Why the regime matters in design:**

| Regime | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **SUPERCRITICAL** | **High velocity → EROSION and scour; a jump will form where it meets tranquil water** |
| **CRITICAL** | **UNSTABLE — small energy changes give large depth changes**; avoid designing at it |
| **SUBCRITICAL** | Stable, the normal condition for canals and rivers |

> **Designing a channel at or near critical depth is a known error**: the E–y curve is flat there, so a small change in energy produces a large and unpredictable change in depth, and the water surface becomes wavy and unstable.

> **Canals are therefore designed comfortably subcritical**, and supercritical flow is confined to chutes and spillways where it is deliberately created and then killed in a stilling basin.

examTip.trick: **Fr compares flow velocity with wave speed.** Supercritical means the water **outruns its own waves** — so disturbances cannot travel upstream, and control is from **upstream**.
examTip.trap: **The source's own note says "greater than 4", which is wrong** — the boundary is **1**. Fr > 4.5 is a *stilling basin* guideline for a steady hydraulic jump, an unrelated idea.
examTip.mnemonic: **Never design a channel at critical depth** — the E–y curve is flat there, so small energy changes give large depth changes and the surface goes unstable. Canals run comfortably subcritical.

questions.stem: Shear stress in a beam is ______ on the neutral axis.
questions.solution:
**Maximum.**

> The source states the pair: **shearing stress in a beam is maximum at the neutral axis and zero at the extreme fibres; the bending stresses are maximum at the extreme fibres.**

**The two stresses are exactly opposite in their distribution** — which is the whole point of the question:

| | **BENDING stress σ = My/I** | **SHEAR stress τ = VAȳ/(Ib)** |
|---|---|---|
| **At the NEUTRAL AXIS** | **ZERO** (y = 0) | **MAXIMUM** |
| **At the EXTREME FIBRES** | **MAXIMUM** | **ZERO** |
| Distribution | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** (rectangle) |

> **Reading the two formulae explains both.** In **σ = My/I**, y is the distance from the neutral axis — zero there. In **τ = VAȳ/(Ib)**, the term **Aȳ** is the first moment of the area **beyond** the level considered, and that area is **greatest at the neutral axis** and **vanishes at the free surface.**

> **So neither result needs memorising** — each follows from its own formula.

**And the top and bottom surfaces must have zero shear for a physical reason:**

> **They are FREE SURFACES with nothing above or below to shear against.** Complementary shear on a free surface is impossible, so τ must be zero there.

**The maximum values for common sections:**

| Section | **τ_max** | Ratio to average |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5 V/(bd)** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **4V/(3A)** | **1.33** |
| **I-section (web)** | **≈ V/(web area)** | **≈ 1.0 – 1.1** |
| Triangle | — | 1.5 |

> **For an I-section the shear is almost entirely carried by the WEB** — about **95%** of it — and it is nearly uniform across the web depth.

> **That is why steel design simply checks V/(web area)**, and why the flanges, which carry almost all the bending, carry almost no shear.

> **The complementary division is elegant: flanges take the MOMENT, the web takes the SHEAR.** It is the reason the I-section is the shape it is.

**Which stress governs a design:**

| Beam | Governed by |
|---|---|
| **LONG, slender** | **BENDING** — moment grows as L² while shear grows as L |
| **SHORT, deep** | **SHEAR** |
| **Heavily loaded near a support** | **SHEAR** |

> **Bending governs the great majority of beams**, because the moment increases with the square of the span while the shear increases only linearly.

> **But shear is decisive in short deep members** — brackets, corbels, transfer beams and deep beams — and a shear failure gives far less warning than a flexural one, which is why codes treat it more conservatively.

**In reinforced concrete this asymmetry is designed for directly:**

> **Diagonal tension from shear is resisted by STIRRUPS**, and IS 456 requires a **minimum shear reinforcement** everywhere, even where calculation shows none is needed.

> **The reason is the failure mode**: a flexural failure is ductile and announces itself through deflection and cracking, while **a shear failure is sudden and brittle.** The minimum stirrups exist to make sure the beam never chooses the second.

examTip.trick: **Read the formulae.** In σ = My/I, y = 0 at the neutral axis. In τ = VAȳ/(Ib), the area beyond the level is greatest there. Neither result needs memorising.
examTip.trap: **Bending and shear are exactly opposite**: bending is zero at the neutral axis and maximum at the fibres; shear is the reverse. Free top and bottom surfaces **cannot** carry shear at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Flanges take the MOMENT, the web takes the SHEAR** — about 95% of it. And **bending governs long beams (M ∝ L²), shear governs short deep ones** — where failure is sudden and brittle.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT used as a media for trickling filters?
questions.solution:
**Paper.**

> The source lists what is used: **coke, pumice, plastic matrix material, open-cell polyurethane foam, clinker, gravel, sand and geotextiles are the most common types of media.** **Paper is not among them.**

**Why paper could never serve:**

| Requirement of a filter medium | Paper |
|---|---|
| **Durable — must last decades under constant wetting** | **DISINTEGRATES in water** |
| **Structurally sound — supports the bed's own weight** | **No strength when wet** |
| **Chemically inert** | **BIODEGRADABLE — it is itself food for the biofilm** |
| **High specific surface area** | — |
| **High void ratio for air circulation** | Collapses, blocking voids |

> **The disqualifying property is that paper is BIODEGRADABLE.** A trickling filter medium must be the one thing in the reactor the micro-organisms do **not** consume — it is the scaffold they live on, not their food.

> **A medium that is itself substrate would be eaten and the bed would collapse**, which settles the question on principle rather than on a list.

**How a trickling filter works:**

> **Sewage is sprayed over a bed of media on which a BIOLOGICAL FILM (biofilm, or zoogleal film) grows.** As the sewage trickles down, organisms in the film absorb and oxidise the organic matter.

> **It is an ATTACHED-GROWTH process** — the organisms live on a surface, in contrast to the **SUSPENDED-GROWTH** activated sludge process where they float in the liquid.

| | **Trickling filter (attached growth)** | **Activated sludge (suspended growth)** |
|---|---|---|
| Organisms | **Fixed on media** | **Suspended in the mixed liquor** |
| Power | **Low — often gravity fed** | **High — continuous aeration** |
| Operation | **Simple, robust** | **Needs skilled control** |
| **Shock loads** | **Tolerant** | **Sensitive** |
| Land | More | Less |
| Effluent quality | Good | **Better** |
| **Sludge produced** | Less | More |

> **The robustness of the trickling filter is what recommends it in Nepal**: it survives flow and load variations, needs little power, and does not fail if an operator is absent for a week. **Activated sludge produces a better effluent but demands reliable electricity and skilled operation.**

**The two essential features of a medium:**

> **1. High SPECIFIC SURFACE AREA** — more surface means more biofilm and more treatment per cubic metre.
>
> **2. High VOID RATIO** — so **AIR can circulate** and the organisms stay aerobic.

> **These two pull against each other**: smaller media give more surface but fewer and finer voids, which clog and go anaerobic.

> **Which is why PLASTIC media largely displaced stone.** Moulded plastic achieves a high surface area **and** a very high void ratio simultaneously, and is far lighter — allowing much deeper filters than the 2–3 m that stone permits.

**Ventilation is the operational essential:**

> **The filter must breathe.** Air moves through the bed by natural draught caused by the temperature difference between the air and the sewage.

> **If the voids clog — PONDING — air is excluded, the film turns anaerobic, and the filter goes septic and smells.** Ponding is the classic trickling filter failure, and it comes from media that are too fine or from excessive organic loading.

**Typical design values:** hydraulic loading **1–4 m³/m²/day** (low rate) and **10–40** (high rate); organic loading **0.08–0.32 kg BOD/m³/day** (low rate); **recirculation** used in high-rate filters to dilute the incoming load and keep the film wet.

examTip.trick: **The medium must be the one thing in the reactor the organisms do NOT eat.** Paper is biodegradable — it is substrate, not scaffold. That settles it on principle, without a list.
examTip.trap: **Sand, gravel AND geotextiles are all genuinely used** — the source names all three. Only one option is disqualified, and it is disqualified absolutely.
examTip.mnemonic: **High surface area and high void ratio pull against each other** — which is why PLASTIC media replaced stone. And **PONDING** (clogged voids → anaerobic → septic) is the classic trickling-filter failure.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an impulse turbine?
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — Pelton, crossflow and Turgo are all impulse turbines.

> The source gives the defining test: **if at the inlet of the turbine the energy available is ONLY KINETIC energy, the turbine is an impulse turbine. Examples: Pelton, Crossflow, Turgo. If at the inlet the water possesses kinetic energy AS WELL AS pressure energy, it is a reaction turbine. Examples: Francis, Kaplan, propeller.**

**The classification test, stated as a single question:**

> **Is there PRESSURE energy at the runner inlet?**
>
> **No → IMPULSE. Yes → REACTION.**

| | **IMPULSE** | **REACTION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Energy at inlet** | **Kinetic ONLY** | **Kinetic + PRESSURE** |
| **Pressure change across the runner** | **NONE — atmospheric** | **Pressure DROPS** |
| **Runner** | **Runs in AIR** | **Fully SUBMERGED** |
| **Flow control** | **Spear / needle valve in the nozzle** | **Adjustable guide vanes** |
| **Draft tube** | **NOT used** | **ESSENTIAL** |
| **Head** | **HIGH** | Medium to low |
| Examples | **Pelton, Turgo, Crossflow** | **Francis, Kaplan, propeller** |

> **In an impulse turbine the NOZZLE has already converted the entire head to velocity before the water reaches the runner.** That is why the runner spins in air at atmospheric pressure, and why no pressure casing is needed.

**The three impulse turbines, and how they differ:**

| Turbine | Jet strikes | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **PELTON** | **Tangentially**, on split buckets | **Very high head (> 250 m)**, low flow |
| **TURGO** | **At an ANGLE (~20°)**, entering one side and leaving the other | **Medium-high head**; **higher flow than Pelton for the same size** |
| **CROSSFLOW (Banki–Michell)** | **THROUGH the runner twice**, across a drum-shaped rotor | **LOW to medium head, higher flow; simple to fabricate** |

> **The Turgo's advantage is that the discharged water does not interfere with the incoming jet**, so it can accept a larger flow than a Pelton wheel of the same diameter — useful where head is high but not extreme.

> **The CROSSFLOW turbine matters greatly in Nepal.** It is simple enough to be **fabricated in a local workshop** from sheet steel, needs no precision casting, holds good efficiency over a **wide range of flows**, and is the workhorse of micro-hydro schemes across the hills.

> **Its part-flow performance is the decisive property**: a run-of-river micro-hydro scheme's flow varies enormously through the year, and a turbine that collapses in efficiency at part load is useless there.

**Why no impulse turbine has a draft tube:**

> **A draft tube recovers the kinetic energy remaining at a reaction turbine's exit and lets the runner sit above tailwater while still using the full head.**

> **An impulse runner must be above the tailwater anyway — it runs in air — and its exit water has already given up its energy.** There is nothing to recover.

> **The consequence is that an impulse turbine WASTES the height between runner and tailwater** — negligible on a 400 m head, unacceptable on a 10 m one. **The economics follow directly from the physics.**

**Selection by head:** **Pelton above 250 m; Francis 45–400 m; Kaplan below 60 m; crossflow across the low and medium range for small schemes.**

> **And specific speed rises as head falls: Pelton 10–35, Francis 60–300, Kaplan 300–1000.**

examTip.trick: **One question classifies every turbine: is there PRESSURE energy at the runner inlet?** No → impulse (the nozzle already converted the head to velocity). Yes → reaction.
examTip.trap: **Turgo and crossflow are less familiar than Pelton but are equally impulse turbines** — which is what makes "All of the above" correct rather than a lazy option.
examTip.mnemonic: **The CROSSFLOW turbine is Nepal's micro-hydro workhorse** — fabricable in a local workshop, and it holds efficiency over a **wide flow range**, which is decisive on a run-of-river scheme.

questions.stem: If D is the scour depth measured below the bed, then the width of the launching apron will generally equal:
questions.solution:
**1.5 D.**

> The source states it: **to protect the face of the guide bank at river bed level a thick stone cover is laid on the bed, called an apron. When the scour undermines the river bed the apron comes down — or LAUNCHES — to cover the face of the scour. The width of the launching apron is generally taken as 1.5 D.**

**Where 1.5 D comes from — it is geometry, and worth deriving:**

> **The apron must contain enough stone to armour the slope that the scour hole exposes.**

> **The launched slope is taken as 2 horizontal to 1 vertical.** For a scour depth **D**, the sloping face has length **D√(2² + 1²) = D√5 = 2.24 D.**

> **The launched stone forms a layer of thickness 1.25 t on that slope** (thickened from the original thickness t, since stone rearranges as it falls).

> **Equating the volume laid flat to the volume needed on the slope gives a width of about 1.5 D** for the standard apron thickness.

> **The 1.5 is therefore a derived proportion, not an arbitrary rule** — and the source's own figure marks both the 1.5 D width and the 1.25 t launched thickness.

**The remarkable idea in this structure:**

> **A launching apron is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED, in a controlled way.**

> **It is laid flat on the bed as a horizontal carpet of loose stone. As the river scours a hole beside it, the stone at the edge FALLS — launches — into the hole, armouring the newly exposed slope as fast as the slope forms.**

> **The apron consumes itself progressively to protect what is behind it**, which is a genuinely different design philosophy from building something strong enough to resist.

> **And it works precisely because the stone is LOOSE.** A rigid, grouted apron would be undermined and would fail as a slab; loose stone follows the scour down.

**Getting the scour depth D:**

> **Lacey's normal scour depth: R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}**, with **f = 1.76√d** (d in mm).

> **Then multiply by the LOCATION FACTOR:**

| Location | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| Straight reach | **1.25** |
| Moderate bend | 1.5 |
| Severe bend | 1.75 |
| **Bridge pier nose** | **2.0** |
| **GUIDE BANK HEAD** | **2.75** |

> **The guide bank head takes the severest scour anywhere in the works** — deeper even than a bridge pier — which is exactly why the heaviest apron is laid there.

**The design points of the apron:**

| Point | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Stone SIZE** | Heavy enough not to be washed away — sized against velocity |
| **Thickness** | Enough to give a **continuous** launched layer |
| **Width** | **1.5 D** |
| **Launched slope** | **2:1** |
| **Launched thickness** | **1.25 t** |

> **Undersizing the stone is the commonest failure**: stone that the flood can carry away does not launch — it simply leaves.

**And what it protects:**

> **GUIDE BANKS prevent OUTFLANKING** — the river going *around* a barrage or bridge and leaving it stranded in a dry bed. **Heavy scour at the curved heads and shanks undermines the stone pitching and destroys the guide bank**, so the apron at the toe is what keeps the whole river training system alive.

examTip.trick: **1.5 D is derived, not arbitrary**: the launched slope is 2:1, so its face is D√5 = 2.24 D long, and at 1.25 t launched thickness the flat apron needs about 1.5 D of width to fill it.
examTip.trap: **1.25 also appears in this structure — as the launched THICKNESS (1.25 t), and as the straight-reach scour factor.** Three different roles for similar numbers; keep them apart.
examTip.mnemonic: **The apron is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED** — loose stone falls into the scour hole as it forms, armouring the slope. A rigid grouted apron would be undermined and fail as a slab.

questions.stem: In a simply supported beam a point load acts at the centre of the span. What will be the strain energy?
questions.solution:
**W²L³/96EI.**

**Working — two steps only:**

> **Step 1 — the deflection under a central point load:**
>
> **δ = WL³/(48EI)**
>
> **Step 2 — the strain energy stored equals the work done by the load, which builds up gradually from zero:**
>
> **U = ½ W δ = ½ × W × WL³/(48EI) = W²L³/(96EI)** ✓

**The factor of ½ is the whole question:**

> **The load does NOT act at full value throughout the deflection.** It grows from zero to W as the beam deflects from zero to δ.

> **The work done is therefore the AREA UNDER the load–deflection line — a triangle — which is ½Wδ, not Wδ.**

> **Omitting the ½ gives W²L³/48EI, which is exactly option (a)** — the distractor built for this error, and the commonest mistake in the topic.

**A DIMENSIONAL check disposes of two options instantly:**

> **Strain energy is an ENERGY — units of N·m.**

| Expression | Dimensions | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **W²L³/EI** | N² · m³ / (N·m²) = **N·m** ✓ | **Correct form** |
| W²L²/EI | N² · m² / (N·m²) = **N** | **A FORCE, not energy** ✗ |

> **Options (b) and (d) carry L², which makes them forces rather than energies** — dimensionally impossible, whatever the coefficient. **Half the options fall without any recall.**

> **(EI has units of N·m², since E is N/m² and I is m⁴.)**

**Strain energy for the standard cases:**

| Loading | **U** |
|---|---|
| **Axial load** | **P²L/(2AE)** |
| **Bending (general)** | **∫ M² dx/(2EI)** |
| **Torsion** | **T²L/(2GJ)** |
| **SS beam, central point load** | **W²L³/(96EI)** |
| **Cantilever, end point load** | **W²L³/(6EI)** |

> **Every one carries a ½ in some form** — from the same triangular work diagram. **Recognising that pattern makes the whole table recoverable.**

> **Note the cantilever stores SIXTEEN TIMES the energy** of the simply supported beam for the same load and span, because it deflects sixteen times as far (WL³/3EI against WL³/48EI).

**Why strain energy is worth having:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **CASTIGLIANO's theorem** | **δ = ∂U/∂P** — deflection is the partial derivative of strain energy with respect to the load |
| **Unit load method** | Deflections in trusses and frames |
| **Analysis of indeterminate structures** | Method of least work: **∂U/∂R = 0** |
| Impact and dynamic loading | Energy absorbed |
| **RESILIENCE and TOUGHNESS** | Material capacity to absorb energy |

> **Castigliano's theorem is the payoff**: differentiate the strain energy with respect to a load and you get the deflection under it — which converts a differential-equation problem into an algebraic one.

> **And where no load acts at the point of interest, a DUMMY load is applied, differentiated, then set to zero.** That trick is what makes the method general.

**And the impact consequence:**

> **A suddenly applied load produces TWICE the deflection and stress of the same load applied gradually**, because the full load acts through the whole deflection — no ½ this time.

> **The same factor of ½, seen from the other side.**

examTip.trick: **U = ½Wδ**, because the load grows from zero to W as the beam deflects — the work is the triangular area, not Wδ. With δ = WL³/48EI that gives **W²L³/96EI**.
examTip.trap: **Omitting the ½ gives exactly option (a).** And options (b) and (d) carry L², which makes them **forces, not energies** — dimensionally impossible. Half the options fall without recall.
examTip.mnemonic: **Castigliano: δ = ∂U/∂P** — differentiate strain energy by the load to get the deflection under it. And the same ½ explains why a **suddenly applied load doubles** the deflection and stress.

questions.stem: Head loss will be small in the case of a:
questions.solution:
**Broad crested weir.**

> The source's reasoning: **broad crested weirs are constructed in rectangular shape only and are suitable for larger flows; hence head loss is less.**

**Why a broad crest loses least energy:**

> **The crest is long enough (in the direction of flow) for the streamlines to become PARALLEL and the flow to settle to a controlled, gradually varied state over it.**

> **Flow separation is minimal, so little energy is dissipated in turbulence.**

> **A SHARP crested weir does the opposite**: the nappe **springs clear** of the crest, air is entrained beneath it, and the jet plunges into the pool below — **a violent, highly dissipative process.**

> **The distinction is simply how much turbulence the geometry forces**, which makes the ranking reasonable rather than arbitrary.

**The weir types compared:**

| Weir | Crest | Energy loss | Chief use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BROAD crested** | **L > 0.5 H — flow parallel over the crest** | **LEAST** | **Large flows; measurement; canal falls** |
| **OGEE (spillway)** | S-shaped, follows the nappe profile | Low | **Dam spillways — highest discharge coefficient** |
| **NARROW crested** | Short crest | Moderate | — |
| **SHARP crested** | **Thin plate — nappe springs clear** | **GREATEST** | **Precise flow MEASUREMENT** |

> **The classification is by the ratio of crest LENGTH to HEAD:** **broad crested when L/H > about 0.5 to 0.6**, sharp crested when the crest is a thin plate.

**The OGEE weir deserves a note, because it is the closest competitor:**

> **Its profile is shaped to follow the underside of the nappe that would spring from a sharp crested weir at the design head.**

> **The water therefore just touches the surface without pressing on it or separating from it** — no negative pressure, no cavitation, and the **highest discharge coefficient of any weir (C ≈ 2.2).**

> **But it is a SPILLWAY profile, designed for passing floods efficiently, not for minimising head loss in a channel.** At heads above the design head the pressure on the crest goes **negative**, risking cavitation, which is why the design head is chosen deliberately below the maximum.

**Why the SHARP crested weir survives despite the highest loss:**

> **Because it is the most ACCURATE flow-measuring device of the four.**

> **The nappe springs clear, so the discharge depends only on the head over a well-defined edge** — no dependence on the crest's condition or on the approach channel's roughness.

| Weir | Discharge formula |
|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **Q = (2/3) C_d L √(2g) H^{3/2}** |
| **V-notch (triangular)** | **Q = (8/15) C_d tan(θ/2) √(2g) H^{5/2}** |
| **Cipolletti (trapezoidal)** | Side slopes **1 H : 4 V**, compensating end contractions |

> **The V-notch is used for SMALL discharges** because its **H^{5/2}** dependence makes the head very sensitive to flow — a small flow still produces a readable head, which a rectangular weir would not.

> **And the Cipolletti weir's 1:4 side slopes are chosen precisely so the added triangular area compensates the loss from end contractions**, letting the simple rectangular formula be used without a contraction correction.

**The practical trade-off in a canal:**

> **A weir in a canal costs head permanently.** Every metre lost to turbulence is a metre of command area given up upstream — so where the purpose is regulation rather than measurement, the **broad crest** is chosen for exactly the reason this question tests.

examTip.trick: **A broad crest lets the streamlines go PARALLEL over it** — little separation, little turbulence, least loss. A sharp crest makes the nappe spring clear and plunge, which is violently dissipative.
examTip.trap: **The OGEE has the highest discharge COEFFICIENT (C ≈ 2.2), which is not the same as the least head loss.** It is a spillway profile for passing floods, not a low-loss channel structure.
examTip.mnemonic: **The sharp crested weir survives because it MEASURES best** — discharge depends only on head over a defined edge. And the **V-notch (H^{5/2})** is for small flows, where a rectangular weir gives no readable head.

questions.stem: The depth of flow at which specific energy is minimum and discharge is maximum is called:
questions.solution:
**Critical depth.**

> The source defines it: **the depth of flow at which the specific energy attains a minimum value and discharge attains maximum value is called the critical depth. The flow at critical depth is called critical flow and the velocity of flow is the critical velocity.**

**The two statements are two views of one point:**

| View | Statement |
|---|---|
| **For a given DISCHARGE** | **Specific energy is MINIMUM at critical depth** |
| **For a given SPECIFIC ENERGY** | **Discharge is MAXIMUM at critical depth** |

> **They describe the same point on the E–y curve** approached from two directions, which is why the definition can be stated either way.

**The four depths — this question is a pure discrimination between them:**

| Depth | Definition |
|---|---|
| **CRITICAL (y_c)** | **Minimum specific energy for the given discharge; Fr = 1** ← |
| **ALTERNATE** | **The OTHER depth with the SAME specific energy** for the same discharge |
| **SEQUENT / CONJUGATE** | **The depths BEFORE and AFTER a HYDRAULIC JUMP — same MOMENTUM flux** |
| **NORMAL (y_n)** | **The depth of UNIFORM flow** in a prismatic channel — set by slope and roughness |

> **ALTERNATE and SEQUENT depths are constantly confused, and the distinction is exact:**

> **ALTERNATE depths have the same SPECIFIC ENERGY. SEQUENT depths have the same MOMENTUM.**

> **A hydraulic jump conserves momentum but LOSES energy**, so the depths across a jump are sequent, not alternate. **The two would coincide only if a jump lost no energy, which it always does.**

**The critical depth relations:**

> **Rectangular channel: y_c = (q²/g)^{1/3}**, q being the discharge per unit width
>
> **V_c = √(g y_c)**, so **Fr = 1** by definition
>
> **E_min = 1.5 y_c**

> **The E_min = 1.5 y_c relation is worth carrying**: it says two thirds of the minimum specific energy is depth and one third is velocity head, which fixes the shape of the E–y curve at its nose.

**Comparing NORMAL and CRITICAL depth classifies the channel:**

| Comparison | Slope | Normal flow |
|---|---|---|
| **y_n > y_c** | **MILD** | **Subcritical** |
| **y_n = y_c** | **Critical** | Critical |
| **y_n < y_c** | **STEEP** | **Supercritical** |

> **"Mild" and "steep" are hydraulic terms, not geometric ones.** A slope is mild or steep relative to the **critical slope for that discharge** — so the *same* physical channel can be mild at one discharge and steep at another.

> **That is a genuinely counter-intuitive point and a favourite examination trap.**

**Why critical depth matters in practice:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **CONTROL SECTION** | Critical flow fixes a unique depth–discharge relation |
| **FLOW MEASUREMENT** | **Flumes and broad crested weirs force critical flow** so discharge follows from depth alone |
| Free overfall | Critical depth occurs a short distance upstream of the brink |
| Water surface profiles | Critical depth is the reference for classifying M, S, C, H and A curves |

> **Forcing critical flow is the whole principle of a measuring flume**: once the flow passes through critical, the discharge depends only on the upstream depth and is independent of downstream conditions.

> **But designing an ordinary channel AT critical depth is a known error** — the E–y curve is flat there, so a small change in energy gives a large change in depth, and the surface becomes wavy and unstable.

examTip.trick: **Minimum energy for a given discharge and maximum discharge for a given energy are the SAME point** on the E–y curve, approached from two directions.
examTip.trap: **ALTERNATE depths share SPECIFIC ENERGY; SEQUENT depths share MOMENTUM.** A jump conserves momentum but loses energy, so jump depths are sequent — never alternate.
examTip.mnemonic: **"Mild" and "steep" are HYDRAULIC, not geometric** — defined by y_n vs y_c, so the same channel can be mild at one discharge and steep at another. And **E_min = 1.5 y_c**.

questions.stem: The number of members nominated by the Nepal Engineering Council itself is:
questions.solution:
**Two.**

> The source quotes the Act's provision directly: **two members nominated by the Council from among engineers holding a degree in engineering with at least seven years of experience in the engineering profession, INCLUDING AT LEAST ONE WOMAN.**

**The two qualifying conditions on these nominees:**

| Requirement | Value |
|---|---|
| **Degree in engineering** | Required |
| **Minimum experience** | **7 years** in the engineering profession |
| **Composition** | **At least ONE must be a woman** |

> **The gender provision is written into the Act itself**, not left to practice — which is why the clause specifies it explicitly rather than merely permitting it.

**How the Council is constituted** — the nominated seats sit among several categories:

| Source of membership | Note |
|---|---|
| **Government-nominated** members | From the ministry and public institutions |
| **Ex-officio** members | By virtue of office held |
| **ELECTED** members | From among registered engineers |
| **Council-nominated** | **2, including at least one woman** ← |
| Representatives of institutions | Universities, professional bodies |

> **The mixture is deliberate.** Elected members give the profession a voice, government nominees give public accountability, and **the Council's own nominations exist to fill gaps — bringing in expertise or representation that election alone would not produce.**

> **That is precisely why the woman-member provision attaches to the NOMINATED seats rather than the elected ones**: nomination is the mechanism available to correct an imbalance that an open election may not.

**What the Nepal Engineering Council does:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTER engineers** and issue **license** certificates | The core statutory function |
| **Recognise engineering qualifications** | Which degrees qualify for registration |
| **Conduct the licensing examination** | The route to registration |
| **Prescribe the CODE OF ETHICS** | Professional conduct |
| **DISCIPLINARY action** | Including suspension and removal from the register |
| Classify categories of engineer | By discipline and level |
| **Report to the Government of Nepal** | Its accountability |

> **The power to remove a name from the register is what makes the Council a regulator rather than an association.** A university cannot un-educate a graduate; the Council can end a career.

**A caution about questions of this kind:**

> **Numbers taken from a statute are the most volatile examination material there is** — an amendment changes the answer without changing the underlying principle.

> **What is durable is the STRUCTURE**: a mixed council of elected, ex-officio, government-nominated and council-nominated members, with a statutory provision for women's representation attached to the nominated seats.

> **Learn the structure and the reason for it; treat the exact count as a fact to check against the current Act.**

**The principal duties in the code of conduct:** **competence** (practise only within your field and level), **public safety paramount** (above the client's interest and your own), **integrity**, **no conflict of interest**, **confidentiality**, and **no supplanting** another engineer already engaged.

> **"Public safety paramount" is the clause that makes engineering a profession rather than a trade** — it requires an engineer to refuse an instruction or report a danger even at commercial cost.

examTip.trick: **Two council-nominated members, needing a degree plus 7 years' experience, including at least one woman.** The gender provision is written into the Act, not left to practice.
examTip.trap: **Statutory numbers are the most volatile exam material there is** — an amendment changes the answer without changing the principle. Learn the **structure**; check the count against the current Act.
examTip.mnemonic: **The nominated seats exist to fill gaps that election cannot** — which is exactly why the woman-member requirement attaches to them rather than to the elected seats.

questions.stem: The value of Poisson's ratio for commonly used engineering materials would be:
questions.solution:
**Less than 1.**

> The source states it: **in practice, Poisson's ratio of commonly used materials ranges from zero to half.**

**What Poisson's ratio is:**

> **μ (or ν) = lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain**, taken as a magnitude.

> **Stretch a bar and it gets THINNER; compress it and it gets FATTER.** Poisson's ratio measures how much.

**Typical values:**

| Material | **μ** |
|---|---|
| **Cork** | **≈ 0** |
| **Concrete** | **0.1 – 0.2** |
| **Cast iron** | 0.23 – 0.27 |
| **STEEL** | **0.25 – 0.33 (commonly 0.3)** |
| Aluminium | 0.33 |
| Copper, brass | 0.34 |
| **Rubber** | **≈ 0.5** |

> **0.3 for steel and 0.2 for concrete are the two values worth carrying**, because they appear in almost every calculation that needs one.

**Why the theoretical upper limit is exactly 0.5** — this is the substance of the question:

> **The BULK MODULUS is K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)].**
>
> **As μ → 0.5, the term (1 − 2μ) → 0, so K → INFINITY.**

> **An infinite bulk modulus means the material cannot change volume at all — it is perfectly INCOMPRESSIBLE.**

> **μ = 0.5 is therefore the incompressible limit, and it cannot be exceeded**: a value above 0.5 would mean the material EXPANDS in volume when compressed, which violates energy conservation.

> **Rubber, at ≈0.5, is very nearly incompressible** — which is why a rubber block confined on all sides behaves almost like a liquid, and why rubber bearings must be free to bulge sideways to work at all.

**And the lower limit:**

> **The theoretical range for an isotropic elastic material is −1 ≤ μ ≤ 0.5.**

> **A NEGATIVE Poisson's ratio is physically possible** — such "auxetic" materials get **fatter** when stretched — but they are engineered structures rather than ordinary materials, and none of the four options offers a negative value.

**Why option (d), "constant for all materials", is wrong:**

> **Poisson's ratio is a MATERIAL PROPERTY and varies widely** — from about 0 for cork to 0.5 for rubber. **It is precisely the property that distinguishes how differently materials deform laterally.**

> **Cork's near-zero value has a practical consequence**: a cork pushed into a bottle neck does not bulge sideways, which is exactly why cork and not rubber is used for the purpose.

**The elastic constant relations** it appears in:

| Relation | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Bulk modulus** | **K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)]** |
| **Rigidity (shear) modulus** | **G = E/[2(1 + μ)]** |
| Combined | **E = 9KG/(3K + G)** |

> **Only TWO of the four constants (E, G, K, μ) are independent for an isotropic material** — any two determine the rest.

> **Check with steel: G = E/[2(1.3)] = E/2.6 ≈ 0.385E**, and with E = 200 GPa that gives **G ≈ 77 GPa**, the standard value ✓

**Where it matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plane stress / plane strain analysis** | Appears throughout |
| **Lateral earth pressure at rest** | **K₀ = μ/(1 − μ)** for an elastic soil |
| **Settlement calculations** | Elastic settlement formulae contain (1 − μ²) |
| Confined concrete | Lateral expansion is what confinement resists |

> **Confinement is the practical one**: concrete fails in compression partly by splitting from lateral expansion, so **stirrups and spirals that restrain that expansion raise both the strength and the ductility** — which is the entire basis of confined-concrete design in seismic detailing.

examTip.trick: **K = E/[3(1 − 2μ)]**, so as μ → 0.5 the bulk modulus → infinity — perfectly incompressible. **0.5 is a hard upper limit**, and every practical material sits between 0 and it.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) claims it is constant — but it is precisely the property that VARIES**, from ~0 for cork to 0.5 for rubber. Cork's near-zero value is why corks don't bulge in a bottle neck.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steel 0.3, concrete 0.2.** And only **two** of E, G, K, μ are independent: G = E/[2(1+μ)] gives steel's 77 GPa from 200 GPa directly.

questions.stem: If the time mean speed is 50 km/h, then the space mean speed is:
options: Time mean speed = 2 × space mean speed
questions.solution:
**Less than 50 km/h.**

> The source states the rule: **the space mean speed will always be less than the time mean speed, and it will be less than 50 km/h.**

**The two speeds, and why they differ:**

| | **TIME mean speed (V_t)** | **SPACE mean speed (V_s)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Measured** | **At a POINT, over TIME** | **Over a LENGTH, at an instant** |
| **Average of** | **Individual spot speeds** | **HARMONIC mean of spot speeds** |
| Formula | **Σv/n** | **n / Σ(1/v)** |
| Magnitude | **ALWAYS the LARGER** | **ALWAYS the SMALLER** |

> **V_s ≤ V_t always**, with equality only when every vehicle travels at exactly the same speed.

**Why the space mean speed is always smaller** — the reasoning is worth having, because it makes the rule impossible to forget:

> **A spot measurement counts vehicles as they PASS. A fast vehicle passes the point more often than a slow one in a given period, so the point sample is BIASED TOWARD FAST vehicles.**

> **A length measurement counts vehicles PRESENT on the road at an instant. A slow vehicle occupies the length for longer, so more slow vehicles are present at any moment — the sample is weighted toward SLOW vehicles.**

> **The same traffic gives two different averages because the two methods sample it differently.** The point method over-represents the quick; the length method represents the road's actual occupancy.

> **And the harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean**, which is the mathematical statement of the same fact.

**A worked illustration** makes the size of the gap clear:

> Two vehicles at **20 and 80 km/h**:
>
> **V_t = (20 + 80)/2 = 50 km/h**
>
> **V_s = 2/(1/20 + 1/80) = 2/(0.05 + 0.0125) = 2/0.0625 = 32 km/h**

> **A very large difference — and note V_t = 50 here, exactly the question's figure.**

**The relation between them:**

> **V_t = V_s + σ²/V_s**, where σ² is the variance of the space speed distribution.

> **The gap widens as the speeds become more VARIED.** In free-flowing uniform traffic the two nearly coincide; in congested or mixed traffic they diverge sharply.

> **Option (c), V_t = 2 V_s, is not a general relation at all** — it would require one particular variance, and there is no reason for traffic to have it.

**Which one to use, and why it matters:**

> **SPACE mean speed is the correct one for the fundamental traffic relation:**
>
> **q = k × V_s**  (flow = density × space mean speed)

> **Using the time mean speed here gives a wrong answer**, because flow and density are both defined over a length of road, and only the space mean speed is consistent with that.

> **It is also the right speed for travel-time and journey-time studies**, since journey time over a length depends on the harmonic average, not the arithmetic one.

**Where each is used:**

| Speed | Used for |
|---|---|
| **SPOT / time mean speed** | **Speed limit setting, enforcement, geometric design (85th percentile)** |
| **SPACE mean speed** | **Traffic flow theory, travel time, level of service** |

> **The 85th PERCENTILE spot speed sets the speed limit** — the speed below which 85% of drivers travel, on the reasoning that the great majority of drivers choose a reasonable speed and the limit should reflect them rather than the slowest or the fastest.

examTip.trick: **A point sample is biased toward FAST vehicles** (they pass more often); **a length sample toward SLOW ones** (they occupy the road longer). Hence V_s ≤ V_t, always.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is not a general relation.** The true link is V_t = V_s + σ²/V_s — the gap depends on the **variance**, and a factor of exactly 2 would need one particular value.
examTip.mnemonic: **Space mean speed is the one in q = k·V_s** — flow and density are both defined over a length, so only the harmonic (space) average is consistent. Time mean speed sets **speed limits (85th percentile)**.

questions.stem: The distribution factor is:
options: Ratio of stiffness of member to member
Ratio of stiffness of the near joint to the far joint
Ratio of stiffness of the member to the joint stiffness (sum of member stiffnesses)
Ratio of stiffness of the joint to the member
questions.solution:
**The ratio of a member's stiffness to the total stiffness of all members meeting at the joint.**

> The source states it: **the DF for a member at a joint is the ratio of the stiffness (or relative stiffness) of the member to the TOTAL stiffness of all the members meeting at that joint.**
>
> **DF = Member stiffness ÷ Joint stiffness**, where **Joint stiffness = Σ Member stiffnesses**

**What it means physically:**

> **When a moment is applied at a joint, the members meeting there share it in proportion to their STIFFNESS.**

> **The stiffer member takes the larger share** — for the sound reason that all members at a rigid joint must rotate by the **same amount**, and the moment each carries is its stiffness times that common rotation.

> **Equal rotation, unequal moment — proportioned by stiffness.** That is the whole of the distribution factor.

**The two checks that catch errors immediately:**

> **1. ΣDF at any joint = 1.** The shares must account for the whole moment; if they do not sum to one, the stiffnesses have been mis-tabulated.
>
> **2. DF = 0 at a FIXED support; DF = 1 at a HINGED end.**

> **A fixed support is infinitely stiff, so it absorbs everything and passes nothing on — DF = 0.** A hinged end has no other member to share with, so it takes the whole — **DF = 1.**

> **Those two boundary values are where most moment-distribution errors originate**, and checking them costs nothing.

**Member stiffness values:**

| Far end | **Stiffness** |
|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** |
| **HINGED / pinned** | **3EI/L** |
| **Free** | **0** |
| Guided roller | EI/L |

> **Note the 3EI/L for a hinged far end** — using 4EI/L there is the standard error. **The modified stiffness is lower because the far end can rotate**, offering less resistance.

> **And using the 3EI/L modification also means the far end needs no carry-over**, which shortens the calculation considerably.

**The CARRY-OVER factor**, which completes the method:

> **When a moment M is applied at one end, a moment of ½M develops at the far end IF that end is FIXED.**

> **Carry-over factor = ½ to a fixed end, and ZERO to a hinged end.**

**The moment distribution (Hardy Cross) procedure:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Compute **FIXED END MOMENTS** with all joints locked |
| **2** | Compute **stiffnesses and distribution factors** |
| **3** | **Release** a joint — distribute the unbalanced moment by DF |
| **4** | **CARRY OVER half** to each far fixed end |
| **5** | **Repeat** until the unbalanced moments are negligible |
| **6** | **Sum each column** for the final moments |

> **It is an ITERATIVE method that converges** — which is exactly what made it valuable before computers, since it needs no simultaneous equations at all.

> **Hardy Cross's insight was to solve a set of simultaneous equations by successive physical approximation**, locking and releasing joints one at a time. **The same idea underlies the Hardy Cross method for pipe networks**, and for the same reason.

**The standard fixed end moments** that feed step 1: **wL²/12** for a UDL, **WL/8** for a central point load, and **Wab²/L², Wa²b/L²** for a general point load.

examTip.trick: **All members at a rigid joint rotate by the SAME amount**, so each carries stiffness × that rotation — the moment splits in proportion to stiffness. That is the distribution factor entire.
examTip.trap: **Far end HINGED gives 3EI/L, not 4EI/L.** Using 4 there is the standard error — and the 3EI/L modification also means **no carry-over** to that end.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two free checks: ΣDF = 1 at every joint; DF = 0 at a FIXED support and 1 at a HINGED end.** Most moment-distribution errors show up there first.

questions.stem: For steady, incompressible two-dimensional flow, the continuity equation is:
questions.solution:
**∂u/∂x + ∂v/∂y = 0.**

**Reading the two qualifiers straight off the stem:**

| Qualifier | What it removes |
|---|---|
| **TWO-DIMENSIONAL** | **Drops the z term — no ∂w/∂z** |
| **INCOMPRESSIBLE** | **Drops ρ — density is constant and divides out** |
| **STEADY** | Removes ∂ρ/∂t, already absent once ρ is constant |

> **Each option fails on exactly one of these**, which makes the question a clean test of reading rather than recall:

| Option | Fault |
|---|---|
| **(a)** | **THREE-dimensional** — correct in itself, but not 2-D |
| **(b)** | **Retains ρ** — the compressible form |
| **(c)** | **Not a continuity equation at all** — a nonsense arrangement of terms |
| **(d)** | **✓ 2-D, incompressible** |

> **Option (a) is the most tempting, because it is a CORRECT equation** — just for a different case. **Match the equation to the stated conditions, not to what looks familiar.**

**What continuity expresses:**

> **CONSERVATION OF MASS. What flows into a control volume must flow out, if nothing accumulates inside.**

> **The general form is ∂ρ/∂t + ∇·(ρV) = 0.** Setting ρ constant makes it **∇·V = 0** — the velocity field is **divergence-free**.

> **"Divergence-free" is the compact statement: an incompressible flow can neither create nor destroy volume at any point.**

**For a stream tube this reduces to the familiar form:**

> **A₁V₁ = A₂V₂ = Q = constant**

> **Which is why a narrowing pipe speeds the flow up** — and it is worth noticing that this everyday result is the same equation as the partial differential form, integrated across the section.

**When is water NOT incompressible?**

> **Almost never in ordinary hydraulics** — water's bulk modulus is **2.07 GPa**, so a 1000 kPa pressure rise compresses it by about **0.05%.**

> **But WATER HAMMER depends entirely on that compressibility.** If water were truly incompressible, stopping a flow instantly would produce an infinite pressure.

> **So the assumption that simplifies everything must be abandoned for the one problem where it matters most** — and the wave speed **C = √(K/ρ) ≈ 1440 m/s** comes directly from the property being assumed away.

**The companion concepts in 2-D flow:**

| Function | Defined by | Exists when |
|---|---|---|
| **STREAM function ψ** | **u = ∂ψ/∂y, v = −∂ψ/∂x** | **Flow is CONTINUOUS (2-D)** — rotational or not |
| **VELOCITY POTENTIAL φ** | **u = −∂φ/∂x, v = −∂φ/∂y** | **Flow is IRROTATIONAL** |

> **The stream function exists for any 2-D continuous flow; the velocity potential only for an irrotational one.** That asymmetry is the point most often missed.

> **Substituting the stream function into the continuity equation satisfies it identically** — which is precisely why ψ is useful: it builds mass conservation into the formulation.

> **And substituting the velocity potential into continuity gives LAPLACE's equation, ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂y² = 0** — the governing equation of potential flow, and of seepage beneath hydraulic structures.

> **Lines of constant ψ and constant φ intersect at RIGHT ANGLES, forming the FLOW NET** — which is how seepage quantities and uplift pressures under a dam are computed.

examTip.trick: **Read the two qualifiers off the stem.** "Two-dimensional" drops the ∂w/∂z term; "incompressible" drops ρ. Each wrong option fails on exactly one of them.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is a CORRECT equation — for 3-D flow.** Match the equation to the stated conditions, not to whichever form looks most familiar.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stream function ψ exists for any 2-D continuous flow; velocity potential φ only for IRROTATIONAL flow.** Substituting φ into continuity gives **Laplace's equation** — the basis of the flow net.

questions.stem: The wheel load is transferred by the:
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — every layer participates in transferring the load.

> The source's own figure sets out the whole structure: **surface course (25–50 mm), binder course (50–100 mm), base course (100–300 mm), sub-base course (100–300 mm) and compacted subgrade (150–300 mm)**, with prime, tack and seal coats between them.

**How a flexible pavement carries load:**

> **The load spreads downward through the layers in a widening cone, roughly at 45°, by GRAIN-TO-GRAIN contact.**

> **Each layer distributes the load over a larger area than the one above, so the STRESS DIMINISHES WITH DEPTH** until the subgrade can carry what reaches it.

> **No single layer carries the load** — which is exactly why the answer is all of them. **A flexible pavement is a system, not a slab.**

**What each layer contributes:**

| Layer | Function |
|---|---|
| **Surface (wearing) course** | **Resists abrasion, provides skid resistance, and SEALS OUT WATER** |
| **Binder course** | Transitional; carries part of the load |
| **Base course** | **The principal load-spreading layer** |
| **Sub-base** | Further spreading; **DRAINAGE and separation from the subgrade** |
| **Subgrade** | Receives what remains and provides the ultimate support |

> **Material quality DECREASES with depth, because stress decreases with depth.** The expensive bituminous material goes where the stress is highest and no deeper.

> **That is the economic logic of the entire layered system**, and it is why a pavement is built in layers at all rather than as one thick slab of good material.

**The three coats in the source's figure, which are constantly confused:**

| Coat | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **PRIME coat** | **On a GRANULAR base**, to bond it to the bituminous layer above and plug its surface voids |
| **TACK coat** | **Between two BITUMINOUS layers**, to bond them together |
| **SEAL coat** | **On top of the surface**, to waterproof it and improve skid resistance |

> **The discriminator is what lies beneath: PRIME goes on granular material, TACK goes on bitumen.** Applying the wrong one gives a poor bond and the layers separate under traffic.

**The contrast with a RIGID pavement makes the point sharper:**

| | **FLEXIBLE** | **RIGID** |
|---|---|---|
| **Load transfer** | **Grain-to-grain, layer by layer** | **SLAB ACTION — bending as a plate** |
| **Design parameter** | **CBR of the subgrade** | **Flexural strength of the concrete** |
| **Depends on subgrade?** | **CRITICALLY** | Much less — the slab bridges weak spots |
| Failure | **Rutting, fatigue cracking** | Corner and edge cracking |

> **A rigid pavement does NOT transfer load through its layers** — it bridges over them, which is why concrete is chosen where the subgrade is poor or variable.

**And the design law worth carrying:**

> **IRC 37 designs on cumulative standard axles, with the standard axle at 80 kN and damage rising as the FOURTH POWER of axle load.**

> **One axle at twice the standard load does SIXTEEN times the damage.** A handful of overloaded trucks can consume more pavement life than all the cars using the road — which is why axle-load control matters more to pavement life than traffic volume does.

**And the factor that actually kills pavements in Nepal:** **DRAINAGE.** Water weakens the subgrade (the CBR test is deliberately run on a **4-day soaked** specimen), strips bitumen from aggregate, and pumps fines under repeated loading. **Most premature failures trace to drainage rather than to inadequate thickness.**

examTip.trick: **A flexible pavement is a SYSTEM, not a slab.** The load spreads in a widening ~45° cone through every layer, so no single one carries it — which is why "all of the above" is right.
examTip.trap: **PRIME coat goes on a GRANULAR base; TACK coat goes between two BITUMINOUS layers.** The discriminator is what lies beneath. Getting it wrong means the layers separate under traffic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Material quality falls with depth because stress falls with depth** — the economic logic of layering. And the **FOURTH POWER law**: double the axle load, sixteen times the damage.

questions.stem: The objective of seasoning of timber is:
options: To increase the structural stability of timber
To increase the resistance to shrinkage, cracking, warping and even decay
questions.solution:
**All of the above.**

> The source states it: **seasoning of timber is the process of reducing the moisture content of timber so as to enhance its engineering properties. The objectives are: to reduce moisture content; to increase the structural stability of timber; and to increase the resistance to shrinkage, cracking, warping and even decay.**

**Why the three are one chain, not three separate benefits:**

> **Reducing the moisture content is the ACTION; the other two are its CONSEQUENCES.**

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| **Moisture reduced** | **Timber shrinks NOW, in the yard, not later in the structure** |
| **Dimensions become stable** | **Structural stability** |
| **Strength rises** as moisture falls | Below fibre saturation, strength increases markedly |
| **Fungi cannot survive below ~20% MC** | **Resistance to DECAY** |

> **So option (d) is not a lazy catch-all — the three statements are the beginning, middle and end of one process.**

**The FIBRE SATURATION POINT is the idea that organises the whole topic:**

> **At about 25–30% moisture content, all free water in the cell cavities has gone and only bound water remains in the cell walls.**

| Above FSP | Below FSP |
|---|---|
| **No shrinkage** | **Shrinkage begins** |
| **No strength change** | **Strength RISES as it dries** |

> **Nothing happens dimensionally until the timber dries past the fibre saturation point** — and everything happens after it. **That single threshold explains why green timber must be seasoned before use and why it is pointless to season it only partly.**

**Target moisture contents:**

| Use | Moisture content |
|---|---|
| **Green (freshly felled)** | **Above 50%, often 100%+** |
| **Structural timber** | **12 – 18%** |
| **Interior joinery, furniture** | **8 – 12%** |
| Fungal attack possible | **Above ~20%** |

> **The governing rule is to season timber to roughly the moisture content it will LIVE at.** Timber that is drier or wetter than its surroundings will move after installation — shrinking, cupping and opening joints.

> **That is the practical reason seasoning matters more than any strength consideration**: a well-made joint in unseasoned timber will open, however strong the material.

**Methods:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **NATURAL (air) seasoning** | **Cheap but SLOW — 2 to 12 months.** Stacked on skids with air gaps, under cover, ends coated |
| **KILN seasoning** | **Fast (days), controlled and more uniform**; costs energy and needs skill |
| Water seasoning | Sap displaced by immersion, then air dried |
| Chemical / boiling | Specialised |

> **Kiln seasoning is not merely faster — it is more UNIFORM**, and it can reach lower moisture contents than air drying in a humid climate ever will. **In Nepal's monsoon air, natural seasoning cannot get below about 15–18%.**

**And why seasoning must not be rushed:**

> **Drying the surface much faster than the interior sets up internal stresses**, producing:

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Case hardening** | Surface dries and sets while the core is still wet |
| **Honeycombing** | Internal splitting from those stresses |
| **Checks and end splits** | Ends dry fastest — hence end-coating |
| **Warping (bow, cup, twist)** | Uneven drying or poor stacking |

> **Which is why the stack matters as much as the schedule**: even spacing, level bearers, weight on top, and shelter from sun and rain.

**Anisotropy governs the shrinkage itself:** timber shrinks about **0.1% longitudinally, 4% radially and 8% tangentially** — so **tangential shrinkage is roughly twice radial**, and that difference is exactly what makes a board **CUP** away from the heart as it dries.

examTip.trick: **The three statements are one chain**: reducing moisture is the action; stability and decay resistance are its consequences. Not a lazy catch-all.
examTip.trap: **Nothing happens until timber dries past the FIBRE SATURATION POINT (~25–30%)** — above it there is no shrinkage and no strength change; below it, both. That threshold explains the whole topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Season to the moisture content the timber will LIVE at**, or it moves after installation. And **tangential shrinkage is ~2× radial**, which is exactly why boards **cup** away from the heart.

questions.stem: The maximum alkalinity value is at:
questions.solution:
**pH = 14.**

> The source's note: **the pH range is commonly given as zero to 14, but a pH value can be less than 0 for very concentrated strong acids or greater than 14 for very concentrated strong bases.**

**Why 14 and not simply "greater than 7":**

> **The question asks for the MAXIMUM, not for the alkaline range.**

> **Option (d), pH > 7, describes every alkaline solution** — correct as a description of alkalinity, but it names a **range**, not a maximum.

> **pH = 14 is the top of the conventional scale**, and therefore the answer to a question about the maximum value.

> **That distinction — a range versus an extreme — is the whole discrimination**, and it is why (a) and (d) are both defensible-looking while only one answers what was asked.

**The pH scale:**

> **pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]**, and it is **LOGARITHMIC.**

| pH | Character |
|---|---|
| **0 – 7** | **Acidic** |
| **7** | **Neutral** (at 25 °C) |
| **7 – 14** | **Alkaline / basic** |

> **Each unit is a TENFOLD change in hydrogen ion concentration.** pH 5 water is **100 times** more acidic than pH 7 water, not slightly more — a point that is constantly underestimated.

> **And the scale's limits come from water's own dissociation: K_w = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C**, so pH + pOH = 14. **The 14 is not arbitrary; it is the negative logarithm of water's ion product.**

> **Which is also why the source is right that values outside 0–14 are possible** — the scale's ends are conventional limits for dilute solutions, not physical barriers.

**But note the distinction between pH and ALKALINITY, which the question's wording invites:**

| | **pH** | **ALKALINITY** |
|---|---|---|
