| Measures | **Hydrogen ion CONCENTRATION** | **CAPACITY to NEUTRALISE ACID** |
| Units | Dimensionless (log scale) | **mg/l as CaCO₃** |
| Due to | Free H⁺ | **Bicarbonates, carbonates, hydroxides** |

> **They are not the same thing.** A water can have a high pH and low alkalinity (a trace of strong base), or a near-neutral pH and high alkalinity (plenty of bicarbonate).

> **ALKALINITY IS BUFFERING CAPACITY** — the ability to resist a change in pH when acid is added. **It is the more useful measurement in water treatment**, because it predicts how the water will behave when a chemical is dosed.

> **Which is why coagulation with alum requires sufficient alkalinity**: alum consumes it, and if there is not enough, the pH crashes and the floc will not form. **Lime or soda ash is then added to supply it.**

**Drinking water standards (NDWQS 2062):**

| Parameter | Limit |
|---|---|
| **pH** | **6.5 – 8.5** |
| **Total alkalinity** | **≤ 500 mg/l as CaCO₃** |
| Total hardness | 500 mg/l |
| Turbidity | 5 NTU |

> **The pH limit is narrow for good reasons at both ends: low pH is CORROSIVE to pipes and dissolves metals into the supply; high pH causes SCALING, impairs disinfection and gives a bitter taste.**

> **And the disinfection point is the operationally important one: HOCl is about 80 times more effective than OCl⁻, and rising pH shifts the balance toward the weak form** — so an alkaline water needs far more chlorine for the same kill.

examTip.trick: **The question asks for the MAXIMUM, not the alkaline range.** pH > 7 describes every alkaline solution; **pH = 14** is the top of the scale, which is what was asked.
examTip.trap: **pH and ALKALINITY are different quantities.** pH measures H⁺ concentration; alkalinity measures the **capacity to neutralise acid** (mg/l as CaCO₃). A water can be high in one and low in the other.
examTip.mnemonic: **pH + pOH = 14 because K_w = 10⁻¹⁴** — the 14 is water's own ion product, not a convention. And **alum consumes alkalinity**: too little and the pH crashes and no floc forms.

questions.stem: If the shear force is zero, then the bending moment will be:
questions.solution:
**Either maximum or minimum.**

> The source is careful about exactly this: **dM/dx = V. The bending moment is maximum OR MINIMUM where the shear force is zero. Zero shear force will not produce a maximum bending moment always.**

**The calculus is decisive:**

> **V = dM/dx**, so **V = 0 means dM/dx = 0** — a **STATIONARY POINT** of the moment diagram.

> **A stationary point may be a maximum, a minimum, or a point of inflexion. The first derivative alone cannot tell you which.**

> **Which one it is depends on the SECOND derivative — that is, on the sign of the load:**

| SFD crosses zero | Moment |
|---|---|
| **From +ve to −ve** | **MAXIMUM** |
| **From −ve to +ve** | **MINIMUM** |

> **The source states both cases explicitly**, and that is precisely why option (a) alone is wrong.

**When is it a maximum, and when a minimum?**

> **On a simple span under downward load, zero shear gives the maximum sagging moment** — which is the case everybody meets first, and the reason "maximum" feels like the whole answer.

> **But on a CONTINUOUS beam the shear crosses zero in every span, and at some of those crossings the moment is a local MINIMUM** — a hogging peak in one sense is a minimum in the signed convention.

> **On an OVERHANGING beam, the shear passes through zero in the back span while the governing moment is the hogging one over the support.**

> **So a beam can have several points of zero shear, and they are not all maxima.**

**Two further cautions the source raises:**

> **1. At a CONCENTRATED LOAD the shear jumps discontinuously**, so dM/dx is **undefined** there. **The moment can be a maximum at a point where the shear never equals zero at all** — it simply changes sign by jumping across it.

> **That is the case for a simply supported beam with a single point load: the maximum moment is under the load, where the SFD jumps from +R₁ to −R₂ without passing through zero as a value.**

> **2. The relation V = dM/dx holds only where the load is distributed or absent.** It cannot be applied across a discontinuity.

**The governing relations, as a set:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change** | **JUMPS by M** |
| **UDL w** | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** |
| **No load** | **Constant** | **Linear** |

> **And the change in moment between two sections equals the AREA of the shear diagram between them** — the fastest hand method there is, and the integral form of the same relation.

**A useful corollary:** **where the moment is constant, the shear is ZERO** — the condition called **PURE BENDING**, and exactly the state assumed in deriving σ = My/I. It is created deliberately in the middle third of a **four-point bending test**.

examTip.trick: **V = dM/dx = 0 marks a STATIONARY point** — maximum, minimum or inflexion. The first derivative cannot say which; the sign change of the SFD does (+→− gives a max, −→+ a min).
examTip.trap: **At a CONCENTRATED LOAD the shear JUMPS** and dM/dx is undefined — so a simply supported beam with one point load has its maximum moment where the shear never *equals* zero at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Change in moment = AREA of the shear diagram** — the fastest hand method, and the integral form of the same relation. And **constant moment ⇒ zero shear = PURE BENDING**.

questions.stem: What is the formula to calculate wind pressure?
questions.solution:
**P_z = 0.6 V_z².**

> The source states it: **P_z = 0.6 × V_z², where V_z is the design wind speed in m/s at height z, and P_z is the wind pressure in N/m² at height z.**

**Where the 0.6 comes from — it is derived, not arbitrary:**

> **Dynamic (stagnation) pressure = ½ ρ V²**
>
> **With air density ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³: ½ × 1.2 = 0.6** ✓

> **So the coefficient is simply half the density of air**, and it can be reconstructed whenever it is forgotten.

> **The units follow directly: kg/m³ × (m/s)² = kg/(m·s²) = N/m²** ✓

**Why the exponent must be 2:**

> **Pressure comes from bringing moving air to rest — a kinetic energy term, so it goes as VELOCITY SQUARED.**

> **A cube would be dimensionally wrong**, and that check disposes of options (c) and (d) without any recall.

> **The physical consequence of the square is worth holding on to: DOUBLING the wind speed QUADRUPLES the pressure.** A 200 km/h cyclone exerts four times the pressure of a 100 km/h gale, not twice — which is why extreme wind events are so disproportionately destructive.

**How the design wind speed is built up (IS 875 Part 3 / NBC 104):**

> **V_z = V_b × k₁ × k₂ × k₃ (× k₄)**

| Factor | Accounts for |
|---|---|
| **V_b** | **Basic wind speed** from the wind map (3-second gust, 10 m height, open terrain) |
| **k₁** | **Risk / return period** — importance of the structure |
| **k₂** | **Terrain, height and structure size** |
| **k₃** | **TOPOGRAPHY** — hills, ridges, escarpments |
| k₄ | Importance for cyclonic regions |

> **k₃ is the factor that matters most in Nepal.** Wind **accelerates over a ridge or up a hill slope**, and a building on a hilltop can experience substantially higher speeds than the same building on the plain.

> **Given how much construction sits on ridges and spurs here, ignoring topography is a real omission**, not a refinement.

**And the pressure is not simply applied to the building:**

> **F = (C_pe − C_pi) × A × P_z**

| Coefficient | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C_pe** | **External pressure coefficient** — varies over the surface |
| **C_pi** | **INTERNAL pressure coefficient** — depends on openings |

> **The internal pressure is the one that causes the damage most often seen.** With a large opening on the windward side — a door left open, a window broken by debris — **internal pressure builds up and acts OUTWARD on the roof and the other walls.**

> **It then ADDS to the external SUCTION on the leeward roof**, and the roof lifts off.

> **This is why light roofs fail in storms**: the critical load case is **UPLIFT**, not downward pressure, and it is why **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** — the combination with dead load factored DOWN — is the one that governs light structures.

> **Wind on a low-pitch roof produces SUCTION on both slopes**, so the roof is being pulled off rather than pushed down, and the anchorage to the walls is what must be designed.

examTip.trick: **0.6 = ½ρ with ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³ for air** — the coefficient is half the density, so it can always be rebuilt. And pressure is a kinetic term, so the exponent is **2**.
examTip.trap: **Options (c) and (d) use V³, which is dimensionally wrong** — that check kills half the options without recall. And remember **doubling the wind speed QUADRUPLES the pressure**.
examTip.mnemonic: **INTERNAL pressure is what lifts roofs off.** A windward opening pressurises the building, that pressure acts outward, and it ADDS to the external suction — which is why **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** governs light roofs.

questions.stem: In the CBR test, comparing the values at 2.5 mm and 5 mm penetration:
options: 2.5 mm normally gives the higher CBR value
5 mm normally gives the higher CBR value
questions.solution:
**2.5 mm normally gives the higher value.**

> The source states the rule and its exception: **generally the CBR value is calculated at 2.5 mm and 5 mm penetration. The CBR value at 2.5 mm penetration will be greater than the CBR value at 5 mm penetration, and in such a case the FORMER is taken as the CBR value. If the CBR for 5 mm exceeds that for 2.5 mm, THE TEST SHOULD BE REPEATED. If the identical result follows, the CBR for 5 mm penetration should be taken for design.**

**Why 2.5 mm normally gives more:**

> **CBR is the ratio of the load carried by the test soil to that carried by a standard crushed stone, at the same penetration, expressed as a percentage.**

| Penetration | **Standard load** |
|---|---|
| **2.5 mm** | **1370 kg (13.44 kN)** |
| **5.0 mm** | **2055 kg (20.55 kN)** |

> **The soil's load–penetration curve normally FLATTENS as penetration increases**, while the standard values rise in proportion — so the ratio falls.

> **The 2.5 mm ratio is therefore the higher one for a normally behaving soil**, and that is what makes it the usual answer.

**And the exception is genuinely informative:**

> **If the 5 mm value is higher, the load–penetration curve has an initial CONCAVE-UPWARD portion — a sign of a surface irregularity or a poorly prepared top surface, not of the soil's real strength.**

> **Hence the instruction to REPEAT the test.** If the same result comes back, the behaviour is real and the 5 mm value is taken.

> **This is one of the few places where a code tells the engineer to retest rather than to accept a number**, which is why it is worth remembering.

**The test conditions, which give the result its meaning:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Plunger diameter** | **50 mm** |
| **Rate of penetration** | **1.25 mm/min** |
| **Soaking period** | **4 DAYS (96 hours)** |
| **Surcharge** | Weights simulating the pavement above |
| Mould | 150 mm diameter |

> **The 4-day SOAKING is the essential feature.** The test measures strength in the **worst likely condition** — a saturated subgrade after prolonged rain — not in the condition the soil happens to be in on the day of testing.

> **In Nepal's monsoon climate that is not a conservatism but a realism**, and the unsoaked value would be dangerously optimistic.

> **The SURCHARGE weights matter too**: they reproduce the confining effect of the pavement layers above, without which the soil would simply heave around the plunger.

**Typical CBR values:**

| Material | CBR |
|---|---|
| **Poor subgrade (soft clay)** | **2 – 5%** |
| **Fair subgrade** | 5 – 10% |
| **Good subgrade** | 10 – 20% |
| **Sub-base** | 20 – 30% |
| **Base course** | **> 80%** |

> **The design relationship is steep**: halving the CBR can require **50% more pavement thickness**, which is why improving a weak subgrade — by replacement, stabilisation or a capping layer — is often cheaper than paving over it.

**And where CBR belongs:**

> **It is the design parameter for FLEXIBLE pavements only** (IRC 37). **A rigid pavement is designed on the FLEXURAL STRENGTH of the concrete** and the subgrade's **modulus of reaction k**, because the slab bridges the subgrade rather than transmitting to it.

verification.notes: The source's options say "penetration rate", which is loose wording — the rate of penetration is 1.25 mm/min for both readings. The source's own explanation makes the intent explicit: it is the CBR VALUE at 2.5 mm that normally exceeds that at 5 mm. The options have been reworded to say "CBR value", which is what the item actually tests, and the keyed letter (a) is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **The soil's load–penetration curve FLATTENS while the standard loads rise in proportion** (1370 kg at 2.5 mm, 2055 kg at 5 mm), so the ratio falls — and the 2.5 mm value is the higher one.
examTip.trap: **If 5 mm gives more, the code says REPEAT the test** — an initial concave-upward curve usually means a poorly prepared surface, not real strength. Only if it repeats is the 5 mm value used.
examTip.mnemonic: **The 4-day SOAK is the point of the test** — strength in the worst likely condition, not on the day of testing. And CBR is for **flexible** pavements; rigid ones use flexural strength and k.

questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a solid hemisphere lies on the central radius at a distance from the plane base of:
questions.solution:
**3r/8 from the plane base.**

> The source's figure marks it directly: **the centroid C of a solid hemisphere lies on the central radius at 3R/8 above the plane base.**

**A sanity check disposes of half the options instantly:**

> **The centroid must lie INSIDE the body**, so its distance from the base must be **less than r** (the hemisphere's height).

| Option | Value | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) 3r/2** | **1.5 r** | **OUTSIDE the body** ✗ |
| (b) 3r/4 | 0.75 r | Inside, but too high |
| (c) 3r/5 | 0.6 r | Inside, but too high |
| **(d) 3r/8** | **0.375 r** | **✓** |

> **Option (a) is impossible without any calculation**, and the remaining choice is settled by a second observation:

> **A hemisphere is WIDEST AT ITS BASE and tapers to a point at the top**, so most of its volume lies in the lower half. **The centroid must therefore sit BELOW the mid-height (0.5 r).**

> **Only 3r/8 = 0.375 r satisfies that**, which answers the question by reasoning alone.

**Standard centroids worth carrying:**

| Solid | Centroid from the base |
|---|---|
| **Solid HEMISPHERE** | **3r/8** |
| **Hemispherical SHELL** | **r/2** |
| **Solid CONE** | **h/4** |
| **Conical shell** | **h/3** |
| **Solid pyramid** | **h/4** |
| Semicircular **area** (lamina) | **4r/3π** |
| Semicircular **arc** | 2r/π |

> **Note the pattern: a SHELL's centroid is always HIGHER than the corresponding SOLID's** — r/2 against 3r/8, and h/3 against h/4.

> **The reason is that a solid concentrates its volume near the wide base, while a shell distributes its material evenly over the surface**, which reaches higher.

> **And the solid cone and solid pyramid share h/4** because the derivation depends only on the linear taper of the cross-section, not on its shape.

**The 4r/3π for a semicircular lamina** is worth separating from these:

> **It is an AREA, not a volume**, and it appears constantly in **section property** calculations — for a semicircular flange, a half-round bar, or the compression zone of a circular section.

**Where centroids matter in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Neutral axis of a section** | **Passes through the centroid** in pure bending |
| **Section properties** | I about the centroid; parallel axis theorem |
| **Stability of dams and walls** | Line of action of self-weight |
| **Hydrostatic force** | Acts at the **centre of pressure**, below the centroid |
| **Buoyancy** | Acts at the **centre of buoyancy** — the centroid of the displaced volume |

> **The last two are worth distinguishing carefully.** For a submerged plane surface, **the centre of pressure is always BELOW the centroid**, by **I_G/(Ay̅)** — because the pressure increases with depth, weighting the resultant downward.

> **And a floating body's stability depends on the METACENTRE being above the centre of gravity**, with **GM = I/V − BG** — a calculation that begins with exactly the kind of centroid this question asks for.

examTip.trick: **Two checks answer it without calculation**: the centroid must lie inside the body (killing 3r/2), and a hemisphere is widest at its base so the centroid sits **below mid-height** (0.5r) — only 3r/8 does.
examTip.trap: **A SHELL's centroid is always higher than the corresponding SOLID's** — r/2 vs 3r/8, h/3 vs h/4. The solid concentrates volume near the wide base; the shell spreads material up the surface.
examTip.mnemonic: **Solid cone and solid pyramid share h/4** — the derivation depends only on the linear taper, not the cross-section's shape. And the semicircular **lamina** is 4r/3π, an area not a volume.

questions.stem: The removal of impurities from an ore is known as:
questions.solution:
**Concentration of the ore.**

> The source explains it: **ores are minerals from which metals can be commercially extracted at low cost and with minimum effort. The REMOVAL OF THE IMPURITIES from the ore is called CONCENTRATION OF ORE — it means increasing the concentration of the minerals. This can be done by hydraulic washing, magnetic separation, froth flotation and leaching.**

**Why the other three are wrong** — and each is wrong in a different way:

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **CRUSHING and GRINDING** | **A PRIOR step** — reduces the ore to a size at which the mineral and the impurity can be separated, but **removes nothing** |
| **MINERALS** | **What is OBTAINED after purification** — the product, not the process |
| **GANGUE** | **The IMPURITY ITSELF** — the unwanted material mixed with the mineral |

> **The source names each of these precisely**, and the set is a good example of a question testing whether the candidate can tell a **process** from a **material** from a **product**.

> **GANGUE is the most interesting distractor**: it is exactly the thing being removed, so it appears in the definition — but it is the object of the operation, not its name.

**The concentration methods, and what each exploits:**

| Method | Property used |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic washing (gravity separation)** | **DENSITY difference** — heavier ore settles, lighter gangue washes away |
| **Magnetic separation** | **MAGNETIC susceptibility** — used for iron ores |
| **FROTH FLOTATION** | **Differential WETTABILITY** — the mineral attaches to air bubbles and floats |
| **Leaching** | **Chemical SOLUBILITY** in a suitable reagent |

> **Each method exploits a physical or chemical difference between the mineral and the gangue**, which is the organising idea: concentration is always separation by some property in which the two differ.

> **Froth flotation is the most widely used of the four** in modern practice, because wettability can be manipulated with reagents even where density and magnetism cannot distinguish the two.

**The full extraction sequence**, for context:

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **1. Crushing and grinding** | **Liberate** the mineral from the gangue |
| **2. CONCENTRATION** | **Remove the gangue** ← this question |
| **3. Roasting / calcination** | Convert to oxide |
| **4. Reduction (smelting)** | **Obtain the metal** |
| **5. Refining** | Purify the metal |

> **Note that crushing must come FIRST**: the mineral and gangue are physically intergrown in the rock, and no separation is possible until the particles are small enough to be individually mineral or individually gangue.

> **That is why crushing is a prerequisite for concentration rather than a form of it.**

**Why this matters to a civil engineer:**

> **It explains where structural materials come from and why they cost what they do.**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Iron and steel** | From iron ore — magnetic separation, then blast furnace reduction |
| **Aluminium** | **From bauxite; extremely energy-intensive**, which is why it costs far more than steel per tonne |
| **Cement** | Limestone and clay, calcined at ~1450 °C |
| Copper, zinc | Froth flotation is standard |

> **Aluminium's price is essentially the price of electricity**, because the reduction step is electrolytic and cannot be done by carbon reduction as iron's can. **That single fact explains most of the material's role in construction** — used where lightness and corrosion resistance justify the cost, and rarely as primary structure.

examTip.trick: **Tell the PROCESS from the MATERIAL from the PRODUCT.** Concentration is the process; gangue is the impurity being removed; minerals are the product; crushing is a prior step that removes nothing.
examTip.trap: **GANGUE is exactly what is being removed**, so it appears in the definition — but it is the object of the operation, not its name. That proximity is what makes it convincing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every concentration method exploits a DIFFERENCE**: density (washing), magnetism, wettability (froth flotation), solubility (leaching). And **crushing must come first** — nothing separates until the particles are liberated.

questions.stem: What is the function of the Nepal Engineering Council?
options: To make the profession effective by mobilizing it in a more systematic and scientific manner and also to register the engineers as per their qualifications
To make the engineering profession effective by mobilizing it in a more systematic and scientific manner and also to register the engineers as per their qualifications
To punish the engineering profession, mobilizing it in a more systematic and scientific manner and also to register the engineers as per their qualifications
questions.solution:
**Option (b)** — to make the **engineering** profession effective by mobilizing it in a more systematic and scientific manner, and to register engineers according to their qualifications.

> The source states the function in exactly these words.

**This is a question about reading, not about knowledge** — the three statements are nearly identical, and the differences are single words:

| Option | Difference |
|---|---|
| (a) | Says **"the profession"** — omits **"engineering"**, so it is unspecific |
| **(b)** | **Complete and correct** ✓ |
| (c) | Says **"to PUNISH the engineering profession"** — a plainly wrong purpose |
| (d) | Cannot be right once (c) is wrong |

> **Option (c) fails on substance, not wording.** A regulator's purpose is to **develop and safeguard** a profession, not to punish it — discipline is a *power* it holds in service of that purpose, never the purpose itself.

> **That distinction is worth stating plainly**, because it is what separates a professional council from an enforcement agency: the Council exists to make good practice possible, and removes a license only when someone puts the public at risk.

> **And once (c) is wrong, (d) falls automatically.** In a set of near-identical options, **finding the one clearly false statement collapses "all of the above" at once** — usually faster than comparing the rest word by word.

**What the Council actually does:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTER engineers** and issue **license** certificates | The core statutory function |
| **Recognise engineering qualifications** | Which degrees qualify |
| **Conduct the licensing examination** | The route to registration |
| **Prescribe the CODE OF ETHICS** | Professional conduct |
| **Disciplinary action** | Suspension, removal from the register |
| Classify categories of engineer | By discipline and level |
| **Report to the Government of Nepal** | Its line of accountability |

> **"Register engineers as per their qualifications" is the phrase carrying the most weight.** Registration is **by category and level** — the Council does not merely admit or refuse, it defines **what each engineer is licensed to do.**

> **That is what makes the COMPETENCE duty enforceable**: an engineer practising outside their registered category is in breach of the Act, not merely of good judgement.

**Why engineering is regulated at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **PUBLIC SAFETY** | Failures kill people who never chose the risk |
| **Information asymmetry** | **The client cannot judge the quality of the work** |
| **Irreversibility** | A defective structure may not reveal itself for years |

> **The information asymmetry is the classic justification.** A client commissioning a building cannot inspect the design or check the calculations — **licensing substitutes an institutional guarantee for a judgement the client cannot make.**

**The principal duties in the code of conduct:** **competence** (practise only within your field and level), **public safety paramount** (above the client's interest and your own), **integrity**, **no conflict of interest**, **confidentiality**, and **no supplanting** an engineer already engaged.

> **"Public safety paramount" is the clause that makes engineering a profession rather than a trade** — it requires refusing an instruction or reporting a danger even at commercial cost.

examTip.trick: **Find the one clearly FALSE option and "all of the above" collapses with it.** Option (c) says "to PUNISH the engineering profession" — that alone settles the question without comparing the rest word by word.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) differ by a single word** — (a) omits "engineering". In near-identical option sets, the difference is always one word, and it is worth finding before choosing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Registration is BY CATEGORY AND LEVEL**, which is what makes the COMPETENCE duty enforceable — practising outside your registered category breaches the Act, not merely good judgement.

questions.stem: Gypsum reacts with which element of cement to reduce its flash setting?
questions.solution:
**C₃A — tricalcium aluminate.**

> The source explains it: **gypsum acts as a RETARDER, slowing the setting time of cement. When gypsum is added it reacts with the TRI-CALCIUM ALUMINATE (C₃A) to form ETTRINGITE, which then acts as a crystal growth inhibitor for the tri-calcium silicate (C₃S).**

**Why C₃A must be retarded:**

> **C₃A hydrates FASTEST of the four compounds and releases the MOST heat.**

> **Left alone it would cause a FLASH SET** — the cement stiffening within minutes of contact with water, before it could be placed, compacted or finished. **The concrete would be unusable.**

> **Gypsum (calcium sulphate) reacts with C₃A to form ettringite, which coats the C₃A grains and slows the reaction to a workable rate.**

**How much and why it matters:**

| Quantity | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gypsum content** | **3 – 5%**, INTERGROUND with the clinker |
| **Too little** | **Flash set — unusable** |
| **Too much** | **UNSOUNDNESS — delayed expansion and cracking** |

> **Both errors are serious, and in opposite ways.** Too little makes the cement unusable immediately; **too much makes it dangerous later**, because excess sulphate forms ettringite after the paste has hardened, and that expansion cracks the concrete from within.

> **This is why the SOUNDNESS test (Le Chatelier for free lime, autoclave for magnesia) exists**, and why sulphate content is a specification limit rather than a target.

**The four Bogue compounds:**

| Compound | % | Contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **C₃S (alite)** | **45 – 55** | **EARLY strength (≤ 7 days)**; 500 J/g heat |
| **C₂S (belite)** | **20 – 30** | **LATER strength (> 28 days)**; 260 J/g — half the heat |
| **C₃A (celite)** | **8 – 12** | **FLASH SET; HIGHEST heat (865 J/g); little strength** ← |
| **C₄AF (felite)** | **6 – 10** | **Colour (grey)**; little strength |

> **The two SILICATES give strength; the two ALUMINATES give heat and colour.** That division organises the whole subject.

> **C₃A is the troublemaker of the four**: it produces the most heat, causes flash set, contributes almost nothing to strength, and is **the compound attacked by sulphates.**

**Which is why the cement types are made by adjusting it:**

| Cement | Composition change | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **SULPHATE RESISTING** | **C₃A limited to below 5%** | **Sulphates attack hydrated C₃A, forming expansive ettringite** |
| **LOW HEAT** | **Less C₃S and C₃A, more C₂S** | **Mass concrete — dams — cannot shed its heat** |
| **RAPID HARDENING** | More C₃S, finer grinding | Early strength; more heat |

> **Note the same reaction — ettringite formation — is HELPFUL before setting and DESTRUCTIVE afterwards.** Controlled by gypsum at mixing it gives workable cement; occurring later through sulphate attack it cracks hardened concrete.

> **That is why sulphate-resisting cement works by limiting the reactant** rather than by adding anything: with little C₃A there is little to attack.

**The setting times (IS 269):**

> **Initial set NOT LESS than 30 minutes; final set NOT MORE than 600 minutes (10 hours).**

> **The directions differ deliberately** — the initial set has a **minimum** (time to transport, place and compact) and the final set a **maximum** (so formwork can be struck and work can proceed). **Reversing them is a common slip.**

examTip.trick: **C₃A hydrates fastest and gives the most heat but almost no strength** — it is the troublemaker. Gypsum forms ettringite around it, slowing the set to a workable rate.
examTip.trap: **Too little gypsum gives flash set; too MUCH gives UNSOUNDNESS** — delayed expansion that cracks hardened concrete. Both errors are serious, in opposite directions and at opposite times.
examTip.mnemonic: **The same ettringite reaction is helpful before setting and destructive after.** That is why sulphate-resisting cement simply **limits C₃A below 5%** — with little reactant, there is little to attack.

questions.stem: The area of A0 paper is:
questions.solution:
**1 m².**

> The source gives the whole series: **A0 is 841 × 1189 mm, area 1 m²; A1 594 × 841, 0.5 m²; A2 420 × 594, 0.25 m²; A3 297 × 420, 0.125 m²; A4 210 × 297, 0.0625 m²; A5 148 × 210, 0.03125 m².**

**The ISO A series is built on two rules, and everything follows from them:**

> **1. A0 has an area of exactly ONE SQUARE METRE.**
>
> **2. Every sheet has an aspect ratio of 1 : √2.**

> **Those two conditions fix every dimension in the series.** Solving them: **width × width√2 = 1**, giving **width = 1/⁴√2 = 0.841 m** and **length = 1.189 m** — exactly the A0 dimensions the source lists.

**Why the √2 ratio is the clever part:**

> **Halving a sheet across its longer side gives a sheet of the SAME aspect ratio.**

> **A √2 : 1 sheet halved becomes 1 : √2/2 = 1 : 1/√2 — which is √2 : 1 again.** No other ratio has this property.

> **So a drawing can be enlarged or reduced between any two A sizes with NO change of proportion and no wasted margin** — which is precisely why the system was adopted, and why photocopier reduction settings are marked 71% (= 1/√2) and 141% (= √2).

**The consequence for area:**

> **Each size down HALVES the area**, since each is one sheet folded in two:

| Size | Area |
|---|---|
| **A0** | **1 m²** |
| A1 | 0.5 m² |
| A2 | 0.25 m² |
| A3 | 0.125 m² |
| **A4** | **1/16 m² = 0.0625 m²** |

> **A4 is therefore exactly one sixteenth of a square metre**, and there are **16 A4 sheets in one A0** — a useful check whenever the sizes are in doubt.

**A dimensional check disposes of option (d) instantly:**

> **AREA has units of m², not m³.** **1 m³ is a VOLUME**, which a sheet of paper cannot have as its area — and that eliminates the option without any recall at all.

> **Option (b), 15 m², is absurd on inspection**: a 15 m² sheet would be about 3.5 m square, larger than most drawing offices.

**Drawing sheet conventions** that accompany the sizes:

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Border and title block** | Title block at the **bottom right** |
| **Filing margin** | **Wider on the LEFT (20 mm)** for binding |
| **Standard scales** | 1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 1:200, 1:500, 1:1000 |
| Line types | Continuous thick for visible edges; **dashed for hidden**; chain for centre lines |

> **The scale ladder runs in 1, 2, 5 steps within each decade**, which is why 1:3 and 1:400 are not standard scales even though nothing prevents them arithmetically.

**And the B and C series exist for related reasons:** **B sizes** sit geometrically between A sizes (B0 = 1 m wide), and **C sizes** are used for **envelopes** — a C4 envelope holds an A4 sheet, because C is the geometric mean of A and B.

examTip.trick: **A0 is defined as exactly 1 m² with a 1:√2 ratio** — those two rules fix every dimension in the series. Each size down halves the area, so A4 = 1/16 m².
examTip.trap: **Option (d) says 1 m³ — a VOLUME, not an area.** A dimensional glance eliminates it without any recall. And 15 m² would be a sheet 3.5 m square.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only the √2 ratio survives halving** — which is why enlargement between A sizes needs no reproportioning, and why photocopiers are marked 71% (1/√2) and 141% (√2).

questions.stem: In the Nepali classification of urban roads, arterial roads are called:
questions.solution:
**Path**, according to the classification the source sets out.

> The source gives the four urban categories: **arterial roads (Path), sub-arterial roads (Sadak), collector roads (Marg), local roads (Upa-Marg)** — classified for geometric design purposes by the function of the road and the traffic level.

**The functional hierarchy itself is the durable part:**

| Class | **MOBILITY** | **ACCESSIBILITY** | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ARTERIAL** | **HIGHEST** | **LOWEST** | **Movement across the city** — long trips |
| **SUB-ARTERIAL** | High | Low | Movement between districts |
| **COLLECTOR** | Moderate | Moderate | **Collects traffic from local roads and feeds it to arterials** |
| **LOCAL** | **LOWEST** | **HIGHEST** | **Direct ACCESS to property** |

> **Mobility and accessibility are inversely related, and necessarily so.** Every access point — a junction, a driveway, a shopfront — is a place where vehicles slow, stop and turn, which is exactly what destroys through movement.

> **So no road can maximise both**, and the hierarchy exists to let different roads specialise.

**The COLLECTOR is the one worth understanding**, because its name states its job:

> **It collects traffic from many local roads and delivers it to the arterial system.** Without it, local roads would connect directly to arterials, and the arterial's mobility would be destroyed by the sheer number of junctions.

> **A well-designed network is a TREE**: property → local → collector → sub-arterial → arterial. **Skipping a level is the classic planning failure**, and it is why direct property access onto a highway is so damaging.

**Ribbon development** is that failure in its commonest form:

> **Shops and houses fronting directly onto an arterial road destroy its mobility function while it is still classified as an arterial.** Speeds fall, accidents rise, and the investment in a through route is lost.

> **This is one of the most visible road problems in Nepal**, and it is why **control of the right of way** matters so much — encroachment is cheap to prevent and ruinous to reverse.

**The rural classification** (Nepal Road Standard), which is separate:

| Class | Right of way | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **National highway (NH)** | **50 m** | Major regions and the capital |
| **Feeder road (F)** | **30 m** | District headquarters to the NH |
| **District road (D)** | **20 m** | Within a district |
| **Village road (V)** | **15 m** | Local access |

> **Right-of-way width falls with class**, because a lower-class road needs no reserve for future widening.

**The design consequences of class:**

| Provision | Arterial | Local |
|---|---|---|
| Design speed | **High** | Low |
| **Access control** | **Restricted or prohibited** | **Unrestricted** |
| Junction spacing | **Wide** | Close |
| Parking | **Prohibited or restricted** | Permitted |

> **ACCESS CONTROL is the defining design tool** — it is what converts a road from one that serves frontage into one that serves movement, and it is applied more strictly the higher the class.

verification.notes: The Nepali names in this item follow the source compilation's own table (arterial = Path, sub-arterial = Sadak, collector = Marg, local = Upa-Marg), and the keyed answer is consistent with it. That mapping is difficult to verify against the Nepal Road Standard and sits awkwardly with ordinary Nepali usage, in which 'path' denotes a minor way rather than the highest urban class — the same difficulty already recorded for the road-name item in Set 5. The FUNCTIONAL hierarchy taught in the solution is not in doubt; only the name mapping is flagged for the owner to confirm against the current standard.

examTip.trick: **The functional hierarchy is the durable part**: arterial (highest mobility, lowest access) → sub-arterial → collector → local (highest access). The Nepali names sit on top of that structure.
examTip.trap: **Ordinary usage and the classification table disagree here**, which is why this item is flagged. Learn the four-level *function* ladder; treat the name mapping as something to check against the current standard.
examTip.mnemonic: **A good network is a TREE: property → local → collector → arterial.** Skipping a level is the classic failure — and **ribbon development** destroys a highway while it is still called one.

questions.stem: Formwork to a column is removed after:
questions.solution:
**24 hours** — in practice 24 to 48 hours, at the engineer's discretion.

> The source's table gives the full schedule: **sides of walls, columns and vertical faces of beams — 24 to 48 hours (as per the engineer's decision); slabs (props left under) — 3 days; beam soffits (props left under) — 7 days; removal of props of slabs spanning up to 4.5 m — 7 days, over 4.5 m — 14 days; removal of props for beams and arches, span up to 6 m — 14 days, over 6 m — 21 days.**

**The organising principle — and it is the whole answer:**

> **VERTICAL faces carry NO LOAD. They are there only to shape the concrete and retain it while it is fluid.**

> **Once the concrete can stand on its own without slumping — a matter of hours — the side shutter has done its job.**

> **SOFFITS and PROPS carry the WEIGHT of the concrete itself, and must stay until the member can carry that weight.** That takes days to weeks.

> **So the schedule sorts itself into two families**: side forms in hours, load-bearing forms in days — and every number in the table follows from which family it belongs to.

**The complete IS 456 schedule:**

| Formwork | Removal time |
|---|---|
| **Vertical faces — walls, columns, beam sides** | **24 – 48 hours** |
| **Slab soffit (props left under)** | **3 days** |
| **Beam soffit (props left under)** | **7 days** |
| **Props to slabs — span ≤ 4.5 m** | **7 days** |
| **Props to slabs — span > 4.5 m** | **14 days** |
| **Props to beams and arches — span ≤ 6 m** | **14 days** |
| **Props to beams and arches — span > 6 m** | **21 days** |

> **Note the two-stage removal for soffits**: the shuttering board comes away at 3 or 7 days but **the props stay**, so the member is still supported while it gains strength.

> **That is why a slab soffit and its props have different times** — a detail candidates often miss when reading the table.

**And why LONGER SPANS need longer:**

> **A longer span carries a larger moment from its own self-weight**, so it needs a greater proportion of its final strength before it can support itself. **The span thresholds (4.5 m and 6 m) exist for exactly that reason.**

**Why premature striking is so damaging:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excessive deflection** | **PERMANENT — the member never recovers** |
| **CREEP** | Concrete loaded young creeps far more, and the deflection grows for years |
| Cracking | Tensile strength not yet developed |
| Collapse | In the worst case |

> **The creep effect is the one most often underestimated.** Concrete loaded at 3 days creeps substantially more over its life than the same concrete loaded at 28 days — so early striking causes a deflection that continues to increase long after the building is occupied.

> **The damage is invisible on the day and permanent thereafter**, which is why the schedule is a code requirement rather than site judgement.

**Temperature governs the times, not the calendar:**

> **The table assumes ordinary Portland cement at about 20 °C.** Times must be **extended in cold weather** — strength gain follows the concrete's maturity, not the passage of days.

> **They may be shortened where cube tests on site-cured specimens prove the strength has been reached**, which is the proper way to accelerate a programme.

**And CURING must not be confused with striking:**

> **Curing continues for at least 7 days (14 for blended cements) regardless of when the formwork comes off.** Removing the shutter exposes the surface and **increases** the need for curing, since evaporation can then begin.

examTip.trick: **Vertical faces carry NO LOAD — they only shape the concrete**, so they come off in hours. **Soffits and props carry the concrete's own weight** and stay for days to weeks. Two families, one principle.
examTip.trap: **Soffit shuttering and its PROPS have different times** — the board comes away at 3 or 7 days but the props remain. Reading only one line of the table is the usual slip.
examTip.mnemonic: **Early striking causes CREEP that never recovers** — concrete loaded at 3 days deflects far more over its life than the same concrete loaded at 28. Invisible on the day, permanent thereafter.

questions.stem: The ultimate bearing capacity of soil is:
options: The load at which the soil fails in shear
The load at which the soil consolidates
The load below the elastic limit
questions.solution:
**The load at which the soil fails in shear.**

> The source's definition: **it is the maximum gross pressure at the base of the foundation which can be applied WITHOUT SHEAR FAILURE — or, the minimum gross pressure at which the soil just fails in shear.**

**The bearing capacity ladder** — four terms that are constantly confused:

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **ULTIMATE bearing capacity (q_u)** | **The pressure at which SHEAR FAILURE occurs** ← |
| **NET ultimate (q_nu)** | **q_u − γD** — the ultimate minus the overburden already there |
| **SAFE bearing capacity** | **q_nu/FOS + γD** — with a factor of safety of **2.5 to 3** |
| **ALLOWABLE bearing pressure** | **The LESSER of the safe capacity and the pressure causing permissible SETTLEMENT** |

> **Option (c), "safe allowable load", is therefore a different quantity — two steps further down the ladder.** It is the ultimate capacity divided by a factor of safety and then checked against settlement.

> **Confusing the two is not a wording error but a factor of about three**, which is why the distinction is worth fixing precisely.

**The two failure criteria, and which one usually governs:**

| Criterion | Governs when |
|---|---|
| **SHEAR failure** | The soil is **weak** — soft clay, loose sand |
| **SETTLEMENT** | **Usually — most of the time in practice** |

> **Settlement, not shear, is the normal control.** A footing with an ample factor of safety against shear failure may still settle more than the structure can tolerate.

> **Which is why the ALLOWABLE pressure is defined as the LESSER of the two** — the design must satisfy both, and it is decided by whichever is smaller.

**Terzaghi's equation** for a strip footing:

> **q_u = c N_c + γ D N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

| Term | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **c N_c** | **COHESION** |
| **γ D N_q** | **SURCHARGE — the depth term** |
| **0.5 γ B N_γ** | **The soil's own weight — the width term** |

> **Which term dominates depends on the soil, and the contrast is sharp:**

| Soil | Dominant term | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Saturated CLAY (φ = 0)** | **Cohesion** — N_c = 5.7, N_q = 1, N_γ = 0 | **q_u is INDEPENDENT of footing WIDTH** |
| **SAND (c = 0)** | **Depth and width terms** | **Capacity rises with BOTH depth and width** |

> **The clay result is genuinely counter-intuitive and worth holding on to: widening a footing on saturated clay does NOT increase its bearing capacity per unit area at all.** It reduces the pressure by spreading the load, but the capacity itself is unchanged.

> **On sand the opposite holds** — a wider, deeper footing has a higher capacity as well as a lower pressure.

**The three failure modes:**

| Mode | Occurs in | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **GENERAL shear** | **Dense sand, stiff clay** | **Sudden, well-defined failure surface, heaving at the surface** |
| **LOCAL shear** | Medium dense | Partial surface, large settlement |
| **PUNCHING shear** | **Loose sand, soft clay** | **Footing punches down; NO heaving, no clear failure load** |

> **Punching failure gives no warning and no identifiable ultimate load**, which is why the reduced-strength parameters (⅔c and tan⁻¹(⅔tanφ)) are used for loose and soft soils rather than the measured ones.

**Why option (d) is wrong** is worth a note: **soil has no meaningful "elastic limit"** in the sense a metal does. Its stress–strain response is non-linear from a very small strain, which is precisely why bearing capacity is defined by **shear failure** rather than by yield.

examTip.trick: **Ultimate = the pressure at SHEAR FAILURE.** Safe and allowable are two steps further down the ladder — divided by a factor of 2.5–3, then checked against settlement.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is a different quantity, not a rewording** — the gap between ultimate and allowable is a factor of about three. And soil has no meaningful **elastic limit**, which disposes of (d).
examTip.mnemonic: **On saturated CLAY (φ = 0), bearing capacity is INDEPENDENT of footing width** — N_γ = 0, so widening spreads the load but does not raise the capacity. On sand it raises both.

questions.stem: The following readings are obtained from levelling: 4.25, 6.81, 2.35, 6.35, 6.25, 4.35, 2.6, with the instrument changed at the 3rd and 5th readings. The readings 2.35 and 6.25 are:
questions.solution:
**Back sight and fore sight** — the readings associated with a CHANGE POINT.

**The three kinds of staff reading, which is the substance worth taking from this item:**

| Reading | Definition |
|---|---|
| **BACK SIGHT (BS)** | **The FIRST reading after the instrument is set up** — always on a point of known elevation |
| **INTERMEDIATE SIGHT (IS)** | **Any reading between the BS and the FS** from the same setup |
| **FORE SIGHT (FS)** | **The LAST reading before the instrument is moved** |

> **The classification depends entirely on the reading's POSITION IN THE SETUP, not on its value or on what it is taken to.**

> **Every setup has exactly ONE back sight and ONE fore sight, and any number of intermediate sights in between.**

**What happens at a CHANGE POINT:**

> **A change point (or turning point) is a staff position on which BOTH a fore sight and a back sight are taken.**

> **The FS is read from the old instrument position; the staff is held still; the instrument is moved; and the BS is read from the new position to the same point.**

> **That is what carries the level forward** — the change point is the link between two setups, and it is why its elevation must be a firm, well-defined object.

> **A change point on soft ground, or a staff that moves between the two readings, breaks the chain and the whole line after it is wrong.**

**The arithmetic checks that follow:**

> **ΣBS − ΣFS = Last RL − First RL**

> **This check works because every intermediate sight cancels out** — it contributes to a reduced level but never to the rise or fall between setups.

| Method | Check |
|---|---|
| **RISE AND FALL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = Σrise − Σfall = Last RL − First RL** — **three checks, fully self-checking** |
| **HEIGHT OF INSTRUMENT (collimation)** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = Last RL − First RL** only — **does NOT check intermediate sights** |

> **That difference decides which method to use.** The **rise and fall** method checks every reading including the intermediates, so it is used where accuracy matters. **The height of instrument method is faster but leaves intermediate sights unverified** — acceptable for a longitudinal section with many IS readings, where speed matters more.

**The other relations:**

> **HI = RL of the point + BS**
>
> **RL of the next point = HI − FS (or IS)**

**And the errors to control:**

| Error | Remedy |
|---|---|
| **Collimation** | **BALANCE the backsight and foresight distances** — it cancels exactly |
| **Curvature and refraction** | **Also cancels with balanced sights**; otherwise 0.0673 d² |
| Staff not vertical | Reading always **too large** — use a staff bubble or wave the staff |
| **Change point moves** | **Use a firm, well-defined point** |

> **Balanced sight distances are the single most effective precaution in levelling** — collimation, curvature and refraction are all proportional to sight length, so equal backsight and foresight lengths cancel all three at every setup.

> **Where balancing is impossible — across a river or ravine — RECIPROCAL LEVELLING achieves the same cancellation** by observing from near each end and averaging.

**Permissible misclosure:** **±12√K mm** for ordinary work and **±3√K mm** for precise levelling, K in kilometres.

verification.notes: The item is ambiguously specified in the source. 'Instrument changed at the 3rd and 5th readings' admits several readings, and none of them yields one back sight and one fore sight: if the change follows readings 3 and 5, both are fore sights; if it precedes them, both are back sights. The source supplies no working, only a restatement of the keyed option. The keyed letter (a) is retained on the reading that 2.35 and 6.25 are the CHANGE-POINT readings, at which both a fore sight and a back sight are taken — but the item cannot be derived as written, and the solution teaches the BS/IS/FS classification rather than defending the arithmetic.

examTip.trick: **Classification depends on POSITION IN THE SETUP, not on the value.** One BS (first reading after setting up) and one FS (last before moving) per setup; everything between is an IS.
examTip.trap: **A CHANGE POINT carries BOTH an FS and a BS** — read from the old position and the new, to the same staff position. That is what links two setups and carries the level forward.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rise and fall is fully self-checking; height of instrument does NOT check intermediate sights.** And **balanced sight distances** cancel collimation, curvature and refraction at every setup.

questions.stem: What is the effect of water table fluctuation above ground level on the effective stress?
questions.solution:
**No effect.**

> The source states it: **the effective stress on a soil mass is INDEPENDENT of the depth of water above the soil surface.**

**Why — the arithmetic is complete in two lines:**

> Consider a point at depth **z** below a soil surface, with water standing to a height **H_w ABOVE that surface.**
>
> **Total stress: σ = γ_w H_w + γ_sat z**
>
> **Pore pressure: u = γ_w (H_w + z)**
>
> **Effective stress: σ′ = σ − u = γ_w H_w + γ_sat z − γ_w H_w − γ_w z = (γ_sat − γ_w) z = γ′ z**

> **The γ_w H_w terms CANCEL EXACTLY.** The free water adds the same amount to the total stress and to the pore pressure, so the difference between them — the effective stress — is untouched.

> **σ′ = γ′ z, depending only on the submerged unit weight and the depth below the soil surface.**

**Why this is a genuinely important result and not a curiosity:**

> **It means the bed of a lake, a river or the sea carries the same effective stress whether the water above it is 1 m or 100 m deep.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **A rising river does NOT consolidate its own bed** | The effective stress is unchanged |
| **Deep-water and shallow-water seabeds** have the same effective stress at a given depth below the mud line | — |
| **A submerged slope's stability is unaffected** by the depth of water over it | Provided it is fully submerged and static |
| Flooding a site does not increase settlement from the water itself | — |

> **The submerged-slope result is the one most often needed**: a slope entirely under still water is no less stable for being deeply submerged.

> **But RAPID DRAWDOWN is a different matter entirely** — and it is the classic failure case. **When the water level falls quickly, the external water pressure that was supporting the slope disappears, while the pore pressure inside the soil has not yet dissipated.** The effective stress falls, and the slope fails.

> **Earth dam upstream slopes are checked specifically for rapid drawdown**, and it is a more critical case than the reservoir being full.

**Contrast with a water table falling BELOW the ground surface**, which is the case that does change things:

| Water table movement | Effect on σ′ at a point below it |
|---|---|
| **Rising ABOVE ground level** | **NO CHANGE** ← this question |
| **Falling BELOW ground level** | **σ′ INCREASES** — soil above becomes moist rather than submerged |
| Rising within the soil | **σ′ decreases** |

> **The reason for the contrast: water above the ground adds to BOTH σ and u; water within the soil changes the unit weight of the soil above the point, which alters σ without an equal change in u.**

> **Which is why groundwater PUMPING causes settlement** — lowering the water table raises the effective stress throughout the soil above the new level, and the ground consolidates.

> **Excessive abstraction has caused metres of subsidence in cities built on soft deposits**, and it is entirely explained by this one equation.

**Terzaghi's principle** underlies all of it:

> **σ′ = σ − u**

> **ALL measurable effects of a change of stress — compression, distortion and a change of shearing resistance — are due exclusively to changes in EFFECTIVE stress.**

> **That is the single most important statement in soil mechanics**, and this question is one of its cleanest illustrations.

examTip.trick: **The γ_w H_w terms cancel exactly.** Free water above the surface adds equally to total stress and pore pressure, so σ′ = γ′z regardless of how deep the water is.
examTip.trap: **Water ABOVE the ground has no effect; water WITHIN the soil does.** Lowering the water table *raises* σ′ — which is exactly why groundwater pumping causes subsidence.
examTip.mnemonic: **A submerged slope is no less stable for being deeply submerged — but RAPID DRAWDOWN is the classic failure.** The supporting water goes, the pore pressure has not dissipated, and σ′ collapses.

questions.stem: A non-ideal (real) fluid flow:
options: Does not follow Newton's law of viscosity
questions.solution:
**Both** — a real fluid **may or may not** follow Newton's law of viscosity.

> The source states it exactly: **non-ideal flow (real flow) MAY follow Newton's law of viscosity OR MAY NOT.**

**The two classifications are INDEPENDENT, and that is the whole point:**

| Classification | Divides fluids into |
|---|---|
| **IDEAL vs REAL** | **Zero viscosity vs finite viscosity** |
| **NEWTONIAN vs NON-NEWTONIAN** | **Constant viscosity vs variable viscosity** |

> **An IDEAL fluid has NO viscosity at all** — a mathematical convenience that does not exist. It cannot follow Newton's law because there is nothing to follow.

> **A REAL fluid has viscosity. The question is then whether that viscosity is CONSTANT (Newtonian) or varies with the rate of shear (non-Newtonian).**

> **Both kinds of real fluid exist**, which is precisely why the answer is "both".

**Newton's law of viscosity:**

> **τ = μ (du/dy)**

> **Shear stress is proportional to the velocity gradient**, with the constant of proportionality μ the **dynamic viscosity.**

> **A NEWTONIAN fluid plots as a STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH THE ORIGIN** on a shear stress against shear rate diagram. Everything else is non-Newtonian.

**The fluid families:**

| Type | Behaviour | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **NEWTONIAN** | **τ ∝ du/dy — straight line through the origin** | **Water, air, most oils, glycerine** |
| **DILATANT (shear-thickening)** | **Viscosity RISES with shear rate** | **Concentrated starch suspensions, some SLURRIES** |
| **PSEUDOPLASTIC (shear-thinning)** | **Viscosity FALLS with shear rate** | Blood, paint, polymer solutions |
| **BINGHAM PLASTIC** | **Needs a YIELD STRESS before it flows at all** | **Toothpaste, drilling mud, FRESH CONCRETE, sewage sludge** |
| **Ideal fluid** | **μ = 0** | **None — a mathematical idealisation** |

> **The civil engineering relevance is direct and often overlooked:**

> **FRESH CONCRETE is a Bingham plastic.** It has a genuine **yield stress** — it will not flow at all until a certain shear is applied, which is exactly why it can stand in a slump cone, hold its shape on a slope, and why **VIBRATION works**: vibration momentarily exceeds the yield stress and lets the mix flow into place and around reinforcement.

> **That single property explains slump, compaction, formwork pressure and self-compacting concrete design.**

> **DRILLING MUD is chosen for the same behaviour**: it must carry cuttings while circulating and hold them in suspension when circulation stops — which requires a yield stress, not merely a high viscosity.

> **And SEWAGE SLUDGE at high solids content is Bingham too**, which is why sludge pumping is calculated differently from water pumping and why a pipeline that stops may not restart.

**Why the ideal fluid idea survives despite not existing:**

> **Outside the boundary layer, viscous effects are genuinely negligible**, so ideal-fluid theory predicts pressure distributions and flow patterns very well.

> **PRANDTL's boundary layer concept is what reconciles the two**: treat the thin layer near the surface as viscous and everything beyond it as ideal. **That insight made modern fluid mechanics possible**, because it let the useful ideal theory be kept without ignoring drag.

**Viscosity's dependence on temperature** is worth noting, since it runs opposite in the two states of matter:

> **LIQUIDS: viscosity FALLS as temperature rises** — molecular cohesion weakens.
>
> **GASES: viscosity RISES as temperature rises** — molecular momentum exchange increases.

examTip.trick: **Two independent classifications**: ideal vs real (zero or finite viscosity), and Newtonian vs non-Newtonian (constant or variable viscosity). A real fluid can be either of the second pair.
examTip.trap: **An IDEAL fluid cannot follow Newton's law because it has no viscosity at all.** The question is about REAL fluids, where both behaviours genuinely occur.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fresh CONCRETE is a Bingham plastic with a real YIELD STRESS** — which is why it holds a slump and why **vibration** works: it momentarily exceeds the yield stress and lets the mix flow.

questions.stem: What is the Laplace equation (for two-dimensional flow in the x–z plane)?
questions.solution:
**∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂z² = 0.**

> The source states it: **Laplace's equation is d²Φ/dx² + d²Φ/dz².**

**The defining feature is that BOTH terms are SECOND derivatives:**

| Option | Fault |
|---|---|
| (a) | **Second derivative in x, FIRST in z** — mismatched order |
| **(b)** | **Both second order** ✓ |
| (c) | **First derivative in x**, second in y — mismatched |
| (d) | **Second in x, first in z** — mismatched |

> **Three of the four mix orders, which cannot be right: the two terms must be dimensionally alike to add.**

> **φ/L² added to φ/L is dimensionally impossible**, so the check is purely mechanical — scan for matching exponents and only one option survives.

**Where the equation comes from:**

> **The velocity potential is defined so that u = −∂φ/∂x and w = −∂φ/∂z.**
>
> **Substituting into the continuity equation ∂u/∂x + ∂w/∂z = 0 gives ∂²φ/∂x² + ∂²φ/∂z² = 0.**

> **So Laplace's equation is simply CONTINUITY expressed in terms of the velocity potential.** It is not an additional physical law but the same one rewritten.

> **The STREAM function ψ satisfies the same equation for irrotational flow**, which is why the two families of curves behave so symmetrically.

**What must be true for it to apply:**

| Condition | Why |
|---|---|
| **IRROTATIONAL flow** | **Only then does a velocity potential exist at all** |
| **INCOMPRESSIBLE** | Otherwise ρ does not divide out of continuity |
| Steady (usually assumed) | — |

> **The irrotationality requirement is the significant one.** A stream function exists for any two-dimensional continuous flow; **a velocity potential exists only if the flow has no rotation.**

> **That asymmetry between ψ and φ is the point most often missed.**

**The FLOW NET, which is the practical payoff:**

> **Lines of constant φ (equipotentials) and constant ψ (streamlines) intersect at RIGHT ANGLES, forming a mesh of curvilinear squares.**

> **Once drawn, the net gives everything:**

| Quantity | From the net |
|---|---|
| **Seepage quantity** | **q = k H (N_f/N_d)** |
| **Pore pressure at any point** | From the number of drops passed |
| **UPLIFT pressure on a structure** | The pressure distribution along its base |
| **EXIT GRADIENT** | **i_e = H/(N_d × l)** at the downstream face |

> where **N_f** is the number of flow channels, **N_d** the number of equipotential drops, and **H** the total head.

**Why the exit gradient matters most:**

> **PIPING — the progressive erosion of soil by seepage at the downstream toe — is the leading cause of failure in earth dams and barrages.**

> **The critical hydraulic gradient is i_c = (G − 1)/(1 + e) ≈ 1.0** for typical soils, and the exit gradient must be kept well below it, with a factor of safety of **4 to 5.**

> **The failure is progressive and rapid**: once a pipe starts at the toe it works backward toward the reservoir, enlarging as it goes, and the structure can be lost in hours.

> **KHOSLA's theory is the analytical solution of exactly this Laplace equation** for barrage floors, giving the uplift pressures and exit gradient without drawing a net — which is why it superseded **Bligh's creep theory**, an empirical rule that took no account of the actual flow pattern.

**And the same equation governs elsewhere:** **steady heat conduction, electrostatics, torsion of non-circular sections, and steady groundwater flow** — which is why solutions found in one field transfer directly to another.

examTip.trick: **Both terms must be SECOND derivatives.** φ/L² cannot be added to φ/L — a purely mechanical scan for matching exponents leaves only one option standing.
examTip.trap: **A stream function exists for ANY 2-D continuous flow; a velocity potential only for IRROTATIONAL flow.** That asymmetry is the condition most often missed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laplace's equation is CONTINUITY rewritten in φ** — not a new law. Its payoff is the **FLOW NET**: q = kH(N_f/N_d), and the **exit gradient** that governs piping, the leading cause of earth-dam failure.

questions.stem: An exceptional gradient is:
options: A gradient steeper than the ruling gradient, used for a limited road length
A gradient steeper than the limiting gradient, which may be used in a very short length in an exceptional case
The maximum gradient within which the designer attempts to design the vertical profile of the road
The minimum longitudinal gradient for longitudinal drainage purposes
questions.solution:
**A gradient steeper than the LIMITING gradient, used in a very short length in an exceptional case.**

> The source sets out all four in order: **RULING gradient (design gradient) — the maximum gradient within which the designer attempts to design the vertical profile; LIMITING gradient — steeper than the ruling gradient, used for a limited or restricted length; EXCEPTIONAL gradient — steeper than the LIMITING gradient, used in a very short length in an exceptional case; MINIMUM gradient — the minimum longitudinal gradient for drainage, 0.5%.**

**The four gradients form a LADDER, and this question tests whether you can climb it in the right order:**

| Gradient | Definition | Length permitted |
|---|---|---|
| **MINIMUM** | **For drainage — 0.5%** | Everywhere in a cutting |
| **RULING (design)** | **The normal design maximum** | **Unrestricted** |
| **LIMITING** | **Steeper than ruling** | **Limited / restricted length** |
| **EXCEPTIONAL** | **Steeper than LIMITING** | **Very short length, exceptional case only** |

> **Each step up is steeper and permitted over a shorter distance.** That single pattern generates the whole set.

**The trap is precise and worth naming:**

> **Option (a) says "steeper than the RULING gradient" — that is the definition of the LIMITING gradient, not the exceptional one.**

> **The exceptional gradient is steeper than the LIMITING gradient — one rung further up.**

> **And option (c) is the RULING gradient's definition; option (d) is the MINIMUM gradient's.** All three distractors are correct definitions of the **other three** members of the set.

> **This is a four-way matching question disguised as a definition question**, and reading only the first few words of each option is exactly how it is failed.

**Typical IRC values:**

| Terrain | Ruling | Limiting | Exceptional |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plain / rolling** | **3.3%** | **5.0%** | **6.7%** |
| **Mountainous / steep (> 3000 m)** | **5.0%** | **6.0%** | **7.0%** |
| **Steep (below 3000 m)** | **6.0%** | **7.0%** | **8.0%** |

> **Note that a steeper gradient is permitted in mountainous terrain, not a gentler one** — the alternative would be enormous lengths of hillside cutting and impossibly long alignments.

**The MINIMUM gradient is a real requirement, not a formality:**

> **0.5% is needed so water flows along the side drains rather than standing.**

> **A perfectly level road in a cutting ponds water, which then softens the subgrade and destroys the pavement from below** — and in Nepal's monsoon climate that is the commonest route to premature failure.

> **It is required in cuttings; on embankment the water sheds sideways and the longitudinal gradient matters less.**

**GRADE COMPENSATION on curves** — the provision most often forgotten:

> **On a horizontal curve the gradient must be REDUCED, because the curve itself adds resistance to a climbing vehicle.**

> **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R per cent, subject to a maximum of 75/R.**

> **It is not applied where the gradient is flatter than 4%.**

> **Failing to apply it is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends** — the combination of a sharp curve and a steep grade exceeds what the vehicle can pull, even though each is individually within limits.

> **That is the practical reason the whole gradient system exists**: the governing case is not the car but the **fully loaded truck at its slowest**, and every limit in the table is set by what such a vehicle can climb without stopping.

examTip.trick: **The four gradients form a ladder: minimum → ruling → limiting → exceptional.** Each rung is steeper and allowed over a shorter length. That pattern generates the whole set.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) defines the LIMITING gradient** (steeper than *ruling*); the exceptional one is steeper than *limiting* — one rung further up. All three distractors define the other three members.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R %, max 75/R**, not applied below 4%. Forgetting it is why trucks stall on hairpins — sharp curve plus steep grade exceeds what each alone would.

questions.stem: The falling head permeability test is used in the case of:
questions.solution:
**Cohesive or less permeable soils.**

> The source gives both tests and their ranges: **constant head method (k > 10⁻⁴ m/s) for coarse-grained, more permeable soil; variable (falling) head method (10⁻⁷ < k < 10⁻⁴ m/s) for fine-grained, less permeable soil.**

**The two laboratory tests:**

| | **CONSTANT HEAD** | **FALLING (variable) HEAD** |
|---|---|---|
| **Suits** | **COARSE — sand, gravel** | **FINE — silt, clayey silt** |
| **k range** | **> 10⁻⁴ m/s** | **10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁴ m/s** |
| **Measured** | **VOLUME collected in a known TIME** | **TIME for the head to fall between two marks** |
| Formula | **k = QL/(Aht)** | **k = 2.303 (aL/At) log₁₀(h₁/h₂)** |

> **The choice follows from what can actually be measured.**

> **In a coarse soil, water pours through — a large volume is collected quickly and can be measured accurately, so the constant head test works.**

> **In a fine soil, the flow is a trickle. Collecting a measurable volume would take days, and evaporation alone would corrupt the reading.**

> **So instead of measuring a tiny volume, the falling head test measures a FALLING LEVEL in a thin standpipe** — and because the standpipe's area **a** is small, even a very small flow produces a visible drop.

> **The narrower the standpipe, the finer the soil it can test.** That is the whole design of the apparatus.

**Darcy's law**, which both tests are built on:

> **v = k i**, and **Q = k i A**, where **i = h/L** is the hydraulic gradient.

> **Note that v is the DISCHARGE VELOCITY through the gross area, not the actual velocity of the water.** The **seepage velocity** through the voids is **v_s = v/n**, which is always larger.

> **Darcy's law holds only for LAMINAR flow** — valid for sands and finer, but it breaks down in coarse gravel and rockfill where the flow becomes turbulent.

**Typical permeability values, spanning eleven orders of magnitude:**

| Soil | **k (m/s)** |
|---|---|
| **Clean GRAVEL** | **> 10⁻²** |
| **Coarse SAND** | 10⁻² – 10⁻³ |
| **Fine sand** | 10⁻³ – 10⁻⁵ |
| **SILT** | **10⁻⁵ – 10⁻⁸** |
| **CLAY** | **< 10⁻⁹** |

> **That enormous range is why no single test covers all soils**, and why clay is treated as effectively impermeable in most engineering problems.

> **For clay itself, even the falling head test is too slow** — permeability is instead computed indirectly from the **consolidation test**, using **k = c_v m_v γ_w.**

**And the FIELD tests, which are more reliable than any laboratory value:**

> **Pumping tests** — from a well with observation boreholes — give a **mass permeability** that accounts for the soil's layering and fissures.

> **A laboratory sample tests a few centimetres of soil in one direction. Real deposits are LAYERED, and their horizontal permeability is often ten times or more the vertical.**

> **k_horizontal ≫ k_vertical is the normal condition**, and a laboratory value from a vertical sample can therefore mislead badly for a problem governed by horizontal flow — such as drainage toward a well, or seepage under a dam.

**Factors affecting k:** **grain size (k ∝ D₁₀² approximately, by Hazen's formula k = C D₁₀²), void ratio, soil structure, degree of saturation, and the fluid's viscosity** — and hence **temperature**, which is why results are corrected to 27 °C.

examTip.trick: **The choice follows from what can be MEASURED.** Coarse soil gives a large volume quickly (constant head); fine soil gives a trickle, so measure a **falling level in a thin standpipe** instead.
examTip.trap: **The narrower the standpipe, the finer the soil it can test** — the small area a is what makes a tiny flow visible. That is the apparatus's whole design, not an incidental detail.
examTip.mnemonic: **k spans eleven orders of magnitude** — gravel 10⁻² to clay 10⁻⁹ — which is why no one test covers all soils. And **k_horizontal ≫ k_vertical** in real layered deposits, so field tests beat laboratory ones.

questions.stem: A point 'P' is above the Horizontal Plane (HP) and in front of the Vertical Plane (VP). The point is in the:
questions.solution:
**First quadrant.**

> The source lists all four: **First quadrant — above HP and in front of VP; Second — above HP and behind VP; Third — below HP and behind VP; Fourth — below HP and in front of VP.**

**The four quadrants:**

| Quadrant | Position of HP | Position of VP |
|---|---|---|
| **FIRST** | **ABOVE** | **IN FRONT** |
| **SECOND** | **ABOVE** | **BEHIND** |
| **THIRD** | **BELOW** | **BEHIND** |
| **FOURTH** | **BELOW** | **IN FRONT** |

> **The pattern is worth reading rather than memorising: going round the quadrants, ABOVE holds for the first two and BELOW for the last two, while IN FRONT holds for the first and fourth.**

> **First and third are the diagonal opposites** — above/front against below/behind — which is why they are the two used in practice.

**Why only the first and third quadrants are used:**

> **In the second and fourth quadrants, rotating the planes into one flat sheet makes the two views OVERLAP.**

> **The projection method requires the horizontal plane to be rotated down into the plane of the vertical one. In the first and third quadrants this separates the views cleanly; in the other two the views land on top of each other and the drawing is unreadable.**

> **So the restriction is geometric, not conventional** — the other two quadrants are unusable, not merely unfashionable.

**FIRST versus THIRD angle projection** — the practical distinction:

| | **FIRST angle** | **THIRD angle** |
|---|---|---|
| Object is | **BETWEEN the observer and the plane** | **BEHIND the plane** — the plane is between observer and object |
| Analogy | The object **casts a shadow** onto the plane | The plane is **transparent** and traced through |
| **Right-hand view appears** | **On the LEFT** | **On the RIGHT** |
| **Top view appears** | **BELOW** the front view | **ABOVE** the front view |
| Used in | **India, Nepal, Europe** | **USA, Canada, Japan, Australia** |

> **The views appear on the OPPOSITE side in first angle and the SAME side in third angle**, and that single sentence covers every layout difference between them.

> **A drawing read in the wrong convention is not merely confusing — it is MIRRORED**, and parts have been manufactured backwards for exactly this reason.

> **Which is why every drawing carries the projection SYMBOL — a truncated cone — in its title block.** It is a safety measure, not decoration, and checking it is the first thing to do on an unfamiliar drawing.

**Notation** used in orthographic projection:

| Element | Notation |
|---|---|
| Point in space | **P** |
| **Front view** (on VP) | **p′** |
| **Top view** (on HP) | **p** |
| **Side view** (on profile plane) | **p″** |
| **Reference line (XY)** | **The intersection of HP and VP** |

> **The XY line is the hinge about which the horizontal plane is rotated**, and both views are measured from it — the front view above, the top view below, in first angle.

**The three principal views** — front elevation, plan and side elevation — are usually sufficient, and **hidden edges are shown DASHED** while visible ones are continuous and thick.

examTip.trick: **Read the pattern rather than memorising**: ABOVE holds for quadrants 1 and 2, BELOW for 3 and 4; IN FRONT holds for 1 and 4. First and third are the diagonal opposites.
examTip.trap: **Only the 1st and 3rd quadrants are usable** — in the 2nd and 4th the views OVERLAP when the planes are rotated flat. The restriction is geometric, not conventional.
examTip.mnemonic: **First angle: views on the OPPOSITE side. Third angle: views on the SAME side.** A drawing read in the wrong convention is MIRRORED — which is why the projection symbol is in every title block.

questions.stem: If SPI < 1 and CPI < 1, then which of the following is true?
options: The project is ahead of schedule and under budget
The project is behind schedule and over budget
The project is ahead of schedule and over budget
questions.solution:
**Behind schedule and over budget.**

> The source gives the definitions: **SV = BCWP − BCWS; negative means behind schedule. SPI = BCWP/BCWS; less than 1.00 means behind schedule. CV = BCWP − ACWP; negative means over budget. CPI = BCWP/ACWP; less than 1.00 means over budget.**

**The rule that makes all four indicators readable at once:**

> **For BOTH indices, LESS THAN 1 IS BAD and GREATER THAN 1 IS GOOD.**
>
> **For both variances, NEGATIVE IS BAD and POSITIVE IS GOOD.**

> **There is no exception and no sign reversal between the schedule and cost pairs**, which is what makes earned value analysis quick to read once the convention is fixed.

**The three basic quantities:**

| Term | Modern name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **BCWS** | **Planned Value (PV)** | **What you PLANNED to have done by now** |
| **BCWP** | **EARNED Value (EV)** | **What you have ACTUALLY done, valued at budget rates** |
| **ACWP** | **Actual Cost (AC)** | **What you actually SPENT** |

> **BCWP — the earned value — is the pivot of the whole method, and it appears in the numerator of both indices.**

> **The insight is that progress must be measured in the SAME UNITS as the plan and the spend.** Comparing money spent against money budgeted tells you nothing about progress; comparing **work done, valued at budget rates**, against both is what makes the comparison meaningful.

**The four indicators:**

| Indicator | Formula | Compares |
|---|---|---|
| **Schedule Variance (SV)** | **BCWP − BCWS** | **Done vs planned** |
| **Schedule Performance Index (SPI)** | **BCWP / BCWS** | Same, as a ratio |
| **Cost Variance (CV)** | **BCWP − ACWP** | **Done vs spent** |
| **Cost Performance Index (CPI)** | **BCWP / ACWP** | Same, as a ratio |

> **Note that the SCHEDULE indicators are measured in MONEY, not time** — which is the method's best-known peculiarity. **SV is a currency figure that tells you about schedule.**

> **And SPI has a real limitation: as a project approaches completion, SPI always tends toward 1.0**, because the earned value eventually equals the planned value even if the work finished late. **It loses its usefulness precisely when a late project most needs watching.**

**The forecasting use, which is where the indices earn their keep:**

> **Estimate At Completion: EAC = BAC / CPI**

> **If a project is running at CPI = 0.8, it is buying 80 paisa of work for every rupee spent — so the final cost will be about BAC/0.8 = 1.25 times the budget.**

> **That is a forecast, available early, from data already collected.** It is the practical reason earned value analysis is used at all: it converts today's performance into tomorrow's number while there is still time to act.

> **Research on large projects has found CPI to be remarkably STABLE after about 20% completion** — a project performing badly early rarely recovers, which makes the early forecast unusually trustworthy.

**The four combinations, for completeness:**

| SPI | CPI | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **> 1** | **> 1** | **Ahead of schedule, under budget — best** |
| > 1 | < 1 | Ahead but overspending |
| < 1 | > 1 | Behind but economical |
| **< 1** | **< 1** | **Behind and over budget — worst** ← this question |

examTip.trick: **For both indices, < 1 is bad and > 1 is good; for both variances, negative is bad.** No sign reversal between the cost and schedule pairs — one convention covers all four.
examTip.trap: **Schedule indicators are measured in MONEY, not time** — SV is a currency figure telling you about schedule. And **SPI always drifts toward 1.0 near completion**, losing value exactly when it is most needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **EAC = BAC/CPI.** At CPI = 0.8 you are buying 80 paisa of work per rupee, so the final cost is ~1.25× budget — a forecast available early, when there is still time to act.

questions.stem: Risk in project management is defined as:
options: An uncertain event that, if it occurs, has a positive effect on project objectives
