examTip.trap: **Three immunities share one cause** — temperature, settlement and lack of fit are all IMPOSED DEFORMATIONS, not applied loads. A structure free to deform absorbs all three by moving.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = EαΔT, and the LENGTH cancels** — steel at 30 °C fully restrained gives **72 N/mm²** whether the member is 1 m or 100 m. That is why expansion joints are not optional.

questions.stem: The influence line diagram (ILD) of statically determinate structures consists of:
questions.solution:
**Straight lines only.**

> The source states it: **the ILD of statically determinate beams consists of only straight lines.**

**Why they must be straight:**

> **In a determinate structure, reactions and internal forces are found from EQUILIBRIUM ALONE — and the equilibrium equations are LINEAR in the load position.**

> **Take a simply supported beam of span L with a unit load at distance x from A:**
>
> **R_A = (L − x)/L, which is LINEAR in x.**

> **Every other quantity follows from the reactions by further linear operations, so every influence line is made of straight segments.**

> **For an INDETERMINATE structure the forces depend on the relative stiffnesses of the members as well as on equilibrium, and the compatibility equations bring in curvature — so its influence lines are CURVED** (Müller-Breslau's principle gives them as deflected shapes).

> **That contrast is the whole content of the question**, and it is a genuine diagnostic: **a curved influence line means the structure is indeterminate.**

**What an influence line actually shows** — and it is worth being precise, because it is constantly confused with a bending moment diagram:

| | **INFLUENCE LINE** | **BM / SF diagram** |
|---|---|---|
| **The load** | **A UNIT LOAD, MOVING** | **Fixed in position** |
| **The section** | **FIXED** | **Varies along the beam** |
| **The ordinate at x means** | **The value AT THE FIXED SECTION when the load is at x** | **The value AT x for the given loading** |

> **They are, in a sense, transposes of one another.** An influence line answers "how does this one section respond as the load moves?"; a BM diagram answers "what happens everywhere for this one loading?"

> **Confusing them is the commonest error in the topic**, and the test is simply to ask what is moving: the **load** or the **section**.

**The standard influence lines for a simply supported beam:**

| Quantity | Shape | Maximum ordinate |
|---|---|---|
| **Reaction R_A** | **Triangle**, 1 at A falling to 0 at B | **1.0 at A** |
| **Bending moment at section C** | **TRIANGLE with apex at C** | **ab/L** |
| **Shear force at section C** | **Two parallel lines, with a JUMP of 1 at C** | a/L and b/L |

> **The BM influence line peaks at the section itself, with ordinate ab/L** — which for mid-span gives **L/4.**

> **The SF influence line is discontinuous at the section**, jumping by exactly 1 as the unit load crosses it, and **changes SIGN there.**

**Why the sign change matters — the practical payoff:**

> **To find the MAXIMUM value, load only the parts of the span where the influence line has the SAME SIGN as the effect wanted.**

| Effect | Load |
|---|---|
| **Maximum BENDING MOMENT** | **The WHOLE span** — the ILD is all one sign |
| **Maximum SHEAR at a section** | **ONE SIDE only** — loading both sides cancels |

> **That is why maximum moment occurs with the span fully loaded but maximum shear does not**, and it is the reason influence lines exist at all.

**And the general rules:**

> **For a point load W: effect = W × (ordinate under the load).**
>
> **For a UDL w over a length: effect = w × (AREA of the influence line under that length).**

> **Which converts a moving-load problem into reading a diagram**, and it is why influence lines are indispensable for bridges, gantry girders and crane runways — anywhere the load's position is not fixed.

**MÜLLER-BRESLAU's principle** unifies it all:

> **The influence line for any force quantity is the DEFLECTED SHAPE obtained by removing the corresponding restraint and imposing a unit displacement in its direction.**

> **For a determinate structure that released shape is a MECHANISM, which moves in straight lines** — which is a second and more elegant proof of exactly what this question asks.

examTip.trick: **Determinate forces come from equilibrium alone, and equilibrium is LINEAR in the load position** — R_A = (L−x)/L. Hence straight lines. A CURVED influence line means the structure is indeterminate.
examTip.trap: **An influence line is not a BM diagram.** In an ILD the **load moves and the section is fixed**; in a BM diagram the load is fixed and the section moves. Ask what is moving.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load only where the ILD has the sign you want** — the whole span for maximum moment, but **one side only** for maximum shear, because the shear ILD changes sign at the section.

questions.stem: The detail about wind load is given in code:
questions.solution:
**NBC 104.**

> The source lists them: **NBC 103 — Occupancy load (imposed load); NBC 104 — WIND LOAD; NBC 105 — Seismic design of buildings in Nepal; NBC 106 — Snow load.**

**The load series of the Nepal National Building Code:**

| Code | Load |
|---|---|
| **NBC 102** | **Unit weights of materials** |
| **NBC 103** | **Occupancy (imposed / live) load** |
| **NBC 104** | **WIND LOAD** ← |
| **NBC 105** | **SEISMIC design of buildings in Nepal** |
| **NBC 106** | **SNOW load** |

> **The numbers run in the order the loads are applied to a structure**: first its own materials (102), then what occupies it (103), then the environmental actions — wind (104), earthquake (105), snow (106).

> **Recognising that sequence makes the whole series recoverable from one remembered number**, which is more reliable than memorising four separate figures.

**NBC 105 is the one that matters most in Nepal:**

> **The whole country lies in a high seismic zone**, on the collision boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates.

> **NBC 105 was substantially revised in 2020**, replacing the 1994 version — and the revision followed directly from what was learnt in the **2015 Gorkha earthquake.**

| The 2020 revision introduced | Note |
|---|---|
| **Updated seismic hazard maps** | Based on modern data |
| **Two-level design** | **Ultimate limit state and serviceability limit state** |
| Revised response spectra | Soil-type dependent |
| **Explicit ductility and detailing requirements** | The lesson of 2015 |

> **The ductility emphasis is the substantive change.** The 2015 earthquake demonstrated that **buildings fail not from a lack of strength but from a lack of DETAILING** — inadequate confinement, poor beam–column joints, short columns, and soft storeys.

> **A ductile building can be shaken far beyond its elastic limit and survive by deforming; a strong but brittle one shatters.**

**Which is why seismic design is philosophically different from every other load case:**

| Design case | Philosophy |
|---|---|
| **Wind, snow, imposed** | **Resist elastically — the structure should not yield** |
| **EARTHQUAKE** | **Deliberately allow INELASTIC deformation and DAMAGE, provided the building does not COLLAPSE** |

> **The seismic design objective is stated in three levels: resist a MINOR earthquake without damage; a MODERATE one with repairable non-structural damage; and a MAJOR one WITHOUT COLLAPSE, even if the building must afterwards be demolished.**

> **Designing a building to remain elastic in a major earthquake would be enormously expensive and is not attempted.** The forces are reduced by a response reduction factor **R**, and the ductility that justifies that reduction must then be **detailed in**.

> **That is the bargain: lower design forces in exchange for guaranteed ductile behaviour.** Take the reduced forces without providing the detailing and the building is unsafe by exactly the factor R.

**The wind load calculation** that NBC 104 governs:

> **P_z = 0.6 V_z²**, with **V_z = V_b k₁ k₂ k₃** — basic speed adjusted for risk, terrain and **TOPOGRAPHY.**

> **k₃ matters greatly here**, because wind accelerates over ridges and hill slopes, and a great deal of Nepali construction sits on exactly such ground.

> **And the force uses (C_pe − C_pi)**: internal pressure from a windward opening acts outward and **adds to the external suction on the roof**, which is why **uplift**, not downward pressure, governs light roofs — and why **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** is the critical combination for them.

examTip.trick: **The numbers run in the order loads are applied**: 102 materials, 103 occupancy, then the environment — 104 wind, 105 seismic, 106 snow. One remembered number recovers the series.
examTip.trap: **NBC 105 (seismic) is the neighbour most likely to be picked by mistake** — and it is the most important code in Nepal, substantially revised in 2020 after the Gorkha earthquake.
examTip.mnemonic: **Seismic design is philosophically different**: wind and snow are resisted **elastically**, but earthquakes are survived by **deliberate inelastic damage without collapse**. Reduced forces are bought with **ductile detailing**.

questions.stem: A sample of ground water at pH 7.0 contains 122 mg/L of bicarbonates. What is the alkalinity of this water in terms of CaCO₃?
questions.solution:
**100 mg/L as CaCO₃.**

**The conversion:**

> **Alkalinity as CaCO₃ = concentration of the ion × (equivalent weight of CaCO₃ ÷ equivalent weight of the ion)**

**Working:**

> **Equivalent weight of CaCO₃ = 100/2 = 50**
>
> **HCO₃⁻: 1 + 12 + (16 × 3) = 61; it carries ONE charge, so its equivalent weight = 61**
>
> **Alkalinity = 122 × 50/61 = 100 mg/L as CaCO₃** ✓

> **The numbers are chosen to be clean: 122 is exactly twice 61**, so the calculation reduces to **2 × 50 = 100.** Noticing that removes the arithmetic entirely.

**Why everything is expressed "as CaCO₃":**

> **A water's alkalinity comes from several different ions — bicarbonate, carbonate and hydroxide — each with a different molecular weight and charge.**

> **Adding milligrams of one to milligrams of another would be meaningless**, because equal masses do not neutralise equal amounts of acid.

> **Converting everything to a COMMON REFERENCE — CaCO₃ — makes the contributions ADDABLE and COMPARABLE.** It is exactly the same device as expressing hardness as CaCO₃.

> **CaCO₃ was chosen because its molecular weight is a convenient 100 and it is the substance that actually precipitates in scaling** — so the number has a physical meaning as well as being a common unit.

**The equivalent weight is the point most often got wrong:**

> **Equivalent weight = molecular weight ÷ charge (valency).**

| Species | Mol. wt | Charge | **Equivalent weight** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CaCO₃** | 100 | **2** | **50** |
| **HCO₃⁻** | 61 | **1** | **61** |
| **CO₃²⁻** | 60 | **2** | **30** |
| **OH⁻** | 17 | 1 | 17 |
| Ca²⁺ | 40 | 2 | 20 |
| Mg²⁺ | 24.3 | 2 | 12.15 |

> **CaCO₃ is divided by 2 because calcium is divalent; bicarbonate is NOT divided, because it carries a single charge.**

> **Forgetting to divide CaCO₃ by 2 gives 122 × 100/61 = 200 mg/L — which is exactly option (d)**, placed there for that error.

> **And using CO₃²⁻'s weight of 60 instead of HCO₃⁻'s 61 would give ≈102** — close enough to mislead but not among the options.

**Why the pH of 7.0 is given:**

> **It tells you which species is present.** At pH 7, essentially **ALL the alkalinity is BICARBONATE** — carbonate and hydroxide are negligible below about pH 8.3.

| pH | Dominant species |
|---|---|
| **< 8.3** | **BICARBONATE (HCO₃⁻) only** |
| 8.3 – 9.4 | Bicarbonate **and** carbonate |
| **> 9.4** | **Carbonate and hydroxide** |

> **The 8.3 threshold is the PHENOLPHTHALEIN end point** and 4.5 the **methyl orange** end point — which is exactly how the two are measured separately in the laboratory.

> **So the pH is not decoration: it confirms that the single conversion applied here is the whole answer**, with no carbonate contribution to add.

**Why alkalinity matters in practice:**

> **It is BUFFERING CAPACITY — the ability to resist a change in pH when acid is added.**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **COAGULATION with alum** | **Alum CONSUMES alkalinity**; too little and the pH crashes and no floc forms |
| Corrosion control | Low alkalinity water is aggressive to pipes |
| **Anaerobic digestion** | The **volatile acids : alkalinity** ratio is the standard stability check |
| Standard | **≤ 500 mg/L as CaCO₃** (NDWQS) |

> **Where alkalinity is insufficient for coagulation, LIME or SODA ASH is added to supply it** — which is a routine adjustment at treatment works drawing soft surface water.

examTip.trick: **122 is exactly twice 61**, so the calculation collapses to 2 × 50 = **100**. Spotting that removes the arithmetic entirely.
examTip.trap: **CaCO₃'s equivalent weight is 50, not 100** — calcium is divalent. Using 100 gives 122 × 100/61 = **200**, which is exactly option (d), placed there for that error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Everything is expressed "as CaCO₃" so different ions become ADDABLE.** And the pH of 7 matters: below 8.3 all alkalinity is bicarbonate, so one conversion is the whole answer.

questions.stem: A sewage sample of 3 ml diluted with distilled water in a 300 ml BOD bottle is incubated at 20 °C for 5 days, and the depletion of dissolved oxygen was 10 mg/L. The initial (ultimate) BOD of the sample is:
questions.solution:
**1463 mg/L.**

**Step 1 — the 5-day BOD from the dilution.**

> **BOD = DO depletion × DILUTION FACTOR**
>
> **Dilution factor = final volume ÷ sample volume = 300/3 = 100**
>
> **BOD₅ = 10 × 100 = 1000 mg/L**

**Step 2 — convert the 5-day value to the ULTIMATE BOD.**

> **BOD_t = L₀ (1 − 10^(−Kt))**, with **K = 0.1/day at 20 °C** — the standard value for domestic sewage.
>
> **10^(−0.1 × 5) = 10^(−0.5) = 0.3162**
>
> **1 − 0.3162 = 0.6838**
>
> **L₀ = 1000/0.6838 = 1462.5 ≈ 1463 mg/L** ✓

**Step 2 is the whole question:**

> **Stopping at 1000 mg/L answers a different question.** The stem asks for the **INITIAL (ultimate)** BOD, not the 5-day value.

> **The ratio BOD₅/L₀ = 0.684 at the standard K = 0.1 — so the 5-day BOD is about 68% of the ultimate.** That figure is worth carrying: it converts between the two in one multiplication and is a quick check on any answer.

> **Note the options are all the same digits at different decimal places** — 146.30, 1.463, 1463, 14.63. **The question is testing whether the dilution factor is applied at all, and in which direction.**

| Error | Result |
|---|---|
| **Dividing by 100 instead of multiplying** | 0.1463 |
| **Omitting the dilution entirely** | 14.63 — **option (d)** |
| **Omitting the ultimate-BOD step** | 1000 (not offered) |
| **Correct** | **1463** ✓ |

> **A sanity check settles the magnitude without any arithmetic: raw domestic sewage has a BOD of a few hundred mg/L, and strong sewage over 1000.** A value of 14.63 mg/L would be **treated effluent**, not raw sewage — and a 3 ml sample would never have been used for something that weak.

> **The dilution itself tells you what to expect.** A 100-fold dilution is chosen precisely because the sample is strong; the analyst's choice of dilution is a statement about the expected result.

**Why dilution is necessary at all:**

> **The BOD bottle can only supply the oxygen dissolved in it — about 9 mg/L at 20 °C.**

> **A sample with a BOD of 1000 mg/L would consume all of it within hours**, and the test would measure only how fast the bottle ran out, not the sample's demand.

> **The rule of thumb: the DO depletion should be at least 2 mg/L and the residual DO at least 1 mg/L.** Here the depletion is 10 mg/L, which is at the upper end — the analyst chose the dilution well.

**Why 5 days and 20 °C:**

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| **5 days** | **Roughly the travel time of English rivers to the sea** — a historical accident that became universal |
| **20 °C** | A representative temperate stream temperature |
| **Dark incubation** | **Prevents algal photosynthesis producing oxygen** and corrupting the result |

> **The 5-day period has no scientific basis at all** — it is a nineteenth-century convention that stuck, and the whole world now reports BOD₅ because everyone else does.

**BOD versus COD:**

| | **BOD** | **COD** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | **BIODEGRADABLE** organic matter | **ALL oxidisable** matter |
| Time | **5 DAYS** | **3 HOURS** |
| Value | Lower | **Higher — COD > BOD always** |

> **The BOD/COD ratio indicates BIODEGRADABILITY**: above about **0.5** the waste suits biological treatment; **below 0.3 it does not**, and a chemical or physical process is needed. **That single ratio is the most useful number in choosing a treatment process.**

examTip.trap: **Stopping at 1000 answers a different question** — the stem asks for the INITIAL (ultimate) BOD. And the options are all the same digits at different decimal places, testing the dilution factor's direction.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate at K = 0.1** — one multiplication converts between them. And the **dilution chosen tells you what to expect**: a 100× dilution means strong sewage, so 14.63 mg/L is absurd.

questions.stem: A C-section is built from two flanges each 5 cm × 1.5 cm and a web 1.5 cm × 7 cm, giving an overall depth of 10 cm and an overall width of 5 cm. The centroid of the section, measured from the outer face of the web and from the bottom, is:
questions.solution:
**1.78 cm, 5 cm.**

**Break the section into three rectangles:**

| Part | Dimensions | **Area** | **x̄ᵢ** | **ȳᵢ** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bottom flange** | 5 × 1.5 | **7.5** | **2.5** | **0.75** |
| **Web** | 1.5 × 7 | **10.5** | **0.75** | **5.0** |
| **Top flange** | 5 × 1.5 | **7.5** | **2.5** | **9.25** |
| **Total** | | **25.5 cm²** | | |

**Horizontal position:**

> **x̄ = (7.5 × 2.5 + 10.5 × 0.75 + 7.5 × 2.5) / 25.5**
>
> **= (18.75 + 7.875 + 18.75)/25.5 = 45.375/25.5 = 1.779 ≈ 1.78 cm** ✓

**Vertical position — by SYMMETRY:**

> **The section is symmetrical about its horizontal centreline, so ȳ = 10/2 = 5 cm exactly.** ✓
>
> **Check: (7.5 × 0.75 + 10.5 × 5 + 7.5 × 9.25)/25.5 = 127.5/25.5 = 5.0** ✓

> **Spotting the symmetry saves the entire second calculation** — and every option gives ȳ = 5, which confirms it and means the question turns wholly on x̄.

**Two checks that dispose of the wrong options at once:**

> **1. The centroid must lie INSIDE the section's overall envelope, so x̄ < 5 cm.** **Option (c), 178 mm = 17.8 cm, is three and a half times the section's width — impossible.** It is the right number with the decimal point moved, and a units check kills it instantly.

> **2. The centroid must lie CLOSE TO THE WEB**, because the web is the largest single area (10.5 cm² of 25.5) and it sits at x = 0.75.
>
> **x̄ = 1.78 is much nearer the web than the mid-width of 2.5**, which is exactly what the area distribution demands. **Option (d), 2 cm, is too far out; option (a), 1.70, is close but does not follow from the arithmetic.**

**Why the centroid matters:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **NEUTRAL AXIS** | **Passes through the centroid** in pure bending |
| **Second moment of area** | Computed about the centroidal axis, via the parallel axis theorem |
| **Section modulus** | **Z = I/y_max** |
| **SHEAR CENTRE** | Where a load must act to avoid twisting |

> **For a channel section the SHEAR CENTRE is the critical extra idea, and it is NOT at the centroid.**

> **It lies OUTSIDE the section, on the opposite side of the web from the flanges.**

> **A load applied through the centroid of a channel therefore TWISTS it** — the section bends and rotates together. **Only a load through the shear centre produces pure bending.**

> **This is why channels are rarely used as isolated beams**, and why they are normally used in pairs, back to back, or restrained against twisting. **It is a genuine design consequence, not a theoretical nicety.**

**The parallel axis theorem** follows on:

> **I = I_centroid + A d²**, with the added term **always positive** — so **the centroidal axis always gives the MINIMUM second moment.**

> **A computed I smaller than the centroidal value is arithmetically impossible**, which is a useful self-check.

**And for a composite section the method is always the same:** divide into simple shapes; take moments of area about a convenient reference; divide by the total area. **Choosing the reference at an edge rather than an arbitrary line avoids sign errors**, which is why x is measured from the web face here.

examTip.trick: **Symmetry gives ȳ = 5 cm without any calculation** — and every option agrees, so the question turns wholly on x̄ = 45.375/25.5 = **1.78 cm**.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) reads 178 mm = 17.8 cm — three and a half times the section's width.** The right digits with the decimal point moved; a units check kills it instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **A channel's SHEAR CENTRE is not at its centroid — it lies OUTSIDE the section.** A load through the centroid TWISTS a channel, which is why channels are rarely used as isolated beams.

questions.stem: A cantilever carries point loads of 300 kN, 500 kN and 800 kN at distances of 0.5 m, 2 m and 4 m respectively from the fixed end. Find the shear force and bending moment at the fixed end.
questions.solution:
**1600 kN and 4350 kNm.**

**Shear force at the fixed end — simply the sum of all the loads:**

> **V = 300 + 500 + 800 = 1600 kN** ✓

**Bending moment at the fixed end — each load times its distance:**

> **M = 300 × 0.5 + 500 × 2 + 800 × 4**
>
> **M = 150 + 1000 + 3200 = 4350 kNm** ✓

**Why a cantilever is the easiest case in structural analysis:**

> **No reactions need be computed at all.** The free end has nothing beyond it, so working from the free end toward the support gives every internal force directly by summing what has been passed.

> **For a simply supported beam you must first solve for the reactions; for a cantilever you never need them.** That is worth remembering under time pressure.

**And both maxima are AT THE FIXED END:**

| Quantity | Maximum | Location |
|---|---|---|
| **Shear force** | **ΣW = 1600 kN** | **Fixed end** |
| **Bending moment** | **ΣWx = 4350 kNm** | **Fixed end** |
| Both | **ZERO** | **Free end** |

> **Which is why a cantilever is deepest at its support and can taper toward its tip** — the section is proportioned to a moment that falls to zero at the free end.

**The distractors, each from a specific error:**

| Option | Error |
|---|---|
| **(b) 1600 N, 4350 Nm** | **Right numbers, wrong UNITS — off by a factor of 1000** |
| **(c) 1680 kN, 4200 kNm** | Arithmetic slip in both |
| **(d) 1450 kN, 4350 kNm** | **Correct moment with a wrong shear** — one load omitted from the sum |

> **Option (b) is the instructive one: the numbers are exactly right and the answer is still wrong.** A shear force of 1600 N is about the weight of two people, which no cantilever carrying 800 kN could possibly have.

> **Always check the magnitude against the given data** — the loads are in kilonewtons, so the answers must be too.

> **And option (d) is worth noticing because it pairs a correct value with an incorrect one.** Checking only the moment, or only the shear, would let it through — both must be verified.

**A dominance check confirms the answer's shape:**

> **The 800 kN load at 4 m contributes 3200 kNm — about 74% of the total moment**, because it is both the largest load and the furthest out.

> **The 300 kN load at 0.5 m contributes only 150 kNm, under 4%.**

> **On a cantilever, distance matters as much as magnitude**, and a load near the support is nearly harmless while one at the tip governs. **That is why the answer must be far closer to 800 × 4 than to the sum of the loads times an average distance.**

**The governing relations, for completeness:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** |
| **No load between loads** | **Constant** | **LINEAR** |

> **So this cantilever's SFD is a set of steps (0 → 800 → 1300 → 1600 kN toward the support) and its BMD is a series of straight segments with kinks under each load** — steepening toward the support as the accumulated shear grows.

> **The change in moment between two points equals the AREA of the shear diagram between them**, which is the fastest way to check the 4350 by hand.

verification.notes: The source presents this item as "find the shear force and bending moment of the given beam" with a figure that the scan does not reproduce legibly. The loading has been recovered exactly from the source's own worked solution — shear force = 300 + 500 + 800 = 1600 kN and moment = 300×0.5 + 500×2 + 800×4 = 4350 kNm — which identifies a cantilever carrying those three loads at 0.5 m, 2 m and 4 m from the fixed end. The stem has been rewritten as an equivalent self-contained text question testing the same computation, and the keyed letter (a) is unchanged.

examTip.trick: **A cantilever needs no reactions at all** — work from the free end. V = ΣW = 1600 kN and M = ΣWx = 4350 kNm, both maximum at the fixed end and both zero at the tip.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) has the right numbers in the wrong UNITS** — 1600 N is the weight of two people. And option (d) pairs a *correct* moment with a wrong shear, so both values must be checked.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a cantilever, distance matters as much as magnitude** — the 800 kN load at 4 m supplies 74% of the moment while the 300 kN at 0.5 m supplies under 4%.

questions.stem: A catchment of 225 ha area has a runoff coefficient of 0.33. A storm of duration more than the time of concentration and intensity 7.78 cm/hr occurs over the area. Find the peak discharge by the rational method.
questions.solution:
**16 m³/s.**

**The rational formula in metric units:**

> **Q = C I A / 360**, with **C** dimensionless, **I in mm/hr**, **A in hectares** and **Q in m³/s.**

**Working:**

> **I = 7.78 cm/hr = 77.8 mm/hr**
>
> **Q = 0.33 × 77.8 × 225 / 360**
>
> **Q = 5776.65/360 = 16.05 ≈ 16 m³/s** ✓

**The unit conversion is the first trap:**

> **The intensity is given in cm/hr but the formula takes mm/hr.** Substituting 7.78 directly gives **1.6 m³/s** — a tenth of the answer, and a value that no option offers, so the error is silent.

> **Where the 360 comes from:** **1 ha·mm/hr = 10⁴ m² × 10⁻³ m ÷ 3600 s = 1/360 m³/s.** The constant is a pure unit conversion, which is why it must be fed the right units.

**The second trap is in the options, and it is the more interesting one:**

| Option | Value | Comparison |
|---|---|---|
| **(a) 16 m³/s** | **16 m³/s** | **✓** |
| (b) 1600 L/s | **1.6 m³/s** | **Ten times too small** |
| (c) 160 cm³/s | **0.00016 m³/s** | **A hundred thousand times too small** |
| (d) 16,000 L/min | **0.267 m³/s** | Sixty times too small |

> **All four options use the digits 16, in four different units.** The question is testing unit fluency as much as the formula.

> **Option (c) is the clearest illustration: 160 cm³/s is about a teacup a second**, which no 225-hectare catchment could produce in a storm. **A magnitude check disposes of it without any conversion.**

**Why the stem says the storm duration exceeds the time of concentration:**

> **That condition is what makes the rational method valid.**

> **The TIME OF CONCENTRATION is the time for runoff to travel from the hydraulically most remote point of the catchment to the outlet.**

> **Only when the storm lasts at least that long does the WHOLE catchment contribute simultaneously — and only then is the peak discharge the full CIA/360.**

> **A shorter storm leaves part of the catchment still draining when the rain stops, and the peak is lower.**

> **Which is why the DESIGN STORM DURATION IS TAKEN EQUAL TO THE TIME OF CONCENTRATION**: any shorter and the whole area does not contribute; any longer and the intensity falls (since intensity decreases with duration in every IDF relationship). **That duration maximises the peak, and it is the whole basis of the method.**

**Runoff coefficients:**

| Surface | **C** |
|---|---|
| **Roofs, concrete, asphalt** | **0.70 – 0.95** |
| Gravel, macadam | 0.35 – 0.70 |
| Lawns, parks | 0.05 – 0.25 |
| **Cultivated land, forest** | **0.10 – 0.30** |

> **C = 0.33 here indicates a largely rural catchment.** A composite catchment uses an **area-weighted average** of the individual coefficients.

> **And URBANISATION is what changes the number most.** Paving a catchment can raise C from 0.2 to 0.8 — **quadrupling the peak discharge from the same rainfall** — while simultaneously **shortening the time of concentration**, which raises the design intensity as well.

> **The two effects compound**, which is why urban drainage systems are so often overwhelmed by development that was never accompanied by drainage upgrading.

**The method's limits:** it assumes uniform rainfall over the whole area and a constant C, so it is reliable only for **small catchments — conventionally under about 50 km²** — and is used for **storm drains, culverts and small bridges** rather than for river flood estimation.

examTip.trick: **Q = CIA/360 takes I in mm/hr** — convert 7.78 cm/hr to 77.8 first. The 360 is a pure unit conversion (1 ha·mm/hr = 1/360 m³/s), so it must be fed the right units.
examTip.trap: **All four options use the digits 16 in different units.** 1600 L/s is 1.6 m³/s (ten times small) and 160 cm³/s is about a teacup a second — absurd for 225 hectares.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design duration = TIME OF CONCENTRATION** — shorter and the whole catchment doesn't contribute, longer and the intensity falls. And **urbanisation raises C and shortens t_c together**, compounding the peak.

questions.stem: Find the discharge through a rectangular orifice 3.2 m wide and 1.7 m deep fitted to a large tank. The water level in the tank is 3.3 m above the top edge of the orifice. Take C_d = 0.6.
questions.solution:
**29.4 m³/s.**

**The large rectangular orifice formula:**

> **Q = (2/3) C_d b √(2g) (H₂^{3/2} − H₁^{3/2})**

**Identifying the heads — this is where the question is won or lost:**

> **H₁ = head to the TOP edge = 3.3 m**
>
> **H₂ = head to the BOTTOM edge = 3.3 + 1.7 = 5.0 m**

> **The 1.7 m is the orifice's DEPTH, not a head.** It must be added to the 3.3 m to reach the lower edge.

**Working:**

> **(2/3) × 0.6 × 3.2 = 1.28**
>
> **√(2 × 9.81) = 4.429**
>
> **5^{1.5} = 11.180; 3.3^{1.5} = 5.995; difference = 5.185**
>
> **Q = 1.28 × 4.429 × 5.185 = 29.4 m³/s** ✓

**Why a LARGE orifice needs this formula at all:**

> **A SMALL orifice is treated as having a single head, because the variation of pressure across its height is negligible: Q = C_d A √(2gH).**

> **A LARGE orifice has appreciably more head at its bottom than at its top, so the velocity varies across the opening** — and the discharge must be found by integrating **dQ = C_d b √(2gh) dh** from H₁ to H₂.

> **That integration produces the 2/3 and the 3/2 power**, which is why the formula looks as it does.

> **The conventional dividing line is H > 5d**, where d is the orifice depth. **Here H₁/d = 3.3/1.7 ≈ 1.9, well under 5** — so the large-orifice treatment is required, and using the small-orifice formula would be wrong.

**Checking against the small-orifice formula shows how much it matters:**

> **Mean head = 3.3 + 0.85 = 4.15 m; A = 3.2 × 1.7 = 5.44 m²**
>
> **Q = 0.6 × 5.44 × √(2 × 9.81 × 4.15) = 0.6 × 5.44 × 9.025 = 29.5 m³/s**

> **Very close here — because the head is still fairly large relative to the depth.** The two diverge sharply as the orifice becomes deep relative to its head, and that is exactly when the distinction becomes essential.

**Note the resemblance to the weir formula:**

> **A rectangular weir is Q = (2/3) C_d b √(2g) H^{3/2}** — the same expression with **H₁ = 0.**

> **A weir IS a large orifice whose top edge is at the water surface**, which is why the formulae are identical in form. Seeing that connection makes both easier to recall and harder to confuse.

**The coefficients, and their relationship:**

| Coefficient | Symbol | Typical | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contraction** | **C_c** | **0.61 – 0.69** | **Vena contracta area ÷ orifice area** |
| **Velocity** | **C_v** | **0.95 – 0.99** | Actual ÷ theoretical velocity |
| **DISCHARGE** | **C_d** | **0.60 – 0.65** | **C_d = C_c × C_v** |

> **C_d ≈ 0.62 is the standard value for a sharp-edged orifice**, and it is close to C_c because C_v is nearly 1 — **the losses are dominated by CONTRACTION, not by friction.**

> **The VENA CONTRACTA — the narrowest section of the jet, about half a diameter downstream — is where the flow area is genuinely smallest**, and it is the reason C_d is well below 1 even for a perfectly smooth orifice.

> **A bell-mouthed or rounded entry eliminates the contraction and raises C_d to about 0.98**, which is why intakes and nozzles are shaped rather than cut square.

examTip.trick: **H₁ = 3.3 m (top edge), H₂ = 3.3 + 1.7 = 5.0 m (bottom edge).** The 1.7 m is the orifice DEPTH, not a head — it must be added. That single step decides the question.
examTip.trap: **Use the LARGE orifice formula when H < 5d.** Here H₁/d ≈ 1.9, so the head varies appreciably across the opening and a single mean head is not strictly valid.
examTip.mnemonic: **A weir IS a large orifice with H₁ = 0** — the formulae are identical in form. And **C_d ≈ 0.62 is dominated by CONTRACTION, not friction**, which is why a rounded entry raises it to 0.98.

questions.stem: The optimistic time is 15 days and the pessimistic time is 30 days. The standard deviation of the project is:
questions.solution:
**2.5 days.**

**The PERT standard deviation:**

> **σ = (t_p − t_o)/6**

**Working:**

> **σ = (30 − 15)/6 = 15/6 = 2.5 days** ✓

**Why divide by 6:**

> **PERT assumes the activity duration follows a BETA distribution, and that the optimistic and pessimistic estimates represent the practical EXTREMES of that distribution.**

> **For a distribution spanning ±3σ about its mean, the total range is 6σ** — so **σ = range/6.**

> **The 6 is therefore not arbitrary: it is the number of standard deviations spanning the full range.** Knowing that means the formula never has to be recalled separately from the expected-time one.

**The companion relation:**

> **Expected time t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6**
>
> **Variance σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²**

> **Both divide by 6, but for different reasons** — the expected time because the weights (1 + 4 + 1) sum to 6, and the standard deviation because the range spans 6σ. **A coincidence of arithmetic, not of meaning.**

> **The weight of 4 on the MOST LIKELY time reflects that it is the mode of the distribution and carries most of the information**, while the two extremes are single estimates each.

**Note that the most likely time is not given here — and is not needed:**

> **σ depends only on the RANGE (t_p − t_o).** The most likely time affects the expected duration but not the spread.

> **That is worth noticing under exam pressure**: an apparently incomplete question may be complete for what is actually asked.

**What σ means in practice:**

> **It measures the UNCERTAINTY in the estimate.**

| Range | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Wide (large σ)** | **Novel or poorly understood work — high risk** |
| **Narrow (small σ)** | Familiar, repetitive work — predictable |

> **Here the range is 15 days on a most-likely duration of the same order — a very wide spread**, indicating an activity whose duration is genuinely uncertain.

**And how the activity variances combine:**

> **For the project as a whole, the VARIANCES of the activities on the CRITICAL PATH are ADDED, and the project standard deviation is the square root of that sum:**
>
> **σ_project = √(Σσᵢ²)**

> **Variances add; standard deviations do NOT.** Adding the σ values directly is a genuine and common error, and it **overestimates** the project's uncertainty.

> **The consequence is important: the project's uncertainty grows more slowly than the number of activities**, because the square root damps the sum. A long chain of individually uncertain activities is more predictable in total than each is alone.

**The probability calculation** PERT exists to support:

> **Z = (T_scheduled − T_expected)/σ_project**, and the normal table then gives the probability of finishing by the scheduled date.

> **That is the whole reason for computing σ at all** — it converts a schedule from a single number into a statement of likelihood, which is what a client actually needs.

**CPM versus PERT:**

| | **CPM** | **PERT** |
|---|---|---|
| Time estimate | **Single, DETERMINISTIC** | **Three — probabilistic** |
| Suits | **Repetitive work — construction** | **Novel work — R&D** |
| Orientation | **ACTIVITY**-oriented | **EVENT**-oriented |
| Cost | **Handles cost–time trade-off (crashing)** | Time only |

> **A caution about PERT's limitation: it considers only the critical path.** A parallel path with high variance may overrun and become critical, and PERT's probability calculation will not have anticipated it — which is why **Monte Carlo simulation** has largely superseded it where the stakes justify the effort.

examTip.trick: **σ = (t_p − t_o)/6 = (30 − 15)/6 = 2.5.** The 6 is the number of standard deviations spanning the full range (±3σ) — not an arbitrary constant.
examTip.trap: **The most likely time is not given and is not needed** — σ depends only on the RANGE. An apparently incomplete question may be complete for what is actually asked.
examTip.mnemonic: **VARIANCES add along the critical path; standard deviations do NOT.** σ_project = √(Σσᵢ²), so project uncertainty grows more slowly than the number of activities.

questions.stem: Activities A, B and C are the immediate predecessors of activity Y. If the earliest finishing times for the three activities are 12, 15 and 10, then the earliest starting time for Y is:
questions.solution:
**15.**

> The source states the rule: **the earliest starting time for activity Y is determined by the MAXIMUM of the earliest finishing times of its immediate predecessors — in this case, 15.**

**Why the MAXIMUM:**

> **Y cannot start until EVERY predecessor is finished.**

> **A and C are done at 12 and 10, but B is not finished until 15 — so Y waits.**

> **The LATEST-finishing predecessor governs**, and that is always the largest number.

> **Taking the minimum (10) would mean starting Y before B is complete, which the precedence relationship forbids.** Option (a) is placed there for exactly that error.

**This is the FORWARD PASS**, and it pairs with the backward pass:

| Pass | Direction | Computes | Rule at a node |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD** | **Start → finish** | **EST, EFT** | **MAXIMUM of incoming** |
| **BACKWARD** | **Finish → start** | **LST, LFT** | **MINIMUM of outgoing** |

> **Forward takes the maximum; backward takes the minimum.** Both express the same physical requirement from opposite ends:

> **An activity cannot start until ALL predecessors are done (hence max), and must finish before ANY successor starts (hence min).**

> **Reversing them is the single commonest error in network analysis**, and the reliable check is to ask what must physically be true rather than to recall which word goes with which pass.

**The relations:**

> **EFT = EST + duration**
> **LST = LFT − duration**
> **TOTAL FLOAT = LST − EST = LFT − EFT**

**What the waiting means:**

> **A and C finish at 12 and 10 but Y starts at 15 — so A has 3 days of slack and C has 5, while B has none.**

> **B lies on the critical path through this node; A and C do not.**

> **That is how the critical path is found: it is the chain of activities with ZERO float, and it is the LONGEST path through the network.**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Zero float** | **Any delay delays the whole project** |
| **Longest path** | Determines the shortest possible project duration |
| **May be more than one** | Multiple critical paths are common |
| **Can SHIFT** | **Crashing one path may make another critical** |

> **The last point is what makes crashing iterative.** Shortening the critical path helps only until a second path becomes critical, after which both must be shortened together — so **the cost of each additional day saved rises in steps**, not smoothly.

**The varieties of float:**

| Float | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | Delay possible **without delaying the PROJECT** |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible **without delaying the SUCCESSOR's early start** |
| **INDEPENDENT float** | Delay possible **without affecting anything on either side** |

> **Free float ≤ total float always**, and **total float belongs to a PATH, not to a single activity** — using one activity's total float consumes the float of everything downstream on the same chain.

> **Which is why two activities on the same chain cannot both use "their" float**, and why float must be managed at the path level rather than activity by activity.

examTip.trick: **Y cannot start until EVERY predecessor is done, so the LATEST one governs** — the maximum, 15. Taking the minimum would start Y before B is complete.
examTip.trap: **Forward pass = MAXIMUM; backward pass = MINIMUM.** Reversing them is the commonest network error. Ask what must physically be true rather than recalling which word goes where.
examTip.mnemonic: **A has 3 days slack, C has 5, B has none — B is on the critical path.** And the critical path can **SHIFT** when crashed, which is why the cost of each saved day rises in steps.

questions.stem: What is the pressure at 1 m below the ground water surface?
questions.solution:
**9.81 kN/m².**

**Working:**

> **P = ρ g h = 1000 × 9.81 × 1 = 9810 N/m² = 9.81 kN/m²** ✓

**The whole question is the UNIT, not the number:**

> **Every option carries the digits 9.81 or something near them, and three of the four are in N/m² rather than kN/m².**

| Option | Value | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| (a) 9.81 N/m² | **Right number, WRONG unit** | **A thousand times too small** |
| **(b) 9.81 kN/m²** | | **✓** |
| (c) 10 N/m² | Wrong number and unit | — |
| (d) 25 N/m² | Unrelated | — |

> **A pressure of 9.81 N/m² is about the weight of a gram spread over a square metre** — utterly negligible, and nothing like the pressure a metre of water exerts.

> **The sanity check is available without any calculation: standing in a metre of water, the pressure at your feet is appreciable, not imperceptible.**

**The relations worth carrying:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **1 m of water** | **9.81 kPa = 9.81 kN/m²** |
| **10 m of water** | **≈ 98.1 kPa ≈ 1 atmosphere** |
| **1 atmosphere** | **101.3 kPa = 10.3 m of water = 760 mm of mercury** |
| **1 bar** | **100 kPa ≈ 10.2 m of water** |

> **"One metre of water is about 10 kPa" is the single most useful approximation in hydraulics** — it converts head to pressure and back in one step, and it is accurate to 2%.

**Why pressure varies only with DEPTH:**

> **In a static fluid, pressure depends solely on the vertical depth below the free surface** — not on the shape of the container, its volume, or the area of the surface.

> **This is the HYDROSTATIC PARADOX**: a narrow tube and a wide reservoir filled to the same level exert the **same pressure** on the base.

> **The force differs, because force is pressure times area — but the pressure does not.**

> **It is why a dam's design depends on the water's DEPTH and not on the size of the reservoir behind it**, and why a small pond 10 m deep loads a wall exactly as a lake 10 m deep does.

**And PASCAL's law completes the picture:**

> **Pressure at a point in a static fluid acts EQUALLY IN ALL DIRECTIONS.**

> **Which is why pressure on a submerged surface always acts NORMAL to it, whatever its orientation.**

**For a submerged plane surface:**

> **Total force F = γ A h̄**, acting at the **CENTRE OF PRESSURE**, at depth
>
> **h_cp = h̄ + I_G/(A h̄)**

> **The centre of pressure is ALWAYS BELOW the centroid**, because pressure increases with depth and weights the resultant downward. **The two coincide only for a horizontal surface**, where the pressure is uniform.

> **Forgetting that offset is a real design error**, since it changes the overturning moment on a wall or gate — the force may be right while the moment is wrong.

**In soil mechanics the same 9.81 kN/m³ appears constantly:**

> **γ_water = 9.81 kN/m³**, and pore pressure **u = γ_w × depth below the water table.**

> **σ′ = σ − u** — Terzaghi's principle, in which every term is a force per unit area, which is why the specific weight rather than the density is the quantity carried through the calculation.

examTip.trick: **P = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 1 = 9810 N/m² = 9.81 kN/m².** The question is entirely about the **unit** — three options give the right digits in N/m².
examTip.trap: **9.81 N/m² is about a gram spread over a square metre** — imperceptible. Standing in a metre of water, the pressure at your feet is clearly not that. A sanity check needs no arithmetic.
examTip.mnemonic: **1 m of water ≈ 10 kPa; 10 m ≈ 1 atmosphere.** And the **hydrostatic paradox**: a narrow tube and a wide reservoir at the same level exert the same *pressure* — depth alone governs.

questions.stem: If the web area of a deep beam is 180,000 mm², the minimum side face reinforcement is:
questions.solution:
**180 mm².**

**Working:**

> **Side face reinforcement = 0.1% of the web area**
>
> **A_s = 180,000 × 0.001 = 180 mm²** ✓

> The source confirms both the rule and the arithmetic: **provide at 0.1% of web area and distribute it equally on both side faces. Minimum side reinforcement area = 180,000 × 0.1% = 180 mm².**

**The 0.1% is easy to misapply, and option (b) exists for that:**

> **0.1% means 0.001, NOT 0.01.**
>
> **Using 1% gives 1800 mm² — exactly option (b).**

> **The percentage-to-decimal conversion is the entire trap**, and it is a factor of ten. **Writing 0.1% as 0.1/100 = 0.001 before multiplying removes any doubt.**

**When side face reinforcement is required (IS 456 cl. 26.5.1.3):**

| Condition | Threshold |
|---|---|
| **Beam NOT subject to torsion** | **Overall depth > 750 mm** |
| **Beam SUBJECT to torsion** | **Overall depth > 450 mm** |

> **The threshold is LOWER for a beam in torsion**, because torsion produces diagonal tension on the side faces themselves — so the steel there is resisting a real force rather than merely controlling cracking.

**And the spacing requirement:**

> **The bars must be distributed EQUALLY on the two faces, at a spacing not exceeding 300 mm or the web thickness, whichever is less.**

> **Spacing matters as much as area here.** The purpose is crack control, and **many small bars close together control cracks far better than a few large bars of the same total area** — a crack can only open as wide as the gap between the bars restraining it.

**Why it is needed at all — this is the substance of the clause:**

> **In a deep beam, the main tension steel is concentrated at the bottom and the compression zone is at the top. The large web between them has NO reinforcement crossing it.**

> **But the concrete there is still in tension over much of the depth**, and it shrinks and moves with temperature like the rest of the member.

> **Without steel, that region develops WIDE, WIDELY SPACED cracks** — because there is nothing to distribute the strain into many fine cracks instead of a few large ones.

| Effect resisted | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shrinkage** | Restrained drying shrinkage of the web |
| **Temperature** | Thermal movement |
| **Crack width control** | **The principal purpose** |
| **Torsional diagonal tension** | Where torsion applies |

> **This is a SERVICEABILITY provision, not a strength one.** The beam would carry its design load without the side bars — but it would look cracked, and wide cracks admit moisture and corrode the main steel.

> **Which is the real argument: crack width governs DURABILITY.** The IS 456 limits are **0.3 mm normally and 0.2 mm in aggressive exposure**, and side face steel is what keeps the web within them.

**The family of minimum reinforcement provisions**, all serving different purposes:

| Provision | Requirement | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum tension steel** | **0.85 bd/f_y** (0.205% for Fe 415) | **DUCTILITY — prevent sudden failure at first cracking** |
| **Maximum tension steel** | **4% of gross area** | **Constructibility — room for concrete to pass** |
| **Minimum shear reinforcement** | **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)** | Prevent brittle shear failure |
| **Side face reinforcement** | **0.1% of web area, D > 750 mm** | **Crack control** ← |
| **Slab minimum** | **0.12% (Fe 415) of gross area** | **Shrinkage and temperature** |

> **Note that these percentages are taken on DIFFERENT reference areas** — bd for tension steel, gross bD for the maximum and for slabs, and the web area here. **Applying the right percentage to the wrong area is as large an error as using the wrong percentage.**

examTip.trick: **0.1% = 0.001.** 180,000 × 0.001 = **180 mm²**. Writing the percentage as 0.1/100 before multiplying removes all doubt.
examTip.trap: **Using 1% instead of 0.1% gives 1800 mm² — exactly option (b).** The percentage-to-decimal conversion is the whole trap, and it is a factor of ten.
examTip.mnemonic: **Required above 750 mm depth — but above only 450 mm if the beam carries TORSION**, because torsion puts real diagonal tension on the side faces rather than mere shrinkage.

questions.stem: If the nominal rate of interest is 10% per annum and there is quarterly compounding, the effective rate of interest will be:
questions.solution:
**10.38% per annum.**

**The effective interest rate:**

> **i_eff = (1 + i_nom/n)ⁿ − 1**, where **n** is the number of compounding periods per year.

**Working:**

> **i_eff = (1 + 0.10/4)⁴ − 1 = (1.025)⁴ − 1**
>
> **(1.025)⁴ = 1.10381**
>
> **i_eff = 0.10381 = 10.38%** ✓

**Why the effective rate EXCEEDS the nominal rate:**

> **Because interest earned in one quarter itself earns interest in the following quarters.**

> **The nominal rate ignores that. The effective rate captures it.**

> **So the effective rate is ALWAYS greater than the nominal rate whenever compounding occurs more than once a year** — which immediately eliminates option (a), and tells you the answer must be the largest plausible figure among the rest.

**How the frequency matters:**

| Compounding | n | **i_eff at 10% nominal** |
|---|---|---|
| **Annual** | 1 | **10.00%** |
| **Semi-annual** | 2 | **10.25%** ← option (c) |
| **QUARTERLY** | **4** | **10.38%** ✓ |
| Monthly | 12 | **10.47%** |
| Daily | 365 | 10.5156% |
| **CONTINUOUS** | ∞ | **e^{0.10} − 1 = 10.517%** |

> **Note that option (c), 10.25%, is the SEMI-ANNUAL answer** — the right method with the wrong n. **That is the distractor to watch**, because it comes from a correct calculation of a different case.

> **And option (b), 10.10%, corresponds to no standard frequency at all.**

**The most interesting feature of the table is that it CONVERGES:**

> **Going from annual to quarterly gains 0.38 percentage points; from quarterly to daily gains only 0.14; and from daily to continuous gains 0.0014.**

> **The effective rate approaches a CEILING of e^i − 1 as the frequency increases without limit.**

> **Compounding more often has rapidly diminishing returns** — which is worth knowing, because it means the difference between monthly and daily compounding is negligible in any practical decision, while the difference between annual and quarterly is not.

**Why this matters in engineering economics:**

> **All the compound interest factors — F = P(1+i)ⁿ, the sinking fund, capital recovery and the rest — require the EFFECTIVE rate for the period being used.**

> **Using a nominal rate in them systematically UNDERSTATES the cost of borrowing and the return on investment.**

> **And the error compounds**: over 20 years at 10% nominal, using 10% instead of 10.38% understates the future value by about **7%** — small annually, substantial cumulatively.

**The disclosure point** worth carrying:

> **A lender quoting "10% per annum, compounded quarterly" is quoting a NOMINAL rate.** The borrower actually pays **10.38%.**

> **This is precisely why consumer credit legislation in many countries requires the EFFECTIVE annual rate (APR) to be disclosed** — the nominal rate understates what is genuinely being charged, and the gap widens with the compounding frequency.

**And the related rules of thumb:**

> **RULE OF 72: money doubles in approximately 72/i years** — at 10%, about 7.2 years.

> **F = P(1 + i)ⁿ is EXPONENTIAL in n**: at 10%, a rupee becomes 2.6 in 10 years, 6.7 in 20, and **17.4 in 30.**

> **The same exponential in reverse is what makes DISCOUNTING so severe on long-lived infrastructure** — at 12%, a benefit 50 years away is worth about **0.3%** of its face value, which is why the choice of discount rate often decides a project appraisal more than any engineering input does.

examTip.trick: **i_eff = (1 + 0.10/4)⁴ − 1 = 1.025⁴ − 1 = 10.38%.** And the effective rate ALWAYS exceeds the nominal one when compounding is more frequent than annual — which eliminates option (a) at sight.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), 10.25%, is the SEMI-ANNUAL answer** — right method, wrong n. A correct calculation of the wrong case is the hardest kind of distractor to spot.
examTip.mnemonic: **The effective rate CONVERGES to e^i − 1 = 10.517%.** Annual→quarterly gains 0.38 points; daily→continuous gains 0.0014. Compounding more often has rapidly diminishing returns.

questions.stem: At a certain point in a strained material two direct stresses of 80 N/mm² (tensile) and 60 N/mm² (tensile) act along with a shear stress of 20 N/mm². Find the major principal stress.
questions.solution:
**92.36 N/mm².**

**The principal stress formula:**

> **σ₁,₂ = (σ_x + σ_y)/2 ± √[((σ_x − σ_y)/2)² + τ_xy²]**

**Working:**

> **Mean stress = (80 + 60)/2 = 70**
>
> **(σ_x − σ_y)/2 = (80 − 60)/2 = 10**
>
> **Radius = √(10² + 20²) = √(100 + 400) = √500 = 22.36**
>
> **σ₁ = 70 + 22.36 = 92.36 N/mm²** ✓
>
> **σ₂ = 70 − 22.36 = 47.64 N/mm²**

**Reading the formula as MOHR'S CIRCLE makes it impossible to forget:**

| Formula term | On the circle |
|---|---|
| **(σ_x + σ_y)/2 = 70** | **The CENTRE** |
| **√[((σ_x−σ_y)/2)² + τ²] = 22.36** | **The RADIUS** |
| **σ₁ = centre + radius** | Rightmost point |
| **σ₂ = centre − radius** | Leftmost point |
| **τ_max = the RADIUS itself = 22.36** | Top of the circle |

> **The centre depends only on the SUM of the direct stresses; the radius only on their DIFFERENCE and the shear.** That is why adding a hydrostatic stress moves the circle without changing its size — and why shear stress is unaffected by it.

**Two checks that verify the answer instantly:**

> **1. σ₁ + σ₂ must equal σ_x + σ_y.**
>
> **92.36 + 47.64 = 140 = 80 + 60** ✓
>
> **The sum of the direct stresses is INVARIANT** — it does not depend on the orientation of the axes, so this check works on any such problem.

> **2. σ₁ must EXCEED the larger applied direct stress (80).**
>
> **Adding shear to a state of direct stress always increases the maximum principal stress.** **Option (a), 90, is plausible; but the value must exceed 80, which rules nothing out here — while a computed σ₁ below 80 would be certainly wrong.**

**The maximum shear stress and where it acts:**

> **τ_max = radius = 22.36 N/mm²**, and it acts on planes at **45° to the principal planes.**

> **This is why a ductile material in a tensile test fails on a 45° plane** — the maximum shear is there, and ductile failure is a shear phenomenon.

> **A brittle material fails perpendicular to the maximum tensile stress instead**, which is why cast iron and concrete crack across the direction of pull while mild steel necks and shears diagonally. **The same stress state, two different failure planes, because two different mechanisms govern.**

**The principal planes themselves:**

> **tan 2θ = 2τ_xy/(σ_x − σ_y) = 40/20 = 2, so 2θ = 63.43° and θ = 31.7°.**

> **On the principal planes the SHEAR STRESS IS ZERO** — that is the defining property, and it is what makes them worth finding. The material is in pure direct stress there.

**Why principal stresses matter in design:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Failure criteria** | **Maximum principal stress (brittle), maximum shear or von Mises (ductile)** |
| **RC design** | **Diagonal tension from shear is what stirrups resist** |
| Crack direction | **Cracks form perpendicular to the maximum principal TENSILE stress** |
| Weld and connection design | Combined states |

> **In a reinforced concrete beam the principal tensile stress near the supports is INCLINED at about 45°**, which is exactly why **shear cracks run diagonally** and why bent-up bars and inclined stirrups follow that direction.

> **Concrete's weakness is in tension, so it cracks along the plane perpendicular to the maximum principal tension** — the whole logic of shear reinforcement follows from this single calculation applied at a point in the web.

examTip.trick: **Read it as Mohr's circle: centre 70, radius √(10² + 20²) = 22.36.** σ₁ = 70 + 22.36 = **92.36**, σ₂ = 47.64, and τ_max is the radius itself.
examTip.trap: **Check σ₁ + σ₂ = σ_x + σ_y**: 92.36 + 47.64 = 140 = 80 + 60 ✓. The sum of direct stresses is INVARIANT with axis orientation, so this verifies any such answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **τ_max acts at 45° to the principal planes** — which is why ductile steel fails on a 45° plane while brittle concrete cracks perpendicular to the maximum tension. Same stress state, two mechanisms.

questions.stem: If the superelevation provided on a highway is zero, then the design speed of a highway having a curve of 200 m radius and coefficient of friction 0.10 is:
questions.solution:
**50 km/h.**

**The governing relation:**

> **e + f = V²/(127 R)**

**Working:**

> **0 + 0.10 = V²/(127 × 200)**
>
> **V² = 0.10 × 25,400 = 2540**
>
> **V = √2540 = 50.4 km/h ≈ 50 km/h** ✓

**With e = 0, FRICTION ALONE resists the centrifugal force** — which is the point of the question.

> **The whole lateral force must be carried by the tyre–road contact**, with no help from the banked cross-fall.

> **That is why the permissible speed is so modest for a 200 m radius**: with e = 0.07 as well, the same curve would allow **√(127 × 200 × 0.17) = 65.7 km/h.**

> **Superelevation is worth about 15 km/h on this curve**, and that comparison shows exactly what banking buys.

**Where the 127 comes from:**

> **The mechanics give R = v²/(g(e + f)) with v in m/s.**
>
> **Converting: v = V/3.6, so v² = V²/12.96, giving R = V²/(12.96 × 9.81 × (e+f)) = V²/(127.1(e+f))**

> **127 = 3.6² × 9.81** — a unit conversion, not a physical constant. It disappears entirely if the calculation is done in m/s.

**Note the friction value given here:**

> **f = 0.10 is LOWER than the usual IRC design value of 0.15.**

> **Both are deliberately conservative.** Actual tyre–road friction on dry asphalt is around 0.7 to 0.8 — several times higher.

> **The design value must hold for the WORST case: a worn tyre on a wet, polished, poorly maintained surface**, and it must leave a margin for the driver who is not concentrating.

> **Using a realistic friction value in design would produce curves that are safe only in good conditions**, which is precisely the situation design exists to avoid.

**Where superelevation is zero in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very large radius curves** | Banking is unnecessary — friction alone suffices |
| **Urban roads with kerbs and drainage constraints** | Cross-fall is set by drainage, not by the curve |
| **Junction approaches** | Banking would conflict with the intersecting road |
| **Existing roads not designed for the speed** | The common real case |

> **In an urban street the cross-fall usually has to serve DRAINAGE**, and it cannot be tilted to suit a curve without ponding water on one side. **So the speed is restricted instead** — which is the correct response and exactly what this calculation determines.

**The IRC design procedure**, for the general case:

> **Step 1 — assume superelevation alone carries the force at 75% of design speed: e = V²/(225 R).**
>
> **Step 2 — if e exceeds e_max, cap it and check that friction can take the remainder.**
>
> **Step 3 — if friction is inadequate, RESTRICT THE SPEED.**

> **The 225 in step 1 is 127 ÷ 0.75²** — the same constant adjusted for designing at three-quarters of the full speed, which is an allowance for **slow-moving vehicles** that the simple formula ignores.

**And the limits on e:**

| Terrain | **e_max** |
|---|---|
| **Plain and rolling** | **7%** |
| **Hilly, not snow-bound** | **10%** |
| **SNOW-BOUND** | **7%** |

> **The limit is set by the SLOW vehicle, not the fast one** — a car stopped on a steeply banked curve in the wet has only friction holding it from sliding down the slope.

> **And snow-bound roads are capped at 7% because ice destroys the very friction a steep cross-fall depends on.**

examTip.trick: **With e = 0, friction alone resists the centrifugal force.** V = √(127 × 200 × 0.10) = √2540 = **50.4 ≈ 50 km/h**.
examTip.trap: **f = 0.10 here, not the usual 0.15** — read the value given rather than substituting the familiar one. And 127 = 3.6² × 9.81, a unit conversion that vanishes if you work in m/s.
examTip.mnemonic: **Superelevation is worth ~15 km/h on this curve** (65.7 vs 50.4). In urban streets the cross-fall must serve **drainage**, so the speed is restricted instead — which is what this calculation finds.

questions.stem: In an inward flow reaction turbine, the velocity of flow at the inlet is 2 m/s. If the guide vanes make an angle of 30° to the tangential velocity direction of the runner, the absolute velocity of the water leaving the guide vanes is:
questions.solution:
**4 m/s.**

**From the inlet velocity triangle:**

> **sin α₁ = V_f1 / V₁**
>
> **V₁ = V_f1 / sin α₁ = 2 / sin 30° = 2/0.5 = 4 m/s** ✓

**Reading the velocity triangle** — the terms, since they are constantly confused:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **V₁** | **ABSOLUTE velocity of water at inlet** |
| **V_f1** | **Velocity of FLOW — the RADIAL component** |
| **V_w1** | **Velocity of WHIRL — the TANGENTIAL component** |
| **u₁** | **Blade (peripheral) velocity** |
| **V_r1** | Relative velocity of water with respect to the blade |
| **α₁** | **Guide vane angle — between V₁ and the TANGENTIAL direction** |

> **The angle is measured from the TANGENTIAL direction, which is why the FLOW (radial) component takes the SINE.**

> **V_f1 = V₁ sin α₁** and **V_w1 = V₁ cos α₁** — the component along the direction the angle is measured from takes the cosine, as always.

> **Here V_w1 = 4 cos30° = 3.46 m/s**, which is the component that actually does the work.

**Why sin 30° = 0.5 makes this a two-second calculation:**

> **Dividing by 0.5 is doubling.** The answer is simply **2 × 2 = 4**, and recognising that removes any need for a calculator.

> **Note the trap in option (b): 2 m/s is the FLOW velocity itself**, offered for anyone who confuses V_f1 with V₁ or forgets to resolve at all.

> **The absolute velocity must ALWAYS EXCEED its own components**, so V₁ > 2 necessarily — which eliminates options (a) and (b) on inspection.

**What each component does:**

> **Euler's turbine equation: Work per unit weight = (V_w1 u₁ − V_w2 u₂)/g**

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **WHIRL velocity V_w** | **Does the WORK — it is the only component in Euler's equation** |
| **FLOW velocity V_f** | **Carries the DISCHARGE: Q = πD b V_f** |

> **The whirl component produces the torque; the flow component delivers the water.** That division explains the entire design of the guide vanes.

> **For maximum efficiency the water should leave the runner with NO WHIRL — V_w2 = 0** — so that all its angular momentum has been given up to the runner.

> **Then the work reduces to V_w1 u₁ / g**, which is the condition every reaction turbine is designed to approach.

**Why the runner cannot simply take everything:**

> **Water leaving with zero whirl still has its FLOW velocity, and that kinetic energy would be lost — which is exactly what the DRAFT TUBE recovers.**

> **A draft tube is a gradually expanding passage from the runner exit to the tailrace.** It does two things:

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Recovers exit kinetic energy** | By decelerating the flow — a diffuser |
| **Allows the runner to be set ABOVE tailwater** | While still using the full head, by creating suction |

> **It is essential in every reaction turbine and absent from every impulse turbine** — because an impulse runner's exit water has already given up its energy and it spins in air anyway.

**INWARD versus OUTWARD flow:**

> **Modern reaction turbines are INWARD flow (Francis type): water enters at the outer periphery and leaves at the centre.**

> **Outward flow turbines are obsolete because they are UNSTABLE at part load** — as the flow increases, the centrifugal effect assists it further, and the machine tends to run away rather than settle.

> **Inward flow is inherently self-regulating**, which is why every practical reaction turbine adopts it.

examTip.trick: **The guide vane angle is measured from the TANGENTIAL direction, so the FLOW component takes the sine.** V₁ = 2/sin30° = 2/0.5 = **4 m/s** — dividing by 0.5 is just doubling.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), 2 m/s, is the FLOW velocity itself** — for anyone who confuses V_f1 with V₁. The absolute velocity must always exceed its own components, which eliminates (a) and (b) at sight.
examTip.mnemonic: **WHIRL does the work (Euler: V_w1u₁/g); FLOW carries the discharge (Q = πDbV_f).** Ideal design leaves the runner with **zero whirl**, and the **draft tube** recovers what flow velocity remains.

questions.stem: The maximum shear stress in a beam of width 300 mm and depth 450 mm with a 50 kN shear force at that section is:
questions.solution:
**0.556 N/mm².**

**For a rectangular section:**

> **τ_max = 1.5 × τ_average = 1.5 V/(b d)**

**Working:**

> **τ_average = 50,000/(300 × 450) = 50,000/135,000 = 0.370 N/mm²**
>
> **τ_max = 1.5 × 0.370 = 0.556 N/mm²** ✓

**Note that option (a), 0.370, is exactly the AVERAGE shear stress** — the answer for anyone who omits the 1.5. **It is the single commonest error in the topic, and the distractor is placed for it precisely.**

**Where the 1.5 comes from:**

> **Shear stress is NOT uniform across the depth. From τ = VAȳ/(Ib), the distribution over a rectangle is PARABOLIC:**

| Position | Shear stress |
|---|---|
| **Top and bottom fibres** | **ZERO** |
| **NEUTRAL AXIS** | **MAXIMUM = 1.5 τ_avg** |

> **The top and bottom are FREE SURFACES with nothing to shear against**, so τ must vanish there — and the parabola therefore peaks at the centre.

> **The 1.5 is simply the ratio of the parabola's peak to its mean value**, which is a geometric fact about parabolas, not a code constant.

**The maximum-to-average ratios worth carrying:**

| Section | **τ_max / τ_avg** |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** | **1.5** |
| **Circle** | **1.33 (4/3)** |
| **Triangle** | 1.5 |
| **I-section (over the web)** | **≈ 1.0 – 1.1** |

> **The I-section's ratio is near 1 because the web carries almost all the shear (about 95%) and carries it almost uniformly.**

> **That is why steel design simply checks V/(web area)** — the refinement of a parabolic distribution is not worth making when the distribution is already nearly flat.

> **And it is the complement of the flanges carrying almost all the bending. Flanges take the MOMENT, the web takes the SHEAR** — the reason the I-section is shaped as it is.

**Is 0.556 N/mm² a problem?**

> **For plain concrete, no. IS 456 permits a design shear strength τ_c of roughly 0.28 to 0.85 N/mm² depending on the grade and the percentage of tension steel** — so this value would typically be within the concrete's own capacity.

> **But the elastic τ_max = 1.5V/bd is NOT what IS 456 uses.** The code works with the **NOMINAL shear stress τ_v = V_u/(b d)** — the average, not the peak — and compares it with τ_c from a table.

> **The 1.5 factor is deliberately absent from the code equation**, because the tabulated τ_c values were themselves derived from tests on the same nominal basis. **Applying the 1.5 to a code check would be double-counting.**

> **Knowing which convention a question is using is essential**, and this item asks for the elastic maximum, which does carry the 1.5.

**And the reason shear is treated so cautiously in concrete:**

> **A flexural failure is DUCTILE** — the beam deflects, cracks widen, and the failure announces itself.

> **A SHEAR failure is SUDDEN and BRITTLE**, with a diagonal crack opening and the beam separating with little warning.

> **That asymmetry is why IS 456 requires MINIMUM shear reinforcement everywhere**, even where calculation shows none is needed: the stirrups exist to ensure the member never chooses the brittle mode.

**Where shear governs:** short deep members — **brackets, corbels, transfer beams, deep beams** — because the moment grows as L² while the shear grows only as L. **In ordinary slender beams, bending governs.**

examTip.trick: **τ_max = 1.5 × V/(bd).** Average = 50,000/135,000 = 0.370, times 1.5 = **0.556 N/mm²**. The 1.5 is the peak-to-mean ratio of a parabola, not a code constant.
examTip.trap: **Option (a), 0.370, is exactly the AVERAGE** — the answer for anyone who omits the 1.5. It is the commonest error in the topic and the distractor exists for it.
examTip.mnemonic: **IS 456 uses the NOMINAL stress τ_v = V_u/bd — the average, WITHOUT the 1.5** — because the tabulated τ_c came from tests on the same basis. Applying 1.5 in a code check double-counts.

questions.stem: For a square footing of effective depth 500 mm and sides of 3 m supporting a column of width 500 mm, what is the critical area to be considered for two-way shear?
questions.solution:
**2.00 m².**

**The critical section for two-way (punching) shear:**

> **A perimeter at a distance d/2 from the face of the column, all the way round.**

**Working:**

> **d = 500 mm = 0.5 m; column side a = 500 mm = 0.5 m**
>
> **Side of the critical perimeter = a + 2(d/2) = a + d = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0 m**
>
> **Perimeter b₀ = 4 × 1.0 = 4.0 m**
>
> **Critical AREA = b₀ × d = 4(a + d) d = 4 × 1.0 × 0.5 = 2.00 m²** ✓

> The source's own figure confirms the form: **Area to be considered = 4(a + d)d = 4(0.5 + 0.5) × 0.5 = 2 m².**

**The idea worth extracting is what "area" means here:**

> **It is NOT a plan area. It is the VERTICAL SURFACE through which the column would punch — the perimeter times the effective depth.**

> **Picture the column pushing a plug of concrete down through the slab.** The plug's sides are the surface that resists, and its area is **perimeter × depth.**

> **That is why the answer has a d in it and why it is not simply 1.0 × 1.0 = 1 m².**

**Why d/2 and not d, or the column face itself?**

> **The punching failure surface is a truncated pyramid sloping outward at about 45° from the column base to the tension steel.**

> **Taking the critical section at d/2 from the face is the code's simplification of that sloping surface into a vertical one** — chosen so that the vertical perimeter has the same average resistance as the real inclined cone.

> **It is an equivalent section, not a physical one**, which is why the d/2 offset must be applied exactly as specified rather than reasoned about afresh.

**ONE-WAY versus TWO-WAY shear** — a footing must be checked for both:

| | **ONE-WAY (beam) shear** | **TWO-WAY (punching) shear** |
|---|---|---|
| **Critical section** | **At distance d from the column face** | **At d/2 from the face, all round** |
| **Shape** | **A straight line across the footing** | **A closed perimeter** |
| Failure | Like a wide beam | **Column punches through** |
| **Permissible stress** | **τ_c from the table** | **τ_c = 0.25√f_ck × k_s — HIGHER** |

> **Note the two different offsets: d for one-way, d/2 for two-way.** Interchanging them is the commonest error, and it changes the answer substantially.

> **The permissible punching stress is HIGHER than the one-way value**, because the concrete around a closed perimeter is confined on all sides and behaves better than an unconfined beam section.

> **k_s = 0.5 + β_c**, capped at 1, where β_c is the ratio of the column's short side to its long side — so a very elongated column gets a reduced allowance, since its behaviour approaches one-way.

**Why punching shear matters so much:**

> **It is a SUDDEN, BRITTLE failure with no warning**, and it is the classic cause of **FLAT SLAB collapses** — where a column punches straight through the slab and the floor above drops onto the one below, often producing progressive collapse through a whole building.

> **In a footing the consequence is equally serious**, since the column would drop through its own base.

> **This is why punching shear is checked before flexure in flat slab design**, and why **shear heads, drop panels, column capitals or shear studs** are provided when the check fails — increasing d or the perimeter b₀ rather than adding tension steel, which does not help.

**The design check:**

> **τ_v = V_u / (b₀ d)**, with V_u the load **outside** the critical perimeter — the soil pressure inside it presses upward on the same plug and is deducted.

> **Forgetting to deduct that inner pressure overestimates the shear**, though conservatively.

examTip.trick: **The "area" is the VERTICAL surface the plug would punch through — perimeter × d**, not a plan area. 4(a + d)d = 4(0.5 + 0.5) × 0.5 = **2.00 m²**.
examTip.trap: **One-way shear is checked at d from the face; two-way at d/2.** Interchanging the two offsets is the commonest error and changes the answer substantially.
examTip.mnemonic: **Punching shear is sudden and brittle — the classic FLAT SLAB collapse.** Fix it by increasing d or the perimeter (drop panels, capitals, shear studs); adding tension steel does not help.

questions.stem: The dimensions of a rectangular channel are 3 m in depth and 4 m in width. Calculate the bed slope of the channel if the specific energy is 3.13 m. Take C = 50.
questions.solution:
**1 in 1200.**

**Step 1 — section properties.**

> **A = B y = 4 × 3 = 12 m²**
>
> **P = B + 2y = 4 + 6 = 10 m**
>
> **R = A/P = 12/10 = 1.2 m**

**Step 2 — find the discharge from the specific energy.**

> **E = y + V²/2g = y + Q²/(2gA²)**
>
> **3.13 = 3 + Q²/(2 × 9.81 × 144)**
>
> **0.13 = Q²/2825.3**
>
> **Q² = 367.3, so Q = 19.16 m³/s**

**Step 3 — apply Chézy's formula.**

> **Q = A C √(R S)**
>
> **19.16 = 12 × 50 × √(1.2 S)**
>
> **√(1.2 S) = 19.16/600 = 0.03193**
>
> **1.2 S = 0.0010196**
>
> **S = 0.00085 = 1/1177 ≈ 1 in 1200** ✓

**The route through the question is what matters:**

> **Specific energy → velocity → discharge → Chézy → slope.**

> **The specific energy is doing one job only: it supplies the VELOCITY.** Everything after that is routine.

> **E − y = V²/2g = 0.13 m**, so **V = √(2 × 9.81 × 0.13) = 1.597 m/s**, and **Q = AV = 12 × 1.597 = 19.16 m³/s** — the same result by a shorter path, and worth using.

**Note how small the velocity head is:**

> **0.13 m out of a total specific energy of 3.13 m — about 4%.**

> **In a deep, slow canal almost all the specific energy is DEPTH**, and the velocity head is a small correction. **That is characteristic of subcritical flow**, and it is a useful check: if the velocity head came out comparable to the depth, the flow would be near critical and the arithmetic should be re-examined.

> **Check the Froude number: V/√(gy) = 1.597/√(9.81 × 3) = 1.597/5.42 = 0.29** — comfortably subcritical, as a canal should be.

**Chézy versus Manning:**

| | **CHÉZY** | **MANNING** |
|---|---|---|
| Formula | **V = C√(RS)** | **V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}** |
| Coefficient | **C — has DIMENSIONS (√L/T)** | **n — effectively constant for a surface** |
| Relation | **C = R^{1/6}/n** | — |

> **Chézy's C is NOT a property of the surface alone** — it varies with the hydraulic radius, which is why the same channel has a different C at different depths.

> **Manning's n is very nearly constant for a given surface**, which is exactly why Manning's formula displaced Chézy's in practice despite being empirical.

> **Check: n = R^{1/6}/C = 1.2^{1/6}/50 = 1.0309/50 = 0.0206** — a plausible value for an earthen canal in fair condition, which confirms the working.

**Typical Manning's n:**

| Surface | **n** |
|---|---|
| **Smooth concrete** | **0.012** |
| Brick, cement plaster | 0.013 – 0.015 |
| **Earthen canal, clean** | **0.018 – 0.025** |
| **Weedy or rough earth channel** | **0.030 – 0.035** |
| Natural stream with stones | 0.040+ |

> **Weed growth can nearly DOUBLE n**, cutting the discharge capacity of a canal by almost half at the same slope and depth — which is why maintenance is a hydraulic matter, not a cosmetic one.

**And a design check on the velocity:**

> **1.6 m/s is a sensible canal velocity** — above the silting limit and below the scouring limit for a lined channel.

> **Too slow and the canal SILTS; too fast and it SCOURS.** Kennedy's and Lacey's regime theories exist precisely to find the velocity that does neither.

examTip.trick: **Specific energy supplies only the VELOCITY**: E − y = V²/2g = 0.13, so V = 1.597 m/s and Q = 19.16 m³/s. Then Chézy gives S directly — no need to go via Q².
examTip.trap: **Chézy's C has DIMENSIONS and varies with R** — it is not a surface property. Manning's n is nearly constant, which is why it displaced Chézy. Check: n = R^{1/6}/C = 0.0206, plausible for earth.
examTip.mnemonic: **Velocity head is only 4% of the specific energy here** — characteristic of subcritical flow (Fr = 0.29). If it came out comparable to the depth, the arithmetic would need re-checking.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Water can be withdrawn from any selected level of the reservoir using dry intake towers
Intake towers have to be designed for the worst combination of hydrostatic, wind, earthquake and wave forces
Dry intake towers are lighter in construction as compared to wet intake towers
In a dry intake tower, the water is directly drawn into the withdrawal conduit through the gated entry ports
questions.solution:
**Statement (c) is incorrect** — dry intake towers are **HEAVIER**, not lighter.

> The source explains: **the water through the entry ports with gates is directly drawn into the withdrawal conduit in a DRY intake tower. Dry intake towers are HEAVIER in construction as they are subjected to additional BUOYANT FORCES even if the gates are closed. There are separate gate-controlled openings for the conduit in a WET intake tower, and openings are also made into the shaft.**

**The distinction between the two:**

| | **DRY intake tower** | **WET intake tower** |
|---|---|---|
| **Interior** | **EMPTY when gates are closed** | **FILLED with water — the shaft floods** |
| **Water path** | **Straight from the ports into the CONDUIT** | Into the **SHAFT**, then into the conduit |
| **Openings** | Gated entry ports to the conduit | **Separate openings into the shaft as well** |
| **BUOYANCY** | **LARGE — the empty tower tries to FLOAT** | **Small — the shaft is flooded, so it is balanced** |
| **Weight of construction** | **HEAVIER — must resist uplift** | Lighter |
| Access for inspection | **Good — the interior is dry** | Poor |

**Why a DRY tower is heavier — and it is a genuinely instructive piece of physics:**

> **An empty tower standing in deep water is a huge submerged VOID.**

> **Archimedes' principle: the upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced** — and the tower displaces its entire submerged volume.
