> **A tower 30 m tall and 6 m in diameter displaces about 850 m³, giving an uplift of roughly 8300 kN — about 850 tonnes of upward force.**

> **It must be built heavy enough that its own weight comfortably exceeds that**, or it would float off its foundation.

> **A WET tower has no such problem: its shaft fills with water, so the buoyancy is balanced from within and only the structure's own volume displaces.**

> **That is the whole reason for the difference, and it is why the statement is exactly backwards.**

**Why a dry tower is nonetheless often preferred:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Dry interior** | **Gates and mechanisms are ACCESSIBLE for inspection and maintenance** |
| **Selective withdrawal** | Ports at several levels, all discharging into one conduit |
| Cleaner operation | No sediment accumulating in the shaft |

> **Being able to inspect and repair the gates without dewatering the reservoir is worth a great deal**, and it usually justifies the extra concrete.

**Why SELECTIVE WITHDRAWAL — statement (a) — matters so much:**

> **A reservoir STRATIFIES: warm, oxygenated water near the surface and cold, oxygen-poor water at depth.**

> **The deep water may be anaerobic, containing dissolved iron, manganese and hydrogen sulphide**, and releasing it downstream damages the river's ecology and burdens the treatment works.

> **Ports at several levels let the operator draw from wherever the quality is best at that season** — which is one of the strongest arguments for a tower intake over a simple submerged one.

> **It also allows warm surface water to be released for downstream fisheries**, rather than the cold deep water that a fixed low intake would deliver.

**Statement (b) is correct and worth noting:**

> **An intake tower is a slender structure standing in deep water and must be designed for the worst combination of hydrostatic pressure, WIND, EARTHQUAKE and WAVE forces.**

> **The seismic case includes HYDRODYNAMIC (added mass) effects** — the water surrounding and inside the tower moves with it during shaking, greatly increasing the effective inertia.

> **That is a large effect, not a refinement**, and it is why intake towers in seismic regions such as Nepal are substantial structures.

**How to answer questions of this form:** **read for the word that reverses a physical fact.** Here "lighter" contradicts buoyancy, and the physics settles it without needing to recall the source at all.

examTip.trick: **An empty tower is a huge submerged VOID** — Archimedes gives it enormous uplift, so it must be built heavy. A wet tower's flooded shaft balances the buoyancy from within.
examTip.trap: **Read for the word that REVERSES a physical fact.** "Lighter" contradicts buoyancy directly, so the physics settles it without needing to recall the source at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dry towers cost concrete but buy ACCESS** — gates inspectable without dewatering. And **selective withdrawal** matters because reservoirs stratify: deep water is cold and often anaerobic.

questions.stem: The stiffness of a member at its near end when the far end is fixed is:
questions.solution:
**4EI/L.**

> The source states the full set: **stiffness for a member at a joint is the moment (or force) required to produce UNIT ROTATION at that joint. Stiffness of a member if the farther end is FIXED = 4EI/L; if the farther end is HINGED = 3EI/L; if the farther end is FREE = 0; when the far end is a GUIDED ROLLER = EI/L.**

**The definition first:**

> **Stiffness is the MOMENT REQUIRED TO PRODUCE UNIT ROTATION at the near end.**

> **A stiffer member resists rotation more, so it takes a larger share of any moment applied at the joint** — which is exactly what the distribution factor expresses.

**The four cases:**

| Far end | **Stiffness** | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **4EI/L** | **The far end resists fully — maximum restraint** |
| **HINGED / pinned** | **3EI/L** | **The far end can rotate freely, offering less resistance** |
| **Guided roller** | **EI/L** | Rotation prevented, translation free |
| **FREE** | **0** | **Nothing to resist against at all** |

> **The ordering follows directly from how much the far end restrains: more restraint, more stiffness.** That makes all four recoverable by reasoning rather than recall.

> **A free far end gives ZERO stiffness** — a cantilever offers no resistance to rotation at its own free end, which is worth checking against intuition and finding correct.

**Why 3EI/L rather than 4EI/L for a hinged far end:**

> **When the far end is hinged, applying a moment at the near end causes the far end to rotate too, and that rotation relieves part of the near-end restraint.**

> **The member is therefore 25% less stiff.**

> **Using 4EI/L where the far end is hinged is the standard error in moment distribution**, and it propagates through the whole calculation.

> **The 3EI/L modification has a second benefit that is easy to miss: with it, NO CARRY-OVER is made to the hinged end.** The pinned end can carry no moment, so there is nothing to carry over — and using the modified stiffness accounts for that automatically, shortening the work considerably.

**The CARRY-OVER factor completes the pair:**

> **A moment M applied at one end induces M/2 at the far end IF that end is FIXED.**

| Far end | Carry-over factor |
|---|---|
| **FIXED** | **½** |
| **HINGED** | **0** |

> **Stiffness and carry-over always go together**: 4EI/L with a carry-over of ½, or 3EI/L with none.

**How stiffness is used — the DISTRIBUTION FACTOR:**

> **DF = member stiffness ÷ Σ(stiffnesses of all members at that joint)**

> **All members at a rigid joint rotate by the SAME amount, so each carries stiffness × that common rotation — the moment splits in proportion to stiffness.**

| Check | Value |
|---|---|
| **ΣDF at any joint** | **= 1** |
| **DF at a FIXED support** | **0** — infinitely stiff, absorbs everything |
| **DF at a HINGED end** | **1** — nothing to share with |

> **Those two boundary values catch most moment-distribution errors**, and they cost nothing to check.

**RELATIVE stiffness is usually enough:**

> **Since only the RATIOS matter in a distribution factor, the 4E cancels and I/L can be used directly** — provided **every** member at the joint is treated the same way.

> **The exception is the hinged far end: its 3EI/L becomes (3/4)(I/L)**, so the modified member must be multiplied by ¾ when relative stiffnesses are used. **Forgetting that ¾ is the same error as forgetting the 3EI/L itself.**

**And the method it feeds:** **moment distribution (Hardy Cross)** — compute fixed end moments with all joints locked, then release each joint in turn, distributing the unbalanced moment by DF and carrying over half to each fixed far end, until the residuals are negligible.

> **It converges without solving a single simultaneous equation**, which is what made it the standard method for indeterminate frames before computers, and why it remains the clearest way to understand how moments actually redistribute.

examTip.trick: **More restraint at the far end, more stiffness**: fixed 4EI/L, hinged 3EI/L, guided EI/L, free 0. The ordering makes all four recoverable by reasoning rather than recall.
examTip.trap: **A hinged far end gives 3EI/L, not 4EI/L** — the far end rotates and relieves 25% of the restraint. Using 4 there is the standard moment-distribution error and it propagates everywhere.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stiffness and carry-over go together: 4EI/L with ½ carry-over, 3EI/L with NONE.** And in relative stiffness (I/L), the hinged member must be multiplied by **¾**.

questions.stem: In a purely cohesive soil (φ = 0), the critical height of an unsupported vertical cut is:
questions.solution:
**4c/γ.**

**The derivation, from Rankine's active earth pressure:**

> **For a cohesive soil, the active pressure at depth z is:**
>
> **p_a = γ z K_a − 2c√K_a**
>
> **With φ = 0, K_a = 1, so p_a = γz − 2c.**

> **The pressure is NEGATIVE (tensile) down to a depth z₀ = 2c/γ** — the soil there is in tension and, being unable to sustain it, opens into a **TENSION CRACK.**

> **Below that depth the pressure is positive.**

> **The critical height is reached when the total thrust on the cut is ZERO — when the negative area exactly cancels the positive area.** Because both are triangles of equal height, that happens at:
>
> **H_c = 2 z₀ = 4c/γ** ✓

**So the two depths are worth keeping apart:**

| Depth | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Tension crack depth z₀** | **2c/γ** | Where the pressure changes sign |
| **CRITICAL height H_c** | **4c/γ** | **Where the net thrust becomes zero** |

> **H_c is exactly TWICE the tension crack depth**, and confusing the two is the commonest error — **option (b) is that error.**

**Why a cohesionless soil cannot do this at all:**

> **With c = 0, H_c = 0.** **A vertical cut in clean dry sand cannot stand to ANY height** — its strength comes entirely from friction, which needs confining pressure, and an unsupported face has none.

> **That contrast is the whole practical significance: clay stands unsupported, sand does not.**

**And the caution that matters on site:**

> **The 4c/γ height is a THEORETICAL maximum with a factor of safety of exactly 1.0** — the cut is on the point of collapse.

> **Practice uses a factor of safety of about 2, giving a safe unsupported height of roughly 2c/γ.**

> **More importantly, the theory assumes the cohesion is PERMANENT. It is not.**

| Effect | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Rain enters the tension crack** | **Water pressure in the crack pushes the block outward** |
| **Softening at the face** | Cohesion falls with time and moisture |
| **Desiccation cracking** | Opens further planes of weakness |
| **Vibration, surcharge, plant nearby** | Additional loading |

> **The tension crack filling with water is the classic trigger.** A crack 2c/γ deep full of water exerts a hydrostatic thrust that the analysis above never included, and the face fails — usually **days after excavation**, in the rain, when nobody expects it.

> **This is why trench collapses so often occur in ground that "stood fine yesterday"**, and why unsupported excavation deeper than about 1.2 m is prohibited in most safety codes regardless of what the soil appears to be doing.

**TAYLOR'S STABILITY NUMBER** generalises the result to sloping faces:

> **S_n = c/(F γ H)**, read from Taylor's charts against the slope angle and φ.

> **For a vertical cut in φ = 0 soil, the chart gives S_n = 0.261**, and **H_c = c/(0.261γ) = 3.83c/γ** — very close to the 4c/γ above, the small difference arising because Taylor assumes a **circular** failure surface rather than a plane one.

**The slope failure modes** for completeness: **face failure** (weak upper soil), **toe failure** (the usual case for steep slopes), and **BASE failure** (flat slopes over a soft deep layer, where the arc passes below the toe).

examTip.trick: **H_c is exactly TWICE the tension crack depth**: z₀ = 2c/γ where the pressure changes sign, and H_c = 4c/γ where the negative and positive triangles cancel.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), 2c/γ, is the TENSION CRACK depth, not the critical height** — the commonest confusion in the topic, and the two differ by a factor of two.
examTip.mnemonic: **A vertical cut in clean sand cannot stand to ANY height (c = 0 → H_c = 0).** And clay's 4c/γ assumes cohesion is permanent — **rain filling the tension crack** is the classic trigger, days later.

questions.stem: The coefficient of earth pressure at rest for a normally consolidated soil is given by:
questions.solution:
**K₀ = 1 − sin φ** — Jaky's formula.

**The three earth pressure coefficients:**

| State | Coefficient | Wall movement required |
|---|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45° − φ/2)** | **Small — about 0.001 H, AWAY from the soil** |
| **AT REST** | **K₀ = 1 − sin φ** | **NONE — the wall does not move at all** |
| **PASSIVE** | **K_p = (1 + sin φ)/(1 − sin φ) = tan²(45° + φ/2)** | **Large — 0.02 to 0.05 H, INTO the soil** |

> **Options (a) and (b) are the PASSIVE and ACTIVE coefficients respectively** — both correct expressions, for the wrong states. **This is a three-way discrimination, and every distractor is a genuine formula.**

**Check the magnitudes for φ = 30°:**

| Coefficient | Value |
|---|---|
| **K_a** | **1/3 = 0.33** |
| **K₀** | **1 − 0.5 = 0.50** |
| **K_p** | **3.0** |

> **K_a < K₀ < K_p always**, and the at-rest value sits between the two — which is exactly what it should do, since it corresponds to no movement in either direction.

> **That ordering is a free check on any answer**: a K₀ outside the range between K_a and K_p is certainly wrong.

**Why the at-rest state matters:**

> **It applies wherever the wall CANNOT move.**

| Structure | Why at-rest applies |
|---|---|
| **BASEMENT walls** | **Braced by the floor slabs at top and bottom** |
| **Bridge abutments** integral with the deck | Restrained by the superstructure |
| **Culverts and box structures** | Rigid, restrained by their own geometry |
| Rigid unyielding retaining walls on rock | No movement possible |

> **A basement wall designed for ACTIVE pressure is UNDER-DESIGNED**, because the active state requires the wall to move away from the soil — and a wall propped by floor slabs cannot.

> **At φ = 30° the error is 0.50 against 0.33 — a 50% under-estimate of the pressure**, which is a serious and entirely avoidable mistake.

**And the movement requirements explain why active is the usual design case elsewhere:**

> **The ACTIVE state develops after only about 0.001 H of movement** — a 5 m wall needs to move just 5 mm. **Any ordinary retaining wall does that during backfilling**, so the active state is what it actually experiences.

> **The PASSIVE state needs 0.02 to 0.05 H — 100 to 250 mm on the same wall.** That is far more movement than a structure can tolerate.

> **Which is why passive resistance is usually discounted or ignored in design**: it exists, but mobilising it fully would make the structure unserviceable first.

**For OVER-CONSOLIDATED soil, K₀ is higher:**

> **K₀(OC) = K₀(NC) × √OCR = (1 − sin φ) √OCR**

> **A heavily over-consolidated clay can have K₀ EXCEEDING 1** — meaning the horizontal stress is greater than the vertical.

> **The reason is that the soil was once loaded far more heavily, compressed horizontally, and when the load was removed the horizontal stress was locked in** by friction and the clay's structure.

> **This is a real and important effect**: excavating in heavily over-consolidated clay releases those locked-in horizontal stresses, and the ground squeezes inward far more than an at-rest calculation with K₀ < 1 would predict.

**Note also that K₀ is not a limiting state:**

> **K_a and K_p are FAILURE conditions — the soil is at its shear strength.**
>
> **K₀ is an ELASTIC condition — the soil is nowhere near failure**, which is why its formula has a completely different form and why it cannot be derived from the Mohr–Coulomb envelope as the other two can.

examTip.trick: **K_a < K₀ < K_p always** — at φ = 30° that is 0.33 < 0.50 < 3.0. The at-rest value sits between, since it corresponds to no movement either way. A free check on any answer.
examTip.trap: **Options (a) and (b) are the PASSIVE and ACTIVE coefficients** — genuine formulae for the wrong states. Every distractor here is real, which is what makes it a proper three-way discrimination.
examTip.mnemonic: **A BASEMENT wall cannot move, so it takes AT-REST pressure** — designing it for active under-estimates by 50% at φ = 30°. And **K₀ can exceed 1 in heavily over-consolidated clay** (× √OCR).

questions.stem: A pile that transfers its load to the soil mainly through skin friction along its shaft is called a:
questions.solution:
**A friction pile.**

**The two load-transfer mechanisms:**

| Pile | Load carried by | Used when |
|---|---|---|
| **END BEARING (point bearing)** | **The TIP, resting on rock or a firm stratum** | **A hard layer exists at a reachable depth** |
| **FRICTION (floating)** | **SKIN FRICTION along the shaft** | **NO firm stratum within reach** |

> **Ultimate capacity: Q_u = Q_p + Q_s = q_p A_p + Σ f_s A_s**

> **In practice EVERY pile carries some of both** — the classification is by which dominates, not by which is present.

**Why a friction pile is called a FLOATING pile:**

> **It does not reach any hard stratum at all. It "floats" in the soil, held entirely by friction along its sides**, in the same sense that a nail in soft wood is held by its shaft rather than its point.

> **That name is worth knowing, because it appears as an alternative in questions.**

**Why the other options are wrong** — each is a real pile type, classified on a different basis:

| Option | Classified by | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| **SHEET pile** | **FUNCTION** | **RETAINS soil or water — a wall, not a load-bearing pile** |
| **BATTER (raker) pile** | **ORIENTATION** | **Driven at an INCLINE, to resist HORIZONTAL loads** |
| **End bearing** | Load transfer | The opposite mechanism |

> **Only option (a) is classified on the same basis as the answer.** Sheet piles and batter piles belong to different classification schemes entirely — which is a useful thing to notice, since a question asking about load transfer can only be answered by a load-transfer category.

> **BATTER PILES are worth a note**: a vertical pile is poor at resisting lateral load, so where horizontal forces are significant — a bridge abutment, a quay wall, a tall structure in wind — piles are **driven at an angle** so that the horizontal force is resolved partly into axial compression, which piles carry well.

**How skin friction is estimated:**

| Soil | Method |
|---|---|
| **CLAY** | **α-method: f_s = α c_u**, with α from 1.0 (soft clay) down to about 0.5 (stiff clay) |
| **SAND** | **β-method: f_s = K σ′_v tan δ**, growing with depth |

> **The α factor falls as the clay gets stiffer** because a stiff clay is disturbed and remoulded more by pile driving, so less of its intact strength is mobilised at the shaft.

> **In sand the friction grows with depth because σ′_v does** — but only up to a **critical depth of about 15 to 20 pile diameters, beyond which it is taken as constant.** Assuming indefinite growth over-predicts the capacity of a long pile substantially.

**NEGATIVE SKIN FRICTION** — the effect that reverses the whole idea:

> **If the surrounding soil settles MORE than the pile, the friction acts DOWNWARD instead of upward — it becomes a LOAD on the pile rather than a support.**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **Recently placed FILL consolidating** | The commonest cause |
| **Groundwater lowering** | Raises effective stress, consolidating the soil |
| Soft clay under a new embankment | — |

> **This is a genuinely dangerous condition**, because it both **adds load** and **removes the support that was counted on** — a double penalty.

> **It is most severe for END BEARING piles**, which do not settle at all, so the whole relative movement is available to drag them down. **A friction pile settles with the soil and suffers less.**

> **The remedy is to coat the upper shaft with bitumen**, giving a slip layer that lets the soil move past without transferring drag.

**Group behaviour**, finally:

> **Group efficiency = group capacity ÷ (n × single pile capacity).** In clay it is usually **less than 1** because the stress bulbs overlap; in sand it can **exceed 1** because driving densifies the soil between the piles.

> **Spacing is normally 2.5 to 3.5 times the diameter** — closer and the group is inefficient, wider and the pile cap becomes uneconomically large.

examTip.trick: **A friction pile is also called a FLOATING pile** — it reaches no hard stratum and is held entirely by its shaft, like a nail in soft wood.
examTip.trap: **Sheet piles and batter piles are classified on different bases** — function and orientation, not load transfer. A load-transfer question can only be answered by a load-transfer category.
examTip.mnemonic: **NEGATIVE skin friction reverses everything**: settling soil drags the pile DOWN, adding load while removing support. Worst for **end bearing** piles, which do not settle at all. Remedy: bitumen slip coat.

questions.stem: For a balanced (limiting) singly reinforced section using Fe 415 steel, the depth of the neutral axis is:
questions.solution:
**x_u,max = 0.48 d.**

**The limiting neutral axis depths (IS 456):**

| Steel grade | **x_u,max/d** |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** |

> **Note that all four options are real numbers from this table plus 0.42** — so the question is a pure test of which grade goes with which value, and guessing the "middle" value would be wrong.

**Where the values come from:**

> **x_u,max/d = 700/(1100 + 0.87 f_y)**
>
> **For Fe 415: 700/(1100 + 0.87 × 415) = 700/(1100 + 361) = 700/1461 = 0.479 ≈ 0.48** ✓

> **The formula makes the pattern intelligible: HIGHER grade steel gives a SMALLER x_u,max**, because a stronger steel reaches its design strain at a higher stress, so the balanced neutral axis sits higher.

**What the limit actually means:**

> **It is the neutral axis depth at which the concrete reaches its ultimate strain (0.0035) at the SAME MOMENT the steel reaches its design yield strain.**

| Condition | Section type | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| **x_u < x_u,max** | **UNDER-reinforced** | **Steel yields FIRST — DUCTILE, with warning** |
| **x_u = x_u,max** | **Balanced** | Both simultaneously |
| **x_u > x_u,max** | **OVER-reinforced** | **Concrete crushes FIRST — BRITTLE, sudden** |

> **IS 456 does not permit over-reinforced sections at all**, and the reason is the failure mode, not the strength.

> **An under-reinforced beam gives ample warning**: the steel yields, the beam deflects visibly, cracks widen, and only then does the concrete crush. **People can leave the building.**

> **An over-reinforced beam fails when the concrete crushes with the steel still elastic — suddenly, explosively, with no deflection to warn anyone.**

> **So the limit is a DUCTILITY requirement**, and it is why the code caps x_u rather than simply allowing more steel to carry more moment.

**Where the value is used:**

> **Limiting moment of resistance: M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b x_u,max (d − 0.42 x_u,max)**

> **For Fe 415: M_u,lim = 0.138 f_ck b d²**

| Grade | **M_u,lim** |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.148 f_ck b d²** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.138 f_ck b d²** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.133 f_ck b d²** |

> **If the applied moment exceeds M_u,lim, the section must be made DOUBLY reinforced** — steel added in the compression zone — or made deeper. **Adding more tension steel alone would only make it over-reinforced and brittle.**

**The two other stress-block constants that appear alongside:**

| Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **0.36** | **Compressive force = 0.36 f_ck b x_u** — the area of the stress block |
| **0.42** | **Centroid of the stress block, at 0.42 x_u from the top** |
| **0.87** | **f_y/1.15** — the steel's design strength |

> **Together, 0.36, 0.42, 0.48 and 0.87 carry the whole of singly reinforced beam design**, and every formula in the topic is built from them.

**And the strains that underlie it:**

> **Concrete ultimate strain = 0.0035** (a fixed value, whatever the grade).
>
> **Steel design yield strain for Fe 415 = 0.87f_y/E_s + 0.002 = 0.0038.**

> **The extra 0.002 is the code's allowance for the non-linear part of the cold-worked bar's stress–strain curve**, which has no sharp yield point — unlike mild steel, where it is absent.

examTip.trick: **x_u,max/d = 700/(1100 + 0.87f_y)** — for Fe 415 that is 700/1461 = **0.48**. Higher-grade steel gives a **smaller** limit, so 0.53 / 0.48 / 0.46 runs Fe 250 / 415 / 500.
examTip.trap: **All four options are real numbers from this area** — 0.53, 0.48, 0.46 are the three grades and 0.42 is the stress-block centroid. Guessing the "middle" value is not a strategy.
examTip.mnemonic: **The limit is about DUCTILITY, not strength.** Under-reinforced: steel yields first, the beam deflects and warns. Over-reinforced: concrete crushes suddenly. Beyond M_u,lim, go **doubly reinforced** — never just add tension steel.

questions.stem: As per IS 800, the maximum slenderness ratio of a steel compression member carrying dead and superimposed loads is:
questions.solution:
**180.**

**The IS 800 slenderness limits:**

| Member | **Maximum λ** |
|---|---|
| **Compression member carrying dead + superimposed loads** | **180** |
| **Compression member carrying loads from wind or earthquake ONLY** | **250** |
| **Member normally acting as a TIE but subject to load reversal** | **350** |
| **Tension member with reversal due to wind or earthquake** | **400** |

> **Every option here is a genuine limit from the same table** — so the question tests which case applies, not whether the numbers are known.

**The pattern is entirely logical once the reason is seen:**

> **The limit RELAXES as the load becomes more temporary and less critical.**

| Load type | Limit | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| **Permanent (dead + superimposed)** | **180 — STRICTEST** | **Always present; buckling under it is a real and constant risk** |
| **Wind or earthquake only** | **250** | Occasional, short duration, and the load is itself uncertain |
| **Occasional reversal in a tie** | **350** | Compression is incidental, not the member's function |

> **So the strictest limit attaches to the load that is always there**, which is the sensible ordering and makes the table recoverable rather than memorised.

**Why a slenderness limit exists at all — this is the substance:**

> **It is NOT a strength calculation.** The design compressive stress already accounts for slenderness through the buckling curves.

> **The limit is a SERVICEABILITY and ROBUSTNESS provision**, and it exists for reasons the strength calculation does not cover:

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Damage during handling, transport and ERECTION** | **A very slender member bends under its own weight** |
| **VIBRATION** | Slender members flutter and buzz under wind or machinery |
| **Sag under self-weight** | Introduces an initial eccentricity the design did not assume |
| **Sensitivity to accidental knocks** | A slight impact can bow the member permanently |
| **Increasing sensitivity to initial imperfections** | The capacity becomes unreliable |

> **The erection argument is the most practical one.** A member with λ = 300 might be perfectly adequate for its calculated load, but it would be **bent before it ever reached the structure** — dropped, dragged, or simply sagging on the truck.

**How λ is computed — and the rule that governs it:**

> **λ = L_e / r_min**

> **ALWAYS use the MINIMUM radius of gyration**, where **r = √(I/A).**

> **A member buckles about its WEAK axis**, so r_min governs. **Using the strong-axis value overestimates capacity, sometimes by a large factor — a real and dangerous error.**

> **Which is also why bracing about the weak axis alone can be so effective**: restraining the weak direction may make the strong direction critical instead, roughly doubling the capacity for very little material.

**The effective lengths:**

| End conditions | **L_e** |
|---|---|
| **Both FIXED** | **0.5 L** (code: 0.65 L) |
| One fixed, one hinged | **0.7 L** (code: 0.8 L) |
| **Both HINGED** | **L** |
| **One fixed, one FREE** | **2 L** |

> **Codes use higher values than theory because perfect fixity never exists** — 0.65 rather than 0.5 — and the adjustment is always in the conservative direction.

**A worked sense of the limit:**

> **For an ISA 90×90×8 angle, r_min ≈ 17.6 mm.** At λ = 180 the maximum effective length is **180 × 17.6 = 3.17 m.**

> **That is a modest length for a common angle**, which shows the limit is a real constraint in practice — particularly for the light members of a truss, where it frequently governs the section chosen rather than the load does.

> **For TENSION members the limit is far less critical**, since a tie carries its load in tension however slender it is — the limits there (350, 400) exist only to control **sag and vibration**.

examTip.trick: **The limit relaxes as the load becomes more temporary**: 180 for permanent loads, 250 for wind/earthquake only, 350 for occasional reversal in a tie. The strictest limit attaches to the load always present.
examTip.trap: **All four options are genuine IS 800 limits from the same table** — the question tests which CASE applies, not whether the numbers are known.
examTip.mnemonic: **The limit is about ERECTION and VIBRATION, not strength** — a λ = 300 member would be bent before it reached the structure. And always use **r_min**: a member buckles about its weak axis.

questions.stem: The appurtenance provided at the summits of a water main to release accumulated air is:
questions.solution:
**An air valve.**

**The four valves and where each belongs on the profile:**

| Valve | **Position** | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **AIR valve** | **At SUMMITS (high points)** | **Releases accumulated air; admits air on emptying** |
| **SCOUR (blow-off) valve** | **At LOW points (valleys)** | **Drains the main and flushes out sediment** |
| **SLUICE (gate) valve** | At intervals along the line | **Isolates a length for repair** |
| **REFLUX (check, non-return) valve** | On a pumping main | **Prevents BACKFLOW** |

> **Air rises and sediment settles** — so the air valve goes at the top and the scour valve at the bottom. **The whole layout follows from that one observation**, and the two are constantly swapped by candidates who have not made it.

**Why trapped air is a serious problem, not a nuisance:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **AIR LOCK** | **A pocket at a summit REDUCES the effective pipe area and can stop the flow entirely** |
| **Increased head loss** | The flow is throttled past the pocket |
| **Corrosion** | Oxygen attacks the pipe wall |
| **Erratic meter readings** | Air is measured as water |
| **Surge amplification** | An air pocket makes water hammer worse, not better |

> **An air lock at a high point can reduce a main's capacity dramatically** — and because the pipe is buried, the cause is invisible. **A main delivering far less than its design flow with no apparent defect is very often air-bound.**

**Where the air comes from:**

> **Water holds about 2% dissolved air by volume**, which comes out of solution as the pressure falls along the main and collects at the high points.

> **Air also enters when the main is filled after repair**, and through pump glands and leaking joints under negative pressure.

> **So air accumulation is continuous and inevitable, not an occasional fault** — which is why air valves are a permanent fixture rather than a commissioning device.

**And the air valve's SECOND function is the one that saves the pipe:**

> **It ADMITS air when the main is being emptied or when a negative pressure develops.**

> **Draining a long main without admitting air creates a partial vacuum, and atmospheric pressure outside can COLLAPSE the pipe** — a large-diameter thin-walled main is far weaker against external pressure than against internal.

> **A double-acting air valve therefore has a large orifice for bulk air movement during filling and emptying, and a small orifice for continuous release under working pressure.**

**The REFLUX valve deserves a note**, because its failure mode is dramatic:

> **It sits on the delivery side of a pump to stop water running back when the pump stops.**

> **Without it, the column reverses and slams into the stationary pump** — and the resulting water hammer can destroy the pump and burst the main.

> **But a reflux valve that slams shut too quickly CAUSES water hammer itself**, which is why slow-closing or damped check valves are used on long rising mains.

**The general layout of a transmission main:**

| Feature | Provision |
|---|---|
| **Summits** | **Air valves** |
| **Valleys** | **Scour valves** |
| Every 1–2 km | **Sluice valves** for isolation |
| Pumping main | **Reflux valve**, plus surge protection |
| Long mains | **Surge tank or air vessel** |

> **The profile itself dictates the fittings**, which is why a longitudinal section is drawn before any of them is specified — and why a main laid "flat" with undulations rather than to a designed profile is difficult to operate for the whole of its life.

examTip.trick: **Air rises, sediment settles** — so air valves go at summits and scour valves at valleys. One observation fixes the whole layout of a transmission main.
examTip.trap: **Scour valves are the natural confusion** — same idea, opposite end of the profile. And a **sluice** valve isolates while a **reflux** valve prevents backflow: four valves, four distinct jobs.
examTip.mnemonic: **An air valve's second job saves the pipe**: it ADMITS air when emptying. Without it a partial vacuum forms and atmospheric pressure can **collapse** a large thin-walled main from outside.

questions.stem: The surface overflow rate of an ideal sedimentation tank is equal to the:
options: Horizontal velocity of flow through the tank
Depth of the tank divided by its length
Settling velocity of the smallest particle that is completely removed
questions.solution:
**The settling velocity of the smallest particle that is completely removed.**

**The definition:**

> **Surface overflow rate (SOR) = Q/A_s** — discharge divided by the **PLAN (surface) AREA** of the tank, in m³/m²/day, or equivalently **m/day** — which is a **VELOCITY.**

> **The units themselves reveal what it is.** A quantity in metres per day is a velocity, and it is precisely the settling velocity of the critical particle.

**Why — the argument is elegant and worth following:**

> **Consider the worst-case particle: it enters at the very TOP of the inlet and must reach the floor by the outlet.**

> **Time available = detention time = V/Q = (A_s × H)/Q**
>
> **Time required to settle = H/v_s**
>
> **For it to just be removed: H/v_s = A_s H/Q**
>
> **v_s = Q/A_s = the surface overflow rate** ✓

> **The DEPTH H CANCELS OUT.** That is the remarkable result.

**The consequence is one of the most important in water treatment:**

> **For ideal settling, removal efficiency depends on the SURFACE AREA ALONE — not on the depth, and not on the detention time.**

> **A shallow, wide tank removes particles just as well as a deep, narrow tank of the same plan area** — even though the deep tank has a far longer detention time.

> **This is counter-intuitive**, because detention time feels as though it should matter. It does not: a deeper tank gives the particle more time, but also more distance to fall, and the two effects cancel exactly.

**The idea has a direct engineering application:**

> **TUBE and PLATE SETTLERS exploit it.** Inserting inclined plates or tubes into a tank multiplies the effective settling area many times over without enlarging the tank at all.

> **A tank fitted with plate settlers can handle several times its original flow**, which is why they are the standard way of uprating an overloaded works on a constrained site.

**Typical design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **SOR — plain sedimentation** | **12 – 18 m³/m²/day** |
| **SOR — after coagulation** | **24 – 30 m³/m²/day** |
| **Detention time** | **2 – 4 hours** |
| **Horizontal velocity** | **0.3 – 1.0 m/min** |
| Depth | 3 – 4.5 m |
| Length : width | 3:1 to 5:1 |

> **The SOR is HIGHER after coagulation** because the flocs are far larger than the original particles and settle much faster — which is the entire purpose of adding a coagulant.

**Why depth still matters in a real tank**, despite cancelling in the theory:

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **SLUDGE storage** | The floor needs volume for accumulated solids |
| **Scour** | Too shallow and the horizontal velocity re-suspends settled sludge |
| **Short-circuiting** | Inlet and outlet turbulence needs depth to dissipate |
| Wind and temperature currents | Disturb a shallow tank more |

> **The ideal theory assumes quiescent, uniform flow.** Real tanks have **short-circuiting and dead zones**, which is why baffles and carefully designed inlet and outlet arrangements matter so much, and why real efficiency falls short of the theory.

**Stokes' law** gives the settling velocity itself:

> **v_s = g d²(G − 1)/(18 ν)**

> **Note v_s ∝ d²** — halving the particle diameter quarters the settling velocity.

> **Which is exactly why COAGULATION is necessary: fine clay and colloidal particles are so small that they would take days or weeks to settle.** Coagulation with alum destabilises them so they aggregate into flocs hundreds of times larger, and the d² relation then does the rest.

examTip.trick: **SOR = Q/A_s has units of m/day — a VELOCITY.** The units alone tell you it is a settling velocity, and the derivation shows the **depth cancels out** entirely.
examTip.trap: **Detention time feels as though it should matter, and it does not.** A deeper tank gives more time but also more distance to fall — the two cancel exactly. Only **surface area** governs ideal removal.
examTip.mnemonic: **Plate and tube settlers exploit the area result** — inclined plates multiply the effective area without enlarging the tank, uprating an overloaded works several-fold on the same footprint.

questions.stem: In sewer design, the invert level is the level of the:
questions.solution:
**The inside bottom of the sewer.**

**The levels used in sewer design:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **INVERT level** | **The INSIDE BOTTOM of the pipe** ← |
| **SOFFIT (crown) level** | **The INSIDE TOP of the pipe** |
| **Obvert** | Another name for the soffit |
| **Cover** | **Depth of soil from the ground surface to the OUTSIDE TOP of the pipe** |

> **Invert level + internal diameter = soffit level**, which is a useful check on any longitudinal section.

**Why the INVERT is the level that matters:**

> **A sewer flows by GRAVITY with a free surface, and the water follows the bottom of the pipe.**

> **The invert therefore controls the HYDRAULIC GRADIENT** — the slope from one manhole to the next is the difference in invert levels divided by the distance.

> **Setting out and checking a sewer is done entirely on invert levels**, and a longitudinal section shows the invert at every manhole.

> **Using the pipe's outside or centre level instead would introduce an error of half a diameter or more at every point** — on a 300 mm sewer laid at 1 in 500, that is equivalent to 75 m of length, which is more than a whole manhole spacing.

**The rule at a manhole where pipe sizes change:**

> **Match the SOFFIT levels, not the inverts.**

> **A larger pipe is set with its soffit at the same level as the smaller pipe's soffit**, so its invert drops by the difference in diameters.

> **The reason is backing up: if the inverts were matched, the smaller upstream pipe's soffit would be BELOW the larger pipe's soffit, and flow could surcharge back into it** when the larger sewer ran full.

> **Matching soffits guarantees the upstream pipe can always discharge freely.**

**And the DROP MANHOLE:**

> **Where an incoming sewer arrives much higher than the outgoing one, the flow is dropped through a vertical pipe outside the manhole rather than allowed to cascade down the chamber wall.**

> **Free-falling sewage would erode the benching, splash, release odour, and endanger anyone working in the manhole** — so the drop is enclosed.

**The design criteria the invert levels must satisfy:**

| Criterion | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Self-cleansing velocity** | **0.6 – 0.8 m/s, achieved at MINIMUM flow** |
| **Maximum (non-scouring) velocity** | **2.4 – 3.0 m/s** |
| **Minimum cover** | **0.9 – 1.2 m** under roads |
| **Depth of flow** | **Partly full — about two-thirds** |
| Manhole spacing | 30 m (small) to 100 m+ (large) |

> **The self-cleansing velocity must be met at the MINIMUM flow, not the design flow** — which is the criterion most often missed. A sewer sized generously for future population may fail to clean itself in its early years, silt up, and turn septic.

**And why the sewer must run partly full:**

> **The space above the flow carries away SEWER GASES.**

> **Septic sewage releases HYDROGEN SULPHIDE, which bacteria on the moist crown oxidise to SULPHURIC ACID** — destroying concrete sewers from the top down. **That is CROWN CORROSION**, and it attacks precisely where the structural arch is most needed.

> **H₂S is also toxic and heavier than air, and it DEADENS the sense of smell at dangerous concentrations** — so the absence of a smell in a manhole is not evidence of safety. **Gas testing and forced ventilation before entry are not precautions but requirements.**

**A hydraulic curiosity worth carrying:** **maximum velocity occurs at about 81% depth and maximum discharge at about 95% depth — NOT when the pipe is full.** A pipe at 95% depth carries **more** than the same pipe running full, because the extra wetted perimeter near the crown adds more friction than the small extra area adds capacity.

examTip.trick: **A sewer flows by gravity along its BOTTOM**, so the invert controls the hydraulic gradient. Invert + internal diameter = soffit, which checks any longitudinal section.
examTip.trap: **Where pipe sizes change at a manhole, match SOFFITS, not inverts** — otherwise the smaller upstream pipe's soffit sits below the larger one's and flow can surcharge back into it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Self-cleansing velocity must be met at MINIMUM flow, not design flow** — the criterion most often missed. Fail it and the sewer silts, turns septic, and **crown corrosion** begins.

questions.stem: In the EIA process, the stage that determines whether an environmental study is required at all is:
questions.solution:
**Screening.**

**The two stages most often confused, stated as a single contrast:**

> **SCREENING asks WHETHER a study is needed.**
>
> **SCOPING asks WHAT that study should contain.**

> **Screening comes first and may end the process entirely** — if a project falls below the threshold, no environmental study follows.

> **Scoping only happens once screening has decided that a study IS required.**

**The EIA process in order:**

| Stage | Question answered |
|---|---|
| **1. SCREENING** | **Is a study needed at all — and at what level?** ← |
| **2. SCOPING** | **What should it cover?** → produces the **Terms of Reference** |
| **3. Baseline study** | What is the existing environmental condition? |
| **4. Impact prediction and evaluation** | What will change, and how much does it matter? |
| **5. Mitigation and the EMP** | How will the impacts be managed? |
| **6. Review and approval** | Is the report adequate? |
| **7. MONITORING and AUDITING** | **What actually happened after implementation?** |

> **Options (c) and (d) are also real stages of the same process — the third and the last.** So this is a four-way ordering question, not a two-way one, and every distractor is genuine.

**How screening is actually done in Nepal:**

> **Under the Environment Protection Act 2076 and Rules 2077, the SCHEDULES list project types and size thresholds**, and the level of study follows from reading the table.

| Level | Applies to | Approving body |
|---|---|---|
| **Brief Environmental Study (BES)** | Smallest projects | Concerned body |
| **IEE** | Medium projects | **Concerned MINISTRY** |
| **EIA** | Large projects | **Ministry of Forests and Environment** |

> **Screening is therefore largely a matter of reading a schedule rather than exercising judgement** — which is deliberate, since a discretionary screening decision would be open to pressure.

> **The thresholds are quantitative: installed capacity for hydropower, length and class for roads, area for irrigation, and so on.**

**And AUDITING — option (d) — is worth defending as a stage:**

> **Environmental auditing is carried out AFTER the project is implemented and operating**, comparing what actually happened with what the EIA predicted.

> **It is the stage most neglected in practice.** An EIA approved and then never checked against outcomes is a **document rather than a safeguard** — and without auditing, the accuracy of prediction never improves, because nobody learns whether the predictions were right.

> **It is also the only stage that can detect impacts nobody anticipated.**

**What SCOPING produces, since it is the near neighbour:**

| Scoping does | Note |
|---|---|
| **Identify the KEY ISSUES** | Focuses effort on what matters |
| **Set spatial and temporal boundaries** | How far, how long |
| **Set evaluation criteria** | — |
| **Identify ALTERNATIVES** | Including the no-project option |
| **PUBLIC CONSULTATION** | A legal requirement |
| **Produce the Terms of Reference** | Its formal output |

> **The "no-project alternative" is a required part of the analysis and is frequently treated as a formality** — but it is the baseline against which every other option's justification rests, and an EIA that dismisses it in a sentence has not done its job.

**PUBLIC CONSULTATION is mandatory** at scoping and again at review, including a public notice and a hearing in the affected area.

> **Its omission is one of the commonest grounds on which an approved EIA is successfully challenged**, which makes it a legal requirement with teeth rather than a procedural courtesy.

examTip.trick: **SCREENING asks WHETHER; SCOPING asks WHAT.** Screening comes first and can end the process entirely; scoping only happens once a study has been found necessary.
examTip.trap: **All four options are genuine stages of the same process** — baseline study is third, auditing is last. This is a four-way ordering question, not a two-way discrimination.
examTip.mnemonic: **Screening in Nepal is reading a SCHEDULE, not exercising judgement** — deliberately, since a discretionary decision would be open to pressure. And **auditing** is the stage most neglected in practice.

questions.stem: The relation between delta Δ (in metres), base period B (in days) and duty D (in hectares per cumec) is:
questions.solution:
**Δ = 8.64 B/D.**

**The derivation — worth doing once so the relation is never mis-remembered:**

> **One cumec flowing for B days delivers a volume of 1 × 86,400 × B m³.**
>
> **That volume irrigates D hectares = 10⁴ D m².**
>
> **Depth Δ = Volume/Area = 86,400 B/(10⁴ D) = 8.64 B/D metres** ✓

> **The 8.64 is simply 86,400 ÷ 10,000** — seconds per day divided by square metres per hectare. **It is a unit conversion, nothing more**, which is why it must be fed B in days and D in ha/cumec.

**The three quantities:**

| Term | Definition | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **DUTY (D)** | **Area a unit discharge can irrigate** | **hectares per cumec** |
| **DELTA (Δ)** | **Total DEPTH of water a crop needs over its base period** | **metres** |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** | **Days from the FIRST to the LAST watering** | days |

**The relationship is INVERSE, and that is the concept:**

> **Δ ∝ 1/D.**
>
> **HIGH duty means water is used EFFICIENTLY — one cumec irrigates a large area — so the depth applied per hectare is LOW.**

| Duty | Delta | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **HIGH** | **LOW** | **Efficient** |
| **LOW** | **HIGH** | **Wasteful** |

> **A quick sanity check on any answer: duty must be in the DENOMINATOR.** Options (a) and (c) put D or B in the wrong place, and (c) inverts the relationship entirely.

> **Option (b), 864 B/D, is off by a factor of 100** — the answer if hectares were confused with a different area unit.

**A worked example gives a feel for the numbers:**

> **For rice with B = 120 days and D = 800 ha/cumec:**
>
> **Δ = 8.64 × 120/800 = 1.30 m**

> **A delta of about 1.3 m is right for rice**, which is a very thirsty crop — and that plausibility check is worth applying to any answer.

**Typical values:**

| Crop | **Delta (m)** | Base period (days) |
|---|---|---|
| **RICE (paddy)** | **1.2 – 1.9** | 120 |
| **Sugarcane** | **0.8 – 1.0** | **320 — the longest** |
| Wheat | 0.35 – 0.40 | 120 |
| Maize | 0.45 | 100 |
| **Gram, pulses** | **0.25 – 0.30** | 100 |

> **Rice needs four to five times the water of a pulse crop**, which is why cropping pattern matters more than any canal improvement in a water-short system.

**Where the duty is quoted matters, and must always be stated:**

| Point of reference | Duty |
|---|---|
| **At the FIELD** | **HIGHEST — no losses counted** |
| At the outlet | Intermediate |
| **At the HEAD (duty on capacity)** | **LOWEST — all losses counted** |

> **Duty on capacity is always the smallest**, because the head discharge is the largest flow in the system. **A duty quoted without saying where it is measured is meaningless.**

**Factors that raise the duty:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CANAL LINING** | **Cuts seepage — the largest single loss** |
| Efficient irrigation method | Drip and sprinkler over flooding |
| Suitable soil | Less deep percolation |
| Good field practices | Levelling, timing, avoiding over-watering |
| Cooler climate, shorter base period | Less evaporation |

> **Lining is the principal economic justification for canal improvement**: the same head discharge then irrigates a larger area, so the duty rises and the project's command area grows without any new water source.

examTip.trick: **Derive it: one cumec for B days gives 86,400B m³ over 10⁴D m², so Δ = 8.64B/D.** The 8.64 is seconds-per-day ÷ m²-per-hectare — a unit conversion, nothing more.
examTip.trap: **Duty must be in the DENOMINATOR** — high duty means efficient use and therefore LOW delta. Option (c) inverts the relationship, and option (b) is out by a factor of 100.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rice needs 4–5× the water of a pulse crop** (Δ ≈ 1.3 m vs 0.28 m), so cropping pattern matters more than canal improvement in a water-short system. And **duty must always state where it is measured.**

questions.stem: The principal benefit of lining an irrigation canal is:
options: An increase in the bed slope
A reduction in the canal's capacity
questions.solution:
**A reduction of seepage losses.**

**Why seepage is the dominant loss:**

> **In an unlined canal, seepage typically accounts for 30 to 45% of the water diverted at the head** — by far the largest single loss, and much greater than evaporation.

| Loss | Typical share |
|---|---|
| **SEEPAGE** | **30 – 45%** |
| Evaporation | 2 – 5% |
| Operational spills | Variable |

> **Lining can cut seepage by 60 to 80%**, which means a very large increase in the water actually reaching the fields from the same diversion.

> **That is the principal benefit, and every other advantage follows from it or from the smoother surface.**

**The full set of benefits:**

| Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Reduced SEEPAGE** | **The primary purpose** |
| **Prevents WATERLOGGING and salinity** | Seepage is the main cause of a rising water table |
| **Higher velocity permitted** | Lining resists scour, so a steeper slope and smaller section are possible |
| **Smaller cross-section** | Lower n means more discharge for the same area |
| **Less maintenance** | No weed growth, no silt clearance, no bank repair |
| **Prevents bank breaching** | A lined bank is not eroded |
| **Higher DUTY** | The same head discharge irrigates more land |

> **The waterlogging benefit deserves emphasis, because it is the one that saves land rather than water.**

> **Canal seepage raises the water table into the crop root zone; capillary rise then brings dissolved salts to the surface, where evaporation leaves them behind.**

> **Waterlogging can be drained away in a season. The SALINISATION it causes may take years to leach out, and in severe cases the land is abandoned.**

> **This is the mechanism that ruined large areas of irrigated land in the Indus and Nile basins**, and it is why lining is defended on land-protection grounds as much as on water-saving ones.

**Why option (d) is exactly backwards:**

> **Lining INCREASES capacity, not reduces it.**

> **Manning's n falls from about 0.025 for an earthen canal to 0.014 for concrete** — and since **V = (1/n)R^{2/3}S^{1/2}**, the velocity rises by roughly **0.025/0.014 = 1.8 times** for the same section and slope.

> **So a lined canal carries nearly twice the discharge of an unlined one of the same size** — or, put the other way, a much smaller section carries the same flow, which is what saves land and earthwork.

**And option (b) is backwards too:**

> **Lining REDUCES silt deposition**, because the higher permissible velocity keeps sediment moving rather than letting it settle.

> **Silt clearance is one of the largest recurring costs of an unlined canal**, and removing it is a substantial part of the maintenance saving.

**The types of lining:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete (cast in situ)** | **Most durable, most expensive** |
| **Shotcrete** | Sprayed; good for irregular sections |
| **Brick / stone masonry** | **Labour-intensive — suits Nepal's conditions** |
| **Compacted CLAY / earth** | Cheapest; moderate reduction only |
| Boulder lining | Local material, rough |
| **Membrane (LDPE) with earth cover** | Very effective against seepage, but vulnerable |

> **Brick and stone lining suits Nepali conditions particularly well**: it uses local materials and local labour, needs no heavy plant, and can be built and repaired by the users themselves.

**The economic test:**

> **Lining is justified where the VALUE OF THE WATER SAVED plus the maintenance saved exceeds the capital cost, discounted over the canal's life.**

> **Which means lining pays best where water is SCARCE and land is VALUABLE** — and it may not pay at all on a canal with abundant supply and low-value cropping. **It is an economic decision, not an automatic improvement.**

examTip.trick: **Seepage is 30–45% of the diverted water** — far larger than evaporation, and lining cuts it by 60–80%. Every other benefit follows from that or from the smoother surface.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) are both BACKWARDS.** Lining *increases* capacity (n falls from 0.025 to 0.014, so V rises ~1.8×) and *reduces* silt deposition, because the higher velocity keeps sediment moving.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging drains away in a season; the SALINITY it causes may ruin the land for years.** That land-protection argument justifies lining as much as the water saving does.

questions.stem: A silt ejector is provided:
options: In the canal, downstream of the head regulator
questions.solution:
**In the canal, downstream of the head regulator.**

**The two silt-control devices, and the distinction between them:**

| Device | **Position** | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Silt EXCLUDER** | **At the HEAD REGULATOR, in the river** | **EXCLUDES silt BEFORE it enters the canal** |
| **Silt EJECTOR (extractor)** | **IN THE CANAL, DOWNSTREAM of the head regulator** | **EJECTS silt that has ALREADY entered** |

> **PREVENTION versus CURE**, and the two names say exactly that:

> **EXCLUDE = keep it out. EJECT = throw it out once it is in.**

> **That single contrast answers the question and every variant of it.**

**How each works:**

> **The SILT EXCLUDER is a set of tunnels in the river bed, in front of the head regulator, inside the under-sluice pocket.**
>
> **The bottom, silt-laden layer of water is drawn into the tunnels and discharged through the under-sluices, while the cleaner upper layer passes over them into the canal.**

> **The SILT EJECTOR is a set of tunnels in the CANAL BED**, some distance downstream of the head regulator.
>
> **By then the sediment has settled toward the bed again, so the bottom layer is drawn off through the tunnels and returned to the river through an escape channel.**

> **Both exploit the same physical fact: coarse sediment travels NEAR THE BED, while cleaner water flows above it.** The devices differ only in where they apply it.

**Why an ejector is needed even when an excluder exists:**

> **No excluder is perfect.** Fine sediment stays in suspension and passes over the tunnels regardless.

> **The ejector catches what the excluder missed**, after the canal's lower velocity has given the sediment time to settle toward the bed.

> **Distance is what makes the ejector work**: it must be far enough downstream for the sediment to have re-concentrated near the bed, which is why it cannot simply be built at the regulator.

**The cost of both:**

> **Each device DISCHARGES WATER along with the silt** — typically **10 to 20% of the canal's flow** is used to flush the sediment away.

> **That water is lost to irrigation entirely**, so silt control is bought at a real price, and the design balances the sediment removed against the water sacrificed.

**Why silt in a canal matters so much:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reduced capacity** | The section silts up and carries less |
| **Raised bed** | **Command area is LOST — land above the new water level cannot be irrigated** |
| **Recurring dredging cost** | The largest maintenance item on many systems |
| **Blocked outlets and field channels** | Distribution fails at the tail |

> **The loss of command is the most damaging, because it is not simply a cost but a permanent reduction in what the project can serve** — and it falls hardest on the tail-end farmers, who are the least able to bear it.

**The other components of the silt-control system at a headworks:**

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Creates a STILL POND in front of the head regulator so silt settles there** |
| **UNDER-SLUICES** | **At bed level — FLUSH the settled silt away** |
| **Raised head regulator sill** | **1.0–1.5 m above the under-sluice crest, so the canal draws the cleaner upper layer** |
| **Silt excluder** | Tunnels in the pocket |
| **Silt ejector** | Tunnels in the canal ← |

> **Five devices, one purpose — and they act in sequence along the water's path.** The wall concentrates the silt, the sluices remove it, the raised sill keeps the remainder out, the excluder catches more at the entrance, and the ejector removes whatever still got through.

> **Sediment control at a headworks is a defence in depth**, and no single device is relied on alone.

examTip.trick: **EXCLUDE = keep it out (at the regulator); EJECT = throw it out once in (down the canal).** Prevention versus cure — the names state the positions.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the EXCLUDER's position.** The two are constantly swapped, and the ejector must be well downstream so the sediment has time to re-concentrate near the canal bed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Both cost 10–20% of the canal's flow** to flush the silt away — silt control is bought with water. And **raised canal beds destroy COMMAND**, which hurts tail-end farmers most.

questions.stem: A spur (groyne) constructed pointing upstream is called:
questions.solution:
**A repelling spur.**

**The three orientations and what each does:**

| Spur | **Orientation** | Effect on the flow |
|---|---|---|
| **REPELLING** | **Points UPSTREAM** (60–75° to the bank, inclined against the flow) | **REPELS the current AWAY from the bank** |
| **ATTRACTING** | **Points DOWNSTREAM** | **ATTRACTS the current TOWARD the bank** |
| **DEFLECTING** | **PERPENDICULAR** to the bank | **Deflects locally only — limited effect** |

> **The rule is direct: a spur pointing UPSTREAM pushes the water away; one pointing DOWNSTREAM draws it in.**

> **Think of holding a hand out of a car window: angled forward it pushes the air out and away; angled back it lets the air run along behind it.** The same reasoning applies to the flow past a spur.

**Why a REPELLING spur is the one usually wanted:**

> **Bank protection means moving the attacking current AWAY from the bank**, and that is exactly what an upstream-pointing spur does.

> **It creates a still-water pocket downstream of itself**, in which sediment deposits — so the bank behind it is not merely protected but progressively rebuilt.

> **Silting up the pocket is a designed outcome, not a side effect**, and a series of repelling spurs eventually re-establishes a new bank line along their tips.

**And why an ATTRACTING spur is ever built:**

> **To hold the channel in a desired position** — for instance to keep the deep flow close to an intake, a ferry ghat, or a bridge opening that would otherwise be abandoned by the river.

> **It attracts the current toward itself and must therefore be very heavily protected**, since it deliberately invites the attack it is designed to withstand. **The nose takes severe scour.**

**The main design points:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Angle to the bank** | **60–75° upstream for repelling** |
| **Length** | Not more than about **⅕ of the river's width** |
| **Spacing** | **2 to 2.5 times the spur length** |
| **Nose protection** | **Heaviest — scour is most severe there** |
| **LAUNCHING APRON at the nose** | Essential |

> **Length is limited to about a fifth of the river width for a real reason: a longer spur constricts the channel excessively**, raising velocities and afflux, and shifting the problem to the opposite bank.

> **Spurs solve a local problem and can create one elsewhere**, which is why they are designed as a system along a reach rather than singly.

**Scour at the nose:**

> **The nose takes the severest attack of any point on the structure**, comparable to a guide bank head. **Lacey's normal scour depth is multiplied by a location factor of 2 to 2.75 there.**

> **A LAUNCHING APRON of loose stone is laid at the toe: as the river scours beside it, the edge stone falls into the hole and armours the newly exposed slope.**

> **It is designed to be destroyed in a controlled way** — and it works precisely because the stone is loose. A grouted apron would be undermined and fail as a slab.

**Option (d) names a real variant:**

> **DENEHY'S T-HEADED SPUR has a T-shaped head at its nose**, which spreads the flow and **reduces the scour at the tip** compared with a plain spur.

> **It is a shape classification, not an orientation one** — which is exactly why it cannot answer a question about which way the spur points.

**The other river training works**, for context: **GUIDE BANKS** (confine the river through a structure and prevent **outflanking**), **MARGINAL BUNDS** (confine floodwater to the flood plain), **CUT-OFFS** (shorten a meander), and **PITCHING or revetment** (armour a bank in place rather than deflecting the flow from it).

> **The choice between a spur and a revetment is the choice between DEFLECTING the attack and RESISTING it** — spurs are cheaper over a long reach; revetment is used where the bank line cannot be allowed to move at all.

examTip.trick: **Pointing UPSTREAM repels; pointing DOWNSTREAM attracts.** Like a hand out of a car window — angled forward it pushes the air away, angled back it lets it run behind.
examTip.trap: **Denehy's T-headed spur is a SHAPE classification, not an orientation one** — it reduces nose scour. It cannot answer a question about which way the spur points.
examTip.mnemonic: **Limit spur length to ~⅕ of the river width** — longer constricts the channel and shifts the attack to the opposite bank. Spurs solve a local problem and can create one elsewhere.

questions.stem: A cross-drainage structure in which the canal is carried over a natural drain and the drain flows under pressure is called a:
questions.solution:
**A syphon aqueduct.**

**The naming rule — learn this and the whole family follows:**

> **The structure is named after WHAT GOES ON TOP, and "syphon" is added when the LOWER channel runs under PRESSURE.**

| Structure | **What is on TOP** | Lower channel |
|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **CANAL over drain** | **Drain flows FREELY (free surface)** |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | **CANAL over drain** | **Drain flows UNDER PRESSURE** ← |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **DRAIN over canal** | Canal flows freely |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | **DRAIN over canal** | **CANAL flows under pressure** |
| **LEVEL CROSSING** | — | **The two MIX and are separated downstream** |
| Inlet and outlet | — | Drain admitted into the canal and taken out later |

> **Two questions settle any of these: which channel is on top, and does the lower one run full?**

> **"Aqueduct" means the canal is above. "Syphon" means the one below is pressurised.** Put together, a **syphon aqueduct** is a canal over a drain that runs full.

**Why a syphon aqueduct is needed rather than a plain aqueduct:**

> **In a plain aqueduct there is enough vertical clearance for the drain's high flood level to pass beneath the canal trough with a free surface.**

> **Where the drain's flood level is HIGHER than the underside of the canal trough, that clearance does not exist** — so the drain must be forced through a barrel below the canal, running full and under pressure.

> **The choice is dictated by the relative LEVELS, not by preference.** A designer does not choose a syphon aqueduct; the site's levels impose it.

**The design consequences of running the drain under pressure:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Head loss through the barrel** | Causes **AFFLUX** — the flood level rises upstream |
| **Higher upstream flood level** | May require the drain's banks to be raised |
| **UPLIFT on the barrel floor** | **The pressurised drain pushes the floor UP** |
| **Uplift on the canal trough** | When the drain runs full and the canal is empty |
| Silting in the barrel | Low velocity at small flows |

> **UPLIFT is the critical structural check**, and it acts in two directions at different times:

> **When the DRAIN is in flood and the CANAL is empty, the drain's pressure lifts the canal trough from below.**
>
> **When the CANAL is full and the drain is dry, the canal's weight and its own seepage pressure act downward.**

> **Both cases must be checked, and the empty-canal case is the one most often forgotten** — exactly as with the empty-reservoir case for a gravity dam.

**And the barrel must be designed for a self-cleansing velocity:**

> **A barrel that silts up loses capacity and cannot be cleaned easily**, since it is buried beneath a working canal. **The section is therefore sized so that even modest flows keep it scoured.**

**Choosing between the alternatives at a crossing:**

| Situation | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Canal bed well ABOVE drain HFL** | **Aqueduct** |
| **Canal bed slightly above drain HFL** | **Syphon aqueduct** |
| **Drain bed above canal FSL** | **Super passage** |
| **Drain bed slightly above canal FSL** | **Canal syphon** |
| **Both at similar level, drain small** | **Level crossing or inlet–outlet** |

> **The decision is made from a longitudinal section showing both channels' beds and their design flood levels** — which is why the survey precedes the choice of structure entirely.

**And note the general principle:** **the canal is normally kept on top wherever possible**, because a canal must maintain its full supply level continuously to keep its command, while a drain flows only intermittently and can afford to be constrained.

examTip.trick: **Named after what goes ON TOP; "syphon" added when the LOWER channel runs under pressure.** Two questions — which is on top, does the lower run full — settle every member of the family.
examTip.trap: **A CANAL SYPHON is the mirror image**: drain on top, canal pressurised. Same word, opposite arrangement — and it is the option most likely to be picked in haste.
examTip.mnemonic: **UPLIFT acts in two directions at different times** — the pressurised drain lifts the trough when the canal is empty. The **empty-canal case** is the one most often forgotten.

questions.stem: In a subsurface (tile) drainage system, the spacing of the drains is computed from:
questions.solution:
**Hooghoudt's equation.**

**What it does:**

> **Hooghoudt's equation relates the SPACING of parallel subsurface drains to the soil's permeability, the drainage coefficient, the depth to an impervious layer, and the height to which the water table is allowed to rise midway between the drains.**

> **S² = (8 k d h + 4 k h²)/q**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S** | **Drain SPACING** |
| **k** | **Permeability of the soil** |
| **h** | **Height of the water table above the drains, MIDWAY between them** |
| **d** | Equivalent depth to the impervious layer |
| **q** | **Drainage coefficient — the rate to be removed** |

> **Note that S is SQUARED.** Halving the permitted water-table rise does not halve the spacing — it changes it by a square-root relation, which is why drainage layouts are less sensitive to the target than intuition suggests.

**Why the other three are wrong — and each is genuinely useful elsewhere:**

| Theory | Its actual field |
|---|---|
| **LACEY's regime equations** | **Stable CANAL section and SCOUR depth** in alluvium |
| **KHOSLA's theory** | **SEEPAGE beneath a barrage floor** — uplift pressures and exit gradient |
| **BLIGH's creep theory** | **The earlier, empirical version of the same seepage problem** |

> **Khosla's and Bligh's both concern seepage under hydraulic structures**, and Khosla's superseded Bligh's precisely because Bligh took no account of the actual flow pattern — treating all creep length as equivalent, whether vertical or horizontal.

> **So three of the four options belong to canal and barrage design**, and only Hooghoudt's addresses land drainage. **Recognising which subject each theory belongs to answers the question without knowing the equation.**

**What subsurface drainage is for:**

> **To LOWER THE WATER TABLE below the crop root zone — the direct remedy for waterlogging.**

| Waterlogging effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Roots deprived of AIR** | Saturated soil has no air-filled pores, and roots must respire |
| **SALT accumulation** | Capillary rise brings salts up; evaporation leaves them behind |
| Soil temperature falls | Wet soil warms slowly |
| Machinery cannot enter | Poor trafficability |

> **SALINISATION is the lasting damage.** Waterlogging can be drained away in a season, but the salt it deposits may take years to leach out — and leaching itself is only possible **if drainage exists to carry the water away.**

> **Which makes drainage doubly necessary: it prevents the problem, and it is the precondition for curing it.**

**The design trade-off:**

> **Closer spacing lowers the water table further and faster, but costs proportionately more.**

> **The drainage coefficient q is the design choice**: a higher value means a faster drawdown and closer drains. **It is set from the crop's tolerance and the local rainfall, not from the soil alone.**

**The alternatives to tile drainage:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Surface drains** | Remove excess water from the surface only |
| **Subsurface (tile / perforated pipe)** | **Lowers the water table — this question** |
| **VERTICAL drainage (tube wells)** | **Pumps groundwater and RE-USES it for irrigation** |
| **Canal lining** | Cuts seepage at source — the largest single cause |
| Deep-rooted trees (phreatophytes) | Transpire groundwater |

> **Vertical drainage is especially attractive because the pumped water is itself a resource** — one operation lowers the water table and supplies irrigation.

> **But it works only where the groundwater is of usable quality.** Pumping saline water onto the land accelerates exactly the damage the scheme was meant to prevent.

**And the most economical remedy is usually upstream of all of them:**

> **LINING THE CANAL.** Seepage from unlined canals is the largest single cause of irrigation waterlogging, and preventing it at source is cheaper than draining the consequences across the whole command.

examTip.trick: **Sort the theories by SUBJECT.** Lacey = canal regime and scour; Khosla and Bligh = seepage under barrages. Only Hooghoudt's concerns land drainage — no equation needed to answer.
examTip.trap: **Khosla's and Bligh's both address the same problem** (barrage seepage), Khosla's having superseded Bligh's empirical creep theory. Two options from one field is a signal neither is the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **S is SQUARED in Hooghoudt's equation**, so spacing responds to the target by a square root — layouts are less sensitive than intuition suggests. And **leaching salt requires drainage to exist first.**

questions.stem: In hydropower planning, firm (primary) power is the power that:
options: Can be guaranteed to be available at all times, including the driest period
Is available only during the monsoon months
Equals the plant's rated installed capacity
Is generated in excess of the guaranteed amount
questions.solution:
**The power that can be guaranteed at all times, including the driest period.**

**The two categories of hydropower output:**

| Type | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FIRM (primary) power** | **Guaranteed to be available at ALL times — corresponds to the MINIMUM flow** |
| **SECONDARY (surplus) power** | **Available only when flows exceed the minimum — INTERMITTENT and cannot be relied on** |

> **Option (d) defines SECONDARY power**, which is the natural distractor, and option (b) describes when secondary power occurs.

> **Option (c) confuses firm power with INSTALLED CAPACITY** — a different quantity entirely, and the confusion matters commercially.

**Why firm power is the number that matters:**

> **A power system must meet its load continuously.** A plant that generates 100 MW in the monsoon and 10 MW in the dry season can only be relied on for **10 MW** — the rest must be backed by something else.

> **Firm power is therefore what a plant is genuinely worth to the system**, and it is what long-term power purchase agreements are priced on.

> **Secondary power is sold at a much lower rate, or dumped**, precisely because the buyer cannot plan around it.

**How firm power is determined:**

> **From the FLOW DURATION CURVE — a plot of discharge against the percentage of time that discharge is equalled or exceeded.**

| Point on the curve | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Q₁₀₀** | **Flow available 100% of the time — the absolute minimum** |
| **Q₉₅ or Q₉₀** | **Commonly used as the design firm flow** |
| Q₅₀ | Median flow |
| Q₁₀ | High flow, exceeded only 10% of the time |

> **Q₁₀₀ is rarely used in practice** because it is set by a single extreme drought year and would make almost every scheme uneconomic. **Q₉₅ or Q₉₀ is the working compromise**, accepting a small risk of shortfall.

> **A reservoir CONVERTS secondary power into firm power** by storing wet-season flow and releasing it in the dry season — which is the fundamental economic argument for storage over run-of-river.

**Why this is the central problem in Nepal:**

> **Most developed schemes are RUN-OF-RIVER, and Nepali rivers carry roughly 80% of their annual flow in the four monsoon months.**

> **So dry-season output — exactly when demand for lighting and heating peaks — can fall to a fraction of the monsoon figure.**

> **The country has a large energy surplus in the monsoon and a deficit in winter**, which is the mismatch that has driven both the load-shedding of past years and the case for storage projects.

**The related planning ratios:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load ÷ PEAK load** |
| **CAPACITY (plant) factor** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED capacity** |
| **Utilisation factor** | Peak load ÷ installed capacity |
| **Diversity factor** | Sum of individual peaks ÷ system peak |

> **Load factor ≤ 1 always, and a HIGH load factor is desirable** — it means the plant's capacity is well used rather than sitting idle between peaks.

> **The DIVERSITY factor is why a system's total capacity need not equal the sum of its consumers' peaks**: not everyone peaks at the same moment, and that statistical fact is what makes an interconnected grid cheaper than isolated supply.

**And why hydropower is valued despite its variability:**

> **It can start and reach full load in MINUTES, against hours for a thermal plant.**

> **That makes it uniquely suited to PEAKING duty and to frequency regulation** — so even a plant with modest firm power can be worth a great deal to a system for its responsiveness alone.

> **Which is also why PEAKING RUN-OF-RIVER schemes, with a few hours of pondage, are attractive**: a small daily storage converts a flat output into a peak-hour one at a fraction of a reservoir's cost.

examTip.trick: **Firm power is what the system can RELY on — set by the minimum flow.** A plant giving 100 MW wet and 10 MW dry is worth 10 MW firm; the rest must be backed by something else.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) defines SECONDARY power and (c) confuses firm power with INSTALLED CAPACITY.** All three wrong options are real quantities from the same topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **A reservoir converts SECONDARY power into FIRM power** — the fundamental economic case for storage. In Nepal, ~80% of flow arrives in four monsoon months, exactly opposite to winter demand.

questions.stem: The ratio of the average load to the peak load during a given period is called the:
questions.solution:
**The load factor.**

**The four factors, which are constantly confused:**

| Factor | **Definition** | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load ÷ PEAK load** | **≤ 1 always** ← |
| **CAPACITY (plant) factor** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED capacity** | ≤ load factor |
| **Utilisation factor** | **PEAK load ÷ installed capacity** | How fully the plant is used at peak |
| **Diversity factor** | **Sum of individual peaks ÷ system peak** | **> 1 always** |

> **Note the pattern: LOAD factor and CAPACITY factor share the same numerator (average load) and differ in the denominator** — peak load for one, installed capacity for the other.

> **And UTILISATION factor is the link between them: Capacity factor = Load factor × Utilisation factor.**

> **Checking that identity is the fastest way to keep the three apart.**

**What a high load factor means:**

> **The load is STEADY rather than peaky, so the plant's capacity is well used instead of sitting idle between peaks.**

| Load factor | Character |
|---|---|
| **HIGH (near 1)** | **Steady demand — efficient use of capacity, LOWER cost per unit** |
| **LOW** | **Peaky demand — capacity idle most of the time, HIGHER cost per unit** |

> **This is why industrial consumers get cheaper tariffs than domestic ones.** An industry running three shifts has a load factor near 0.8; a household's is perhaps 0.2, with everything switched on for three hours in the evening and almost nothing overnight.

> **The household requires the same generating capacity to be built but uses far less of its output**, so the cost per unit delivered is much higher.

> **Tariff structures — off-peak rates, time-of-day metering, demand charges — all exist to raise the system load factor**, which is cheaper than building capacity that will be idle.

**Why the DIVERSITY factor is always greater than 1:**

> **Consumers do not all peak at the same instant.**

> **The sum of everyone's individual maximum demands exceeds the system's actual maximum**, because the peaks are spread through the evening.

> **A system serving 1000 households each with a 2 kW individual peak does not need 2000 kW** — it might need 700 kW, giving a diversity factor of about 2.9.

> **That statistical fact is what makes an interconnected grid fundamentally cheaper than isolated supply**, and it is the strongest technical argument for interconnection.

**And it is also why load factor and diversity factor pull in the same direction:**

> **Both express the same underlying idea — that a system serves many varied loads more efficiently than a few uniform ones**, because the variation itself smooths the total.

**Where hydropower fits:**
