> **A run-of-river plant with no pondage runs at a nearly constant output, giving a HIGH capacity factor but supplying BASE load only** — it cannot follow the evening peak.

> **A storage or peaking plant runs at a LOW capacity factor by design**, generating only during peak hours — which looks inefficient by that measure but is exactly what the system needs.

> **A low capacity factor is therefore not necessarily a fault**, and judging a peaking plant by it would be a category error.

> **Hydropower can start and reach full load in MINUTES**, against hours for a thermal plant — which is what makes it uniquely suited to peaking and to frequency regulation.

**And the related planning quantities:** **firm (primary) power**, guaranteed at all times and set by the minimum flow, against **secondary power**, available only when flows exceed it. **A reservoir converts the second into the first**, which is the economic case for storage.

examTip.trick: **Load and capacity factors share the numerator (average load)** and differ only in the denominator — peak load vs installed capacity. And **Capacity = Load × Utilisation** links all three.
examTip.trap: **Diversity factor is ALWAYS > 1**, unlike the other three — it compares the sum of individual peaks with the system peak. That alone distinguishes it at sight.
examTip.mnemonic: **A low capacity factor is not necessarily a fault** — a peaking plant is designed for one. Judging it by that measure is a category error, and hydro's minutes-to-full-load is why it peaks.

questions.stem: The hoop (circumferential) stress in a thin cylindrical penstock of internal diameter d and thickness t under internal pressure p is:
questions.solution:
**σ_hoop = pd/(2t).**

**The derivation — it takes one diagram and one equation:**

> **Cut the cylinder along a longitudinal plane and consider a length L.**
>
> **Bursting force = pressure × projected area = p × (d × L)**
>
> **Resisting force = stress × the two cut walls = σ × (2 t L)**
>
> **Equating: p d L = σ × 2 t L, so σ = pd/(2t)** ✓

> **The projected area is d × L, not the curved surface area** — that is the step worth understanding, and it is why the answer contains d rather than πd.

**The two stresses in a thin cylinder:**

| Stress | Formula | Acts |
|---|---|---|
| **HOOP (circumferential)** | **pd/(2t)** | **Around the circumference** |
| **LONGITUDINAL (axial)** | **pd/(4t)** | **Along the axis** |

> **The hoop stress is exactly TWICE the longitudinal stress.**

> **Option (d), pd/4t, is the LONGITUDINAL stress** — a genuine formula for the other direction, which is what makes it the natural distractor.

**Why hoop stress is twice — the physical reason:**

> **The longitudinal stress resists the pressure on the END, acting over an area πd²/4, and it is carried by the full circumference πdt.**
>
> **The hoop stress resists the pressure over dL and is carried by only 2tL.**

> **The geometry of the two cuts differs by a factor of two, and that is the whole explanation.**

> **The consequence is visible: a pressurised cylinder BURSTS ALONG A LONGITUDINAL SEAM, not around its circumference** — because the hoop stress reaches the material's limit first.

> **A sausage splits along its length, not across it, for exactly this reason.**

**Which is why penstock construction follows the stress:**

> **Longitudinal welds carry the hoop stress and are therefore the critical ones**, subject to full radiography and the strictest quality control.

> **Circumferential welds carry only half as much and are less critical.**

> **Spiral (helically wound) pipe distributes the stress across the seam at an angle**, which is one reason spiral-welded pipe is used for large penstocks.

**When is "thin" valid?**

> **The thin-cylinder theory assumes the stress is UNIFORM across the wall, which holds while d/t > about 20** (some texts use 15).

> **Below that the radial stress is no longer negligible and LAMÉ's equations for a thick cylinder must be used**, which give a stress varying through the thickness — **highest at the inner surface.**

> **A high-head penstock can become a thick cylinder**, and applying the thin formula there would under-estimate the peak stress at the bore.

**Designing the penstock thickness:**

> **t = pd/(2 σ_allowable η) + corrosion allowance**, where **η is the joint (weld) efficiency**, typically 0.85 to 1.0.

> **And the pressure p must be the DESIGN pressure, which includes the WATER HAMMER surge — not merely the static head.**

| Pressure component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Static head** | The gross head at that point |
| **WATER HAMMER surge** | **Can add 25–50% or more on sudden closure** |
| Design pressure | The sum of both |

> **Joukowsky: Δp = ρCΔV, with the wave celerity C ≈ 1440 m/s in water in a rigid pipe.**

> **Stopping a flow of 2 m/s instantaneously gives about 2.9 MPa — roughly 300 m of extra head**, which for a moderate-head scheme can exceed the static pressure itself.

> **This is why penstock thickness is governed by the transient, not the steady state**, and why **surge tanks, slow-closing valves and pressure relief valves** are provided — they reduce the design pressure and therefore the steel.

**And thickness usually INCREASES down the penstock**, since the head grows toward the powerhouse — so a long penstock is built in several thicknesses rather than one.

examTip.trick: **Bursting force pdL against resisting force σ·2tL** gives σ = pd/2t. The **projected** area is dL, not the curved surface — which is why there is no π in the answer.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), pd/4t, is the LONGITUDINAL stress** — a real formula for the other direction. Hoop is exactly **twice** longitudinal, which is why pipes burst along a **longitudinal** seam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design pressure includes WATER HAMMER, not just static head** — Δp = ρCΔV with C ≈ 1440 m/s, so stopping 2 m/s adds ~300 m. The transient governs the thickness, which is why surge tanks save steel.

questions.stem: The test that measures the resistance of road aggregate to abrasion is the:
questions.solution:
**The Los Angeles abrasion test.**

**Each of the four tests measures a DIFFERENT property**, which is what makes this a clean four-way discrimination:

| Test | **Property measured** | Method |
|---|---|---|
| **CRUSHING value** | **Resistance to a gradually applied COMPRESSIVE load** | 40 tonnes applied over 10 minutes |
| **LOS ANGELES ABRASION** | **Resistance to ABRASION and wear** ← | **Rotating drum with STEEL BALLS** |
| **IMPACT value** | **Resistance to sudden SHOCK or impact** | **15 blows of a falling hammer** |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **Resistance to WEATHERING** | **Alternate wetting/drying in sodium or magnesium sulphate** |

> **The distinction between them is the RATE and NATURE of the load: gradual crushing, sudden impact, prolonged rubbing, or chemical weathering.**

> **Naming the loading tells you the test**, which makes the set recoverable without memorising four procedures.

**How the Los Angeles test works:**

> **A graded aggregate sample is placed in a rotating steel drum with a charge of steel balls and a shelf that lifts and drops the material.**

> **The drum rotates for 500 to 1000 revolutions at 30–33 rpm.**

> **The abrasion value is the PERCENTAGE of material passing a 1.7 mm sieve afterwards** — the fines produced by grinding.

> **A LOWER value means a HARDER, more abrasion-resistant aggregate**, which is the direction of every one of these tests: the value is a measure of damage, so less is better.

**IRC limits:**

| Layer | **LA abrasion (max)** | Impact value (max) | Crushing value (max) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bituminous SURFACE course** | **30%** | **24%** | **30%** |
| Bituminous base / binder | 35 – 40% | 27 – 30% | 30 – 45% |
| **WBM base course** | **40 – 50%** | 30 – 35% | 45% |
| Sub-base | 50 – 60% | — | — |

> **The limits TIGHTEN toward the surface**, and the reason is direct: **the surface course takes the traffic's rubbing and impact directly**, while lower layers are protected by the material above them.

> **That gradation of quality with depth is the same economic logic that governs the whole layered pavement** — good material where the stress is, cheaper material below.

**Why abrasion resistance matters specifically:**

| Consequence of poor abrasion resistance | Note |
|---|---|
| **Loss of surface texture** | **SKID RESISTANCE falls — a safety failure** |
| **Polishing under traffic** | Especially with soft, rounded aggregate |
| **Generation of fines** | Fines clog the mix and reduce drainage |
| Rutting and ravelling | The surface breaks up |

> **The skid resistance point is the serious one.** An aggregate that polishes smooth under traffic gives a surface that is perfectly sound structurally and **dangerously slippery when wet** — a failure that is invisible until it causes accidents.

> **This is why the POLISHED STONE VALUE (PSV) is specified separately** for surfacing aggregate on high-speed roads and at junctions, in addition to the abrasion value.

**The other aggregate properties tested:**

| Test | Measures |
|---|---|
| **Shape — flakiness and elongation index** | **Particle shape; limited to 15% for surface courses** |
| **STRIPPING value** | **Resistance to bitumen being displaced by water — retention > 95%** |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity; usually limited to 2% |
| **Specific gravity** | For mix design calculations |

> **FLAKY particles are specifically excluded because they BREAK under compaction and traffic**, and they pack poorly, leaving voids.

> **And STRIPPING is the failure that drainage problems produce**: water displaces the bitumen film from the aggregate surface, the binder loses its grip, and the mix ravels. **It is a common cause of premature failure in Nepal's monsoon conditions**, and it is countered with anti-stripping agents or by choosing aggregate with better affinity for bitumen.

examTip.trick: **Each test names its own loading**: gradual crushing, sudden impact, prolonged rubbing (abrasion), chemical weathering (soundness). Naming the loading identifies the test.
examTip.trap: **All four are genuine aggregate tests** — the question is which property is *abrasion*. And in every one of them a **lower value is better**, since the number measures damage.
examTip.mnemonic: **Limits TIGHTEN toward the surface** (LA 30% for surface, 50–60% for sub-base) — the same logic as the layered pavement. And **polishing destroys SKID RESISTANCE** invisibly, hence the separate PSV.

questions.stem: The maintenance operation in which a thin layer of binder followed by a cover of aggregate is applied to an existing bituminous surface to restore texture and waterproofing is called:
questions.solution:
**Surface dressing, also called a seal coat.**

**What it is:**

> **A thin film of bituminous binder is sprayed on the existing surface, and a single layer of clean stone chippings is spread over it and rolled in.**

> **It adds NO structural strength at all** — the layer is only one stone thick.

**What it does:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **WATERPROOFS the surface** | **Seals fine cracks against water entry — the principal purpose** |
| **Restores SKID RESISTANCE** | New angular chippings give texture |
| **Arrests ravelling** | Binds a surface that has begun to lose aggregate |
| **Very cheap per square metre** | Its great advantage |

> **The waterproofing is the point.** Water entering through fine surface cracks reaches the base and subgrade, weakens them, and destroys the pavement from below.

> **A timely surface dressing costing a fraction of a reconstruction can add many years to a pavement's life** — which makes it the single most cost-effective maintenance operation there is.

**Why the distinction from the other three matters:**

| Operation | What it does |
|---|---|
| **PATCH repair** | **Localised — repairs potholes and defined failed areas** |
| **MILLING** | **REMOVES the existing surface by cold planing**, usually before resurfacing |
| **OVERLAY** | **Adds a NEW STRUCTURAL layer of bituminous concrete — INCREASES strength** |
| **SURFACE DRESSING** | **Thin, NON-structural seal over the whole surface** ← |

> **The key contrast is with an OVERLAY: an overlay adds strength, a surface dressing does not.**

> **They are used for entirely different conditions — a pavement that is structurally sound but surface-worn needs a dressing; a pavement that is structurally inadequate needs an overlay, and dressing it would be wasted money.**

**Which is why the diagnosis precedes the treatment:**

| Distress | Cause | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Ravelling, fine cracking, loss of texture** | **Surface ageing** | **Surface dressing** |
| **RUTTING in the wheel path** | **Structural or mix deficiency** | Overlay, or reconstruction |
| **ALLIGATOR (fatigue) cracking** | **STRUCTURAL failure — subgrade or thickness** | **Overlay or reconstruction; dressing it merely hides it** |
| Potholes | Localised failure | Patch repair, then seal |
| **BLEEDING** | Excess binder | **Blot with sand or coarse aggregate** |

> **Surface dressing an alligator-cracked pavement is a classic false economy** — the cracks reflect through within a season, and the underlying structural failure has been concealed rather than addressed.

**The two practical hazards of surface dressing:**

| Problem | Cause and remedy |
|---|---|
| **Loose chippings** | **Traffic must be restricted and speed limited for a few days** until the chippings are embedded, or windscreens are broken |
| **BLEEDING in hot weather** | **Too much binder** — the bitumen rises through and the surface becomes slippery |

> **The binder rate is therefore critical and is calculated from the chipping size (the ALD — average least dimension), the existing surface's hardness, and the traffic.**

> **Too little binder and the chippings are swept away; too much and the surface bleeds.** It is a genuinely narrow window, and it is why surface dressing looks simple and is often done badly.

**Where the maintenance categories fit:**

| Category | Examples |
|---|---|
| **ROUTINE** | **Drain clearing, vegetation control, pothole patching — continuous** |
| **PERIODIC** | **Surface dressing, overlay, renewal — every few years** |
| **Special / emergency** | Landslide clearance, flood damage |
| **Rehabilitation** | Major reconstruction |

> **DRAIN CLEARING is the cheapest routine item and the one that saves the most pavement**, because water is the principal destroyer of a flexible pavement — weakening the subgrade, stripping the binder and pumping out fines.

> **In Nepal's monsoon climate, a road maintenance budget spent on drainage buys more pavement life than the same money spent on surfacing.**

examTip.trick: **An OVERLAY adds strength; a surface dressing does NOT.** One stone thick, purely a seal — which is why the two suit entirely different conditions.
examTip.trap: **Surface dressing an ALLIGATOR-cracked pavement is a false economy** — the structural failure is concealed, not repaired, and the cracks reflect through within a season.
examTip.mnemonic: **Too little binder and the chippings sweep away; too much and it BLEEDS** — a narrow window, which is why dressing looks simple and is often done badly. And **drain clearing buys more pavement life than surfacing.**
